Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: With Preface
“Rhapsody on the Horseback Archery at Huálín Garden on the Third Day of the Third Month, with Preface”
Your servant has heard that Yáo, in the mid-spring month,
carved jade and journeyed upon the river;
Shùn, on a jiǎzǐ morning,
unrolled maps and patrolled Luò.
Upon the jade terrace of Xiàhòu,
sometimes two dragons were harnessed;
before the Mystic Garden of the Zhōu king,
still eight steeds were yoked.
As for the founding of our great Zhōu,
the Southern Regulator governed heaven,
the Northern Regulator governed earth,
pacifying the rebellion of the Jiǔlí,
settling the crimes of the Sānwēi.
Clouds marked the official titles,
birds oversaw the duties;
the August King possessed the tally of receiving the calendar,
the dark jade tablet held the omen of accomplished merit.
How could it be merely that heaven and earth joined in virtue,
and the sun and moon shone with splendor!
The Emperor, with the bearing of highest sagehood,
receives the destiny of succeeding the martial,
comprehends the numinous signs of the celestial phenomena,
and reveals the virtue of the divine and enlightened.
Yí, in charge of the ancestral rites,
appears in the Three Rituals;
Kuí, as Music Director,
is heard in the Nine Completions.
Self-restraint is fully expressed in ritual demeanor,
awesome majesty is gathered in military governance.
Added to this, he humbles himself and eats plain fare,
uses black tents and coarse silk garments,
takes the common people as his heart,
and holds the Four Seas as his concern.
If no rain falls in the western suburbs,
the imperial mind is immediately stirred;
if the eastern plowing has not yielded harvest,
heavenly care turns all the more.
With arms and armor not assembled for meetings,
there is no need to await the crimson crow;
with palaces and towers not relocated,
truly there is no labor for the white swallow.
Silver urns and golden boats,
mountain carts and marsh horses.
How could it be limited to bamboo and reeds, two plants,
together dripping sweet dew;
the azure and crimson, three vapors,
simultaneously forming the propitious star?
Those with tattooed foreheads and filed teeth,
recognize the sea water and come to pay homage;
Wūyì and Huángzhī,
verify the east wind and accept official posts.
At this time, the dark bird governs the calendar,
the azure dragon directs the movement;
lambs are offered, ice breaks open,
paulownia blossoms, duckweed grows.
The Emperor proceeds to the garden of Huálín,
the Jade Balance is upright and the Grand Steps are level,
the Gate of Heaven opens and the Hooked Array turns,
a thousand chariots rumble like thunder,
ten thousand riders gather like clouds.
Falling blossoms fly together with the mushroom-shaped canopies,
willows share the same color with the spring banners.
Then he commands the assembled ministers,
to present the ritual of the Great Archery.
Though performing the feast of purification,
they immediately employ the rites of the spring hunt.
They halt and set up the traveling palace,
merely unfold the tented hall.
The steps lack jade discs,
already differing from the stele of Héjiān;
the doors have no golden fittings,
greatly unlike the rhapsody of Xǔchāng.
The cavern hall is already spread,
and “Bearing Clouds” is then performed.
“Zōuyú” in nine sections,
“Líshǒu” in seven movements.
They correct the five-colored clouds of paintings,
the pot calms the wine of a hundred blessings.
Táng bows joined nine times,
with winter-dried and spring-glued [sinew];
summer arrows finished threefold,
with green shafts and crimson feathers.
Thereupon, horses of crimson sweat are selected,
and the golden-marked track is measured.
Hóngyáng, Flying Magpie,
Purple Swallow, Morning Wind,
the Sùshuāng of Duke Tángchéng,
the Thousand-Li Steed of Marquis Hǎixī.
None fail to drink the feathers and grasp the pole,
singing gibbons and falling geese.
Bells and drums shake the earth,
dust and haze swell to the sky.
Wine is passed in léi vessels,
dishes are presented from dǐng tripods.
Silks and brocades are all moved as if from a market,
coins are transferred as if from a copper mountain.
The Grand Historian listens to the drums and discusses merits,
the Minister of War unfurls banners and rewards the captures.
Above, clouds spread and rain bestows;
below, mountains conceal and seas receive.
Truly, it is the utmost joy of heaven and earth,
the delight of abundant blessings.
As the Ruòmù tree is about to lower,
and golden waves about to rise,
heaven looks on, serene and solemn,
guests sing, only drunk.
Though again briefly departing the northern palace gates,
they feast for a while in the western city,
it is akin to the morning assembly at Fēng River,
and even more the gathering at Qí Mountain.
This petty minister, lacking in talent,
receives the command to compose this text.
Viewing heaven through a tube,
measuring the sea with a ladle,
how could a mere outline describe
such magnificent virtue?
The year falls under Zhāoyáng,
the moon is in Dàliáng.
The day is the Upper Sì,
the time is Shàoyáng.
The Spring Scribe performs his duty,
the Green Spirit manifests auspicious signs.
Summon ten thousand riders to Pínglè,
open a thousand gates at Jiànzhāng.
Attendant carriages strain wine,
covered passageways burn incense.
The Emperor arrays the four enclosures in the imperial stables,
turns the six dragons in the heavenly park,
faces the level woods of Xuānqū,
gazes upon the long slope of Gānquán.
The canopy flies level,
the wind bird turns gently.
The road is straight, the city distant,
the forest long, the riders far.
The curtained palace is set overnight,
the tented hall opens for feasting,
adjacent to the slender willows,
bordering obliquely on Qínián.
Deploy the array of crane wings,
wave the banners of fish whiskers.
The traveling clepsydra holds the marks,
the forward banners bear the kites.
By the river’s edge, weeds are cleared,
at the Wèi’s mouth, springs are channeled.
The target cloud is five-colored,
the bullseye halo doubly round.
The yang pipes are already tuned,
the spring strings are truly strummed.
Harmonizing the pitch with the general standard,
setting up feathers at the perfected balance.
Soaring phoenixes form a forest,
numinous mushrooms make a garden.
Grass holds long ribbons,
paulownia trees hang fine tassels.
Birds warble, songs arrive,
flowers thicken, snow gathers.
Jade pitch-pipes tune the bells,
golden chún regulate the drums.
Thereupon, biting bridles and pulling irons,
chasing the sun and pursuing the wind,
together they test the track of the tall catalpas,
all descending to the palace of Lánchí.
Cracking whips brings forth crimson sweat,
entering the track raises red dust.
Having observed the worthy in the great archery,
then policies are promulgated to the Bow Director.
Changing the three drives, they paint deer,
ascending the hundred-foot pole, they hang a bear.
Fánruò bows shake the earth,
iron-black steeds tread the air.
Ritual corrects the six pairs,
poetry sings of nine knots.
Seven layers of armor are all pierced,
five boars share the same lair.
Bows like bright moons face the target,
horses like floating clouds head for the track.
Geese, separated from the flock, break formation;
gibbons, seeking the forest, find the path cut off.
Gripping jade bridles, they shake the stars;
straddling golden saddles, they stir the moon.
Then there were fine families from six commanderies,
and heroic selections from the five mausoleum districts.
Freshly returned from the troops at Mǎyì,
just concluded the battle at Lóngchéng.
Generals in military attire,
came to join the martial banquet.
Still bearing the shooting stars,
still riding the galloping lightning.
First hearing the drums and singing tallies,
then moving the pole and marking arrows.
Horses snort, soaking the clothes,
dust startles, sprinkling the face.
Stone weirs water to irrigate gardens,
flowers ride the wind to circle the hall.
Xióng’ěr carved cups,
Fēiyún painted jars.
Water-heng coins piled like mountains,
weaving-chamber brocades spread like rosy clouds.
Feast supervisors award prizes,
wine stewards bring cups.
The utmost joy surpasses the autumn waters,
laughter and mirth exceed the spring terrace.
Then as the sun sets over the archery hall,
the feast ends at the archery range.
Regretful for the lingering joy of the halted carriage,
longing for the remaining dance as the imperial carriage turns back.
Wishing to make stone bridges catch arrows,
copper mountains drink feathers.
Draw the bow at the river serpent of Chǔ waters,
shoot arrows at the pavilion tiger of Wú.
Moreover, reverently self-restrained and non-interfering,
with the "South Wind" present here,
not intentionally toward mantis wings,
how could one linger affection on halberd branches?
Only observe the ritual of bowing and yielding,
to adopt the demeanor of majestic might.
○From Wényuàn Yīnghuá, chapter 58.
From Yìwén Lèijù, chapter 4.
From Chūxué Jì, chapter 4.
"Rhapsody on a Small Garden"
As for a single branch above,
Cháo Fù found a place to settle his nest;
within a single gourd,
Gourd Elder had a space to accommodate his body.
How much more so, Guǎn Níng’s goosefoot-wood bed,
though worn through, could still be sat upon;
Jī Kāng’s forging stove,
once warmed, was fit for sleeping.
Must one necessarily have interconnected gates and deep chambers,
like the mansion of Fán Zhòng of Nányáng;
green steps and blue ring-knockers,
like the residence of Wáng Gēn of the Western Hàn?
I have several acres of a humble hut,
secluded beyond the human world,
by which to approximate the winter and summer sacrifices,
by which to avoid wind and frost.
Though again, like Yàn Yīng near the market,
I do not seek the profits of morning and evening;
like Pān Yuè facing the city,
I merely enjoy the pleasure of leisurely dwelling.
Moreover, the yellow crane warns of dew,
with no intention toward carriages with canopies;
the yuānjū avoids the wind,
fundamentally without feeling for bells and drums.
Lù Jī, then, dwelt together with his brother;
Hán Kāng, then, did not separate from his maternal uncle.
The tip of a snail’s horn, the lash of a mosquito’s eyelid—
these too are sufficient to accommodate one another.
Thus I pace within my cave-room,
somewhat akin to chiseling through a wall.
Between the paulownias, dew falls,
beneath the willows, wind comes.
A zither named Pearl Pillar,
a book titled Jade Cup.
There are pear trees but no hall,
enough sour jujubes but no terrace.
Still, it slopes eight or nine zhang,
extends several tens of paces across,
with two or three rows of elms and willows,
over a hundred pear and peach trees.
Part the dense growth to see the window,
walk the crooked path to find the way.
Cicadas, having cover, are not startled;
pheasants, without nets, what have they to fear?
Grasses and trees intermingle,
branches and limbs intertwine.
The hill is but a basket of soil,
the ground has puddles like hall hollows.
Hidden raccoon-dogs share burrows,
nursing magpies build layered nests.
Linked beads of fine moss,
long-handled cold gourds—
they can relieve hunger,
they can provide rest.
Precarious and slanting, the narrow room,
leaking and pierced, the thatched roof.
Eaves straight and low hinder one’s hat,
doors level and low obstruct one’s brows.
No crane sits on the tent,
but a turtle props the bed.
Birds are mostly leisurely,
flowers follow the four seasons.
My heart is like the withered tree of Lìlíng,
my hair like the tangled silk of Suīyáng.
Not summer, yet it can be feared;
different from autumn, yet it can be saddened.
Fish of one or two inches,
bamboos of two or three poles.
Cloud-qi shades the clump of yarrow, metal essence nourishes the autumn chrysanthemum. Sour dates, tart pears, peaches, wild plums, and cherry plums.
Fallen leaves half cover the bed,
wild flowers fill the room.
Called the home of a rustic man,
deemed the valley of Foolish Old Man.
Try reclining in the lush woods,
then long have I admired pulling out the hairpin.
Though there is a gate, it is always closed;
truly without water, yet constantly submerged.
In third spring, hoe-bearing acquaintances,
in fifth month, fur-clad seekers come.
Ask about Gé Hóng’s medicinal properties,
inquire of Jīng Fáng’s divination grove.
Grasses lack the intent to forget worries,
flowers lack the heart for lasting joy.
Why should birds chase after wine?
What feeling makes fish listen to the zither?
Moreover, cold and heat differ in their commands,
contrary and violating one’s virtuous nature.
Cuī Yīn, through displeasure, shortened his years;
Wú Zhì, with constant sorrow, nurtured illness.
Pacify the house spirit with buried stones,
repress the mountain sprite with a mirror.
Often stirred the lament of Zhuāng Xì,
nearly carried out the command of Wèi Kē.
Towards dusk in the idle women’s quarters,
old and young support each other,
disheveled-haired son of Wáng Bà,
coiled-bun wife of Liáng Hóng.
Two jars of parched wheat,
one plot of cold vegetables.
Wind rustling, trees urgent,
heavens gloomy, clouds low.
Gathering at empty granaries, sparrows clamor;
startling the lazy wife, cicadas shrill.
In former times, undeservedly inflated by flattery,
relying on the auspicious legacy of the "Wén Yán."
At the gate was the virtue of access,
the family received bestowed books.
Sometimes accompanied at the Xuánwǔ Observatory,
at times joined the ruins of the Fènghuáng Tower.
Witnessed receiving auspices in the Xuānshì Hall,
composed the "Chángyáng" rhapsody in the duty chamber.
Then came mountains collapsing and rivers drying up,
ice shattering and tiles cracking,
the great thief stealthily shifted,
the long separation eternally extinguished.
Broken the straight rein at Sānwēi,
shattered the level road at Jiǔzhé.
Jīng Kē had the sorrow of cold water,
Sū Wǔ had the parting of autumn wind.
At frontier passes, wind and moon are desolate;
at Lǒng River, liver and intestines are severed.
The turtle speaks of this land’s cold,
the crane marvels at this year’s snow.
A hundred years—how fleeting!
Splendor and glory—already late.
Not redeeming the stumble at Yànmén,
first mindful of the distant wild goose on land.
Not like the Huái sea, transformable;
not like the golden elixir, convertible.
Not exposing bones at Lóngmén,
in the end, bowing head at Mǎbǎn.
Truly, Heaven’s creation is obscure,
alas, the people are benighted.
○From Yìwén Lèijù, chapter 65.
From Wényuàn Yīnghuá, chapter 97.
"Rhapsody on a Bamboo Staff"
When Marshal Huán Xuānwǔ pacified Jīngzhōu,
an attendant announced from outside:
"There is one who calls himself Master Chǔqiū,
come to visit at your gate."
Duke Huán said:
"The son of a renowned father,
wandering displaced by the Jiāng and Hàn rivers—
this is my responsibility!"
He then ordered him to be brought in,
and said:
"Alas,
you have grown old!
With crane-white hair and chicken-skin,
disheveled head and sparse teeth.
Yet you are the outstanding spirit of the Jiāng and Hàn,
the fine timber of Héng and Jīng.
Though your fame is heard even in ten households,
fortunately you do not seek from a thousand miles.
I have a spirit-longevity staff with copper rings,
and a peach-branch cane with silver corners.
Its wood-apple blossom has not yet fallen,
the lotus it nurtures does not wither.
It welcomes immortal guests in brocade markets,
and sends off roaming dragons at Gěbēi.
This, sir, may be used to support your old age,
and to aid you in times of peril."
The master laughed and said:
"The Central States are clear about ritual and righteousness,
but dim in understanding people.
The sorrow in my heart
is only for our common people.
Even if there are sparse branches and sturdy柘,
tight-knotted joints and steadfast bamboo,
with birds carved on the staff's end,
and a unicorn depicted on its horned head,
how could they assist me in this affliction,
or support this body of mine?
As for when the world changes like marketplaces and courts,
and years shift like hills and valleys,
with gibbons wailing and falcons fierce,
wind and霜 bleak and dark;
when Chǔ and Hàn contended for supremacy,
and Yuán and Cáo vied in pursuit,
beasts found no grass to eat,
birds no trees for nests.
At such times, one trembles without fear,
shivers without cold.
Barbarian horses mournfully neigh,
Qiāng flutes sadly turn;
kinsfolk and friends are parted and severed,
wife and children drift and scatter.
Jade Pass sends letters,
Zhāngtái leaves bracelets;
cold frontier bleak and desolate,
sojourner's journey sad and dreary.
Sparse fur withstands arrows and strings,
brittle bones are exposed to wind and霜.
Hair, thinning and种, grows ever shorter,
eyebrows, long and髟, vie in length.
Thus sorrow's trunk spreads wide,
grief's branches knot and tangle.
Formerly awkward and丑,
suddenly aged and耄耋.
Tián Fèng changed in Chénggōng,
Yángwén altered in Zōngmiè.
Pān Yuè in autumn stirred,
Jī Kāng weary of travel,
Huán Tán found no joy,
Wú Zhì long in sorrow—
all were years not yet at dusk,
but appearance先于 autumn.
As for this decline of mine,
though there is cause,
it is neither ghost nor蜮,
but rather heart's sorrow.
Before attaining随心,
first seek顺耳.
Why did Bóyù sigh?
Qiūmíng felt only shame.
Pulling tigers and parting bears,
I was still a稚童;
observing form and inspecting appearance,
you truly are a悲翁.
Moreover, there are those with庞眉 among the nine棘,
and暮齿 under the three槐,
like Kǒng Guāng pleading illness,
Yuán Féng retiring from office,
Wú Bì not attending court,
Yáng Biāo losing a son.
Your esteemed gift,
perhaps is not contrary to reason."
The master then sang:
"Autumn goosefoot with tight joints,
white藋 sharing the same heart.
In the end fit to carry a bamboo basket,
sufficient to drive off birds.
Once传到大夏,
it merely becomes a Dèng forest."
○From *Yìwén Lèijù*, scroll 69.
From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, scroll 109.
〈Rhapsody on the Qióng Bamboo Staff〉
Shěn Míngzǐ traveled to the peaks of Bā Mountain,
and gathered bamboo on its northern shade.
Graceful with lofty joints,
serene and无心.
Frost-wind colored it ancient,
dew-dye streaked it deep.
Often with the tottering clan,
in secluded gloom沉沉.
Its grain not naturally exceptional,
yet its substance found appreciation,
imbued with the pitch of the crying phoenix,
fashioned into a dragon-formed staff.
Plucked stem firm and straight,
lustrous and斌, color rich,
harmonious with the wheelwright's lack of weight,
awaiting the feather-guest to be presented.
Green spring about to dusk,
white clouds slow to come.
Consulting with elders,
grasping it to follow them.
Holding the tip to offer it,
no means to support oneself.
Sugar cane though sweet,
cannot be leaned upon;
that goosefoot though solid,
cannot be deemed fine.
Not like dwelling among the unfit,
at the beginning of being useful.
Lǔ apportioned by rank,
Hàn bestowed by seniority.
Formerly they honored your age,
now they favor my worth.
Books laid across the table,
jade-dust mat筵,
then placed behind,
brushed before.
You may pluck fragrance in forest ponds,
stroll for pleasure on verandas and steps,
distinguish尊卑 by hanging帨,
follow上下 in winding paths.
Roots寄 in Jiāngnán,
vast and淼幽潭;
joints传 to Dàxià,
far and悠悠广野.
How could it compare to receiving the master's hall slippers,
or being the master's seat-right inscription,
and thus joining silken sashes and jade珮,
leaving fragrant chambers for huì courtyards?"
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, scroll 109.
Together with Preface
〈Rhapsody Lamenting Jiāngnán〉 together with its Preface
In the year of Wùchén,
in the month of Jiànhài,
a great usurper overturned the state,
and Jīnlíng collapsed.
I fled into the desolate valleys,
as both public and private affairs fell into ruin.
Summoned to duty in Huáyáng,
I departed never to return.
The path of restoration was cut short,
ending in the year of Jiǎxū.
For three days I wept at the capital’s pavilion;
for three years I was held captive in a foreign lodge.
Heaven’s way revolves like the stars,
yet when things reach their extreme, they do not turn back.
Like Fù Xiè, I can only lament my fate,
with nowhere to seek life;
like Yuán Ān, whenever I think of the royal house,
tears flow unbidden.
In the past, Huán Jūnshān with his aspirations,
and Dù Yuánkǎi in his lifetime,
both wrote books,
and each could narrate his own story.
Pān Yuè, with his literary brilliance,
first recounted his family’s traditions;
Lù Jī, in his poetry and rhapsodies,
first proclaimed his ancestral virtues.
I, Xìn, had just reached the age of graying hair,
when I encountered the chaos of collapse and rebellion,
remained distant in my wanderings,
until my twilight years.
The “Song of Yān” tells of distant parting,
grief too heavy to bear;
meeting an elder of Chǔ,
what use are tears now?
Fearing the rain of Nánshān,
I suddenly trod the court of Qín;
yielding by the shores of the Eastern Sea,
I ended up eating the grain of Zhōu.
Drifting by Xiàtíng,
a traveler lodged at Gāoqiáo.
The songs of Chǔ are no means for joy;
the wine of Lǔ holds no power to forget sorrow.
I pursue this task of writing a rhapsody,
merely to record words,
not without expressions of peril and bitterness,
but with sorrow as its essence.
The day wanes, the road is long—
what age is this in the human world!
The general departed,
and the great tree withers;
the brave man does not return,
amidst the cold wind’s mournful sigh.
The jade of Jīng presented at the pillar,
accepted the linked cities but was deceived;
the covenant document laid across the steps,
the pearl tray held but unsettled.
Zhōng Yí, a noble man,
entered as a captive wearing a southern cap;
Jìsūn the envoy,
detained in a lodge west of the river.
Shēn Bāoxū dashed his head upon the ground,
shattering it with his skull;
Cài Wēigōng’s tears were exhausted,
followed by blood.
The willows moved at Diàotái—
not something to be seen from Yùguān;
the cranes cry at Huátíng—
how could they be heard at Héqiáo!
Sūn Cè divided the world into three parts,
with a force of only one brigade;
Xiàng Jí used the sons of Jiāngdōng,
men merely eight thousand.
Thus they split mountains and rivers,
carved up the realm.
How could a million righteous troops,
in a single day roll up their armor,
be mowed down and slaughtered,
like grass and trees?
The Jiāng and Huái offered no bank-like barriers,
the fortresses no fence-like solidity.
Those who collected taxes with heads and baskets,
formed alliances and pacts;
those who wielded hoes and thorn-spears,
seized advantage and convenience.
Was it not that the royal aura south of the river,
ended after three hundred years?
Thus we know that even one who swallowed the six directions,
could not avoid the disaster at Zhǐdào;
even one who unified chariots and script,
could not avert the calamity at Píngyáng.
Alas!
Mountains and peaks crumble,
having trodden the fate of peril and ruin;
spring and autumn alternate,
inevitably bringing sorrow of leaving the old.
Heaven’s will and human affairs—
how they can cause anguish and wound the heart!
Moreover, with boats and oars, the road ends;
the Milky Way is not a place to reach by raft.
Winds and storms block the way;
Pénglái has no date of arrival.
The desperate wish to express their words;
the toiling must sing of their affairs.
Should Lù Shìhéng hear it and clap his hands,
I would be content;
should Zhāng Píngzǐ see it and deem it crude,
that is only fitting.
My family’s stewardship of granaries succeeded Zhōu,
forming a clan through generations of service;
governing the state and aiding Hàn,
serving as officials through discourse on the Way.
Endowed with the jade and stone of Sōng and Huà,
moistened by the waves of Hé and Luò.
Dwelling north of Luò for generations,
settlements by the river in peace and safety.
Then came the hardships of Yǒngjiā,
when the Central Plains lacked a lord.
People leaned against walls for rest,
roads crisscrossed by wolves and tigers.
When the five horses fled south,
and three stars gathered in the east.
They crossed the river and founded a state,
beginning the relocation of our ancestors.
Lands granted from Nányáng,
fiefs carved from the eastern peak.
Clearing weeds at Sòng Yù’s residence,
Waters and woods exchanged their fortunes,
mountains and rivers collapsed and dried.
The family upheld the straight path,
many preserved their integrity wholly.
Teaching sons seen in purity and depth,
serving the lord manifested in righteousness and fervor.
Xīnyě has a temple of living sacrifice,
Hénán a stele with foreign script.
Moreover, there was the true man of Shǎowēi,
the recluse of Tiānshān.
Courtyards like empty valleys,
gateways with carriage wheels of rushes.
Conversations moved to the lecturing tree,
writings simplified on bamboo slips.
Descended were generations of virtue,
born were loyal ministers.
Literary talent higher than Jiǎguān,
models flourishing by the Zhāng River.
Alas, for a virtuous way but no phoenix;
sigh for an untimely age yet a qílín appears.
Since treacherous and hidden forces arose,
they never pleased the benevolent.
In the year Prince Zǐ roamed the Luò,
Lánchéng sat for the examination.
First bearing fragrance at Jiànlǐ,
then soaring high at Chóngxián.
Studied at the repeated thunder of lecture halls,
sat among the bright heirs at feasts.

Jìyáng's loyal and brave,

Some, like hawks with sparrow wings,

Troops weak, enemies strong,

Blowing on leaf-like skiffs,

Originally not versed in perilous conduct,

In the past, three generations passed without shame,

At that time, the Overlord of Western Chǔ,

Commanding troops from the golden chamber,

Grey hawks and red sparrows,

Destroying nests and smoking out dens,

Using bellies as lamps,

Straight rainbows piercing the barracks,

Gazing westward toward Bówàng,

Moonlit pavilions and windy terraces,

The Minister of War, skilled in strategy and governance,

The merit of pacifying Wú,

Nányáng reviewing texts,

The Defender of the North, proud of past fame,

The water god struck by arrows,

Thus, the hibernating bear injures the horse,

The Middle Ancestor quelling violence and chaos,

Leaving the Dàidǐ to inherit the foundation,

Restoring old statutes at the Office of the Capital,

When suspicions sink, desires run wild,

Words filled with jealousy and harshness,

The land but a black mole,

“Rùnfǎ” with Preface
I lack evidence of the five blessings,
the three spirits have reproached me,
as for my heirs,
most met early demise.
Two sons and one daughter,
all just reaching the age to wear proper robes,
when the chaos and loss of Jīnlíng struck,
they perished together, guarding each other.
Sojourning through passes and rivers,
suddenly my hair turned white,
seedlings that never flowered,
repeatedly bringing grief.
One daughter reached adulthood,
one eldest grandson still a toddler,
suddenly buried in dark earth,
what pain compares to this!
Grieving over these events,
mourning those lost before,
I feel only heartbreak,
thus I made “Heartbreak” a rhapsody.
As for entering a room that once shone,
it is beyond hope to reach again;
governing districts across the river,
the road ahead grows ever more distant.
Jiéyú had her self-lamenting rhapsody,
Yáng Xióng had his mourning texts,
Wáng Zhèngcháng had the sorrow of the northern outskirts,
Xiè Ānshí had the regret of the eastern hills,
how could it be otherwise?
As for Cáo Zǐjiàn, Wáng Zhòngxuān, Fù Chángyú, Yìng Déliǎn, the mother of Liú Tāo, the kin of Rèn Yán,
their letters full of sharp grief,
their words laden with sorrow and pain,
a thousand griefs, ten thousand regrets,
how can they be fully expressed!
The paulownia of Lóngmén,
its branches already broken;
the juǎnshī grass,
its heart truly wounded.
Alas, sorrow!
The rhapsody says:
Sorrowful, the autumn wind,
shaking leaves, turning to decay.
Soul, you have gone far,
where have you gone, what do you lean on?
Gazing with longing, no hope,
returning, yet not returning.
Not understanding the meaning of the eastern gate,
only fearing the ridicule of Xīhé.
In former times, in Jīnlíng,
the world was in chaos and loss,
the royal house turbulent,
the people in dire distress.
Brothers were scattered across five commanderies,
fathers and sons separated in three provinces.
The land seethed like Yuán and Cáo’s strife,
people became wolves like Chǔ and Hàn.
Some held trees and met disaster,
hid clothes and suffered calamity,
before setting the mulberry bow,
the zhè pavilion stood empty first.
A person is but a single mound,
yet the pavilion endures a thousand autumns.
Biān Sháo’s eternal regret,
Sūn Chǔ’s lasting sorrow.
Zhāng Wǔzhuàng’s heart ailment,
Yáng Nánchéng’s flowing tears.
Grieving over these heirs,
following this generation’s record.
Heaven’s way is thus compassionate,
human relations hold this love.
Dragon destroyed at the knee,
pearl shattered in the palm.
The orchid in the room withers first,
the orchid growing in the courtyard cut early.
The length of life’s span,
alas, already full.
The crane’s cry, lonely and cut off,
the gibbon’s wail, heart-rending.
Between Yíng and Bó,
the road resembles Xīn’ān.
Vines bind the coffin cart, brambles seal the casket,
stumps cover the Yú coffin.
No mound, no marker,
only thorns, only goldenrain trees.
Heaven gloomy and colorless,
clouds gray and bitterly cold.
Moreover, I have drifted and taken residence in Qínchuān,
floating and wandering, displaced and relocated,
serving in office yet not truly an official,
returning to the fields yet without land to till.
Facing the Jade Pass, I remain a traveler in exile,
sitting by the long river, I face my twilight years.
Already my eyes are struck by countless sorrows,
and my heart is further wounded by thoughts of the Nine Springs.
As for the three tigers and two dragons,
the three pearls and two phoenixes,
all possessing the spirit of mountains and marshes,
each entered the dreams of bears and panthers.
Gazing toward Lǒngshǒu, they never return,
passing through the capital gates, they are seen off forever.
Facing the precious bowl, my heart aches with pain,
stroking the "Xuán Jīng," tears of grief flow.
Shíhuá was taken in vain,
rhinoceros horn pointlessly adorned.
The wind holds no maiden,
the grass bears no male child.
Black feathers merely cover,
beast's milk emptily held.
"Zhèn" is the palace of the eldest son,
"Xùn" is the position of the eldest daughter,
in the years of my life,
they withered first in this place.
How long is a human life?
A hundred sorrows all arrive!
The two Wángs revered Buddha,
the two Xìs revered Daoism,
the time of arrival is certain,
how can they preserve each other?
Chilly are the falling dews,
rustling are the autumn grasses.
Gone are the common people,
alas, Zhòngrén!
I hoped for Yáng Hù's foresight,
and awaited Zhāng Héng's rebirth.
Once the candle flame in the wind,
eternal dust through the ages.
O hills and mounds, how can you bear it!
How many people can remain?

"Rhapsody on a Withered Tree"
Yīn Zhòngwén was a man of refined elegance and grace,
renowned throughout the land.
As times changed and circumstances shifted,
he was sent out to serve as Governor of Dōngyáng.
Often he felt disconsolate and unhappy,
and gazing at the locust tree in his courtyard, he sighed:
"This tree, once lush and spreading,
now has its vitality utterly exhausted!"
As for the steadfast pines where white deer dwell,
the patterned catalpas where blue oxen roam,
their roots coil with mighty spirit,
through mountain cliffs, inside and out.
Why did the cassia wither and perish?
Why is the phoenix tree half-dead?
In the past, some were transplanted to Sānhé,
others had roots moved to Jiǔwǎn.
They bloomed flowers in Jiànshǐ Palace,
bore fruit in Suīyáng Garden.
Their sounds held the echoes of Xiègǔ,
their melodies embraced "Cloud Gate."
Nurturing fledglings, phoenixes gathered,
wing to wing, mandarin ducks nested.
By the Wind Pavilion, cranes cried,
facing Moon Gorge, apes chanted.
Then there were gnarled and knotted ones,
coiled and twisted, turning back and forth,
like bears and tigers glancing around,
like fish and dragons rising and falling.
Their nodes stood like linked mountains,
their grain stretched like rippling water,
Master Shí the carpenter stared in amazement,
Gōngshū Bān himself grew dizzy at the sight.
Carving and engraving just completed,
chiseling and cutting still added;
scales leveled, armor planed,
horns removed, teeth broken;
layer upon layer like shattered brocade,
piece by piece like real blossoms;
scattered among grasses and trees,
strewn amidst mist and rosy clouds.
As for pines, catalpas, ancient trees,
Píngzhòng, Jūnqiān,
their dense branches cover a hundred acres,
their stumps and sprouts span a thousand years.
In Qín, a Grand Master received his post beneath one,
in Hàn, a General sat in its shade.
All are buried under moss, pressed by fungus,
pecked by birds, bored through by insects.
Some droop low under frost and dew,
some are shaken and battered by wind and mist.
In the Eastern Sea stands a temple of white wood,
in the Western River lies a shrine of withered mulberry,
in the Northern Land, poplar leaves mark the pass,
in the Southern Hills, plum roots forge the furnace.
On Little Hill, clusters of cassia detain the traveler,
in Fúfēng, tall pines tether the horses.
Is it only by the city atop Xìliǔ,
or the fortress beneath Táolín?
If then mountains and rivers block the way,
drifting and scattered, parting in sorrow,
uprooted, they shed tears,
wounded at the root, they drip blood.
Fire enters their hollow hearts,
sap flows from broken joints.
Lying askew across the cave mouth,
broken halfway, collapsed on the mountainside.
Those with slanted grain—hundred-armspan ice shattered; those with straight grain—thousand-fathom tiles cracked.
Bearing goiters, carrying tumors,
hiding boreholes, embracing cavities.
Tree spirits flicker their gaze,
mountain demons work their mischief.
Moreover, wind and clouds bring no inspiration,
a traveler in exile with no return,
unable to gather kudzu,
instead forced to eat bracken.
Sunk in obscure lanes,
overgrown, buried behind bramble gates,
already grieving the falling leaves,
all the more lamenting the decline.
The "Huáinánzǐ" says:
"When tree leaves fall,
the elder feels sorrow."
This is what it means.
Thus I sing:
"Jiànzhāng Palace burned for three months,
on the Yellow River, rafts float for a thousand miles.
If not the garden full of trees at Jīngǔ,
then surely the county-wide blossoms of Héyáng."
Grand Marshal Huán heard it and sighed:
"In former years I planted willows,
lovingly in Hànnán;
now I see them wither and fall,
desolate by the river pool.
If trees are still thus,
how can humans endure!"

"Rhapsody on Spring"
In Yíchūn Park, spring has already returned,
in Pīxiāng Hall, they make spring garments.
New Year's birds sing with a thousand warbles,
in second month, willow catkins fill the road, flying.
Héyáng's whole county is nothing but blossoms,
Jīngǔ has always been full of garden trees.
A cluster of fragrant grass is enough to hinder a person,
a few feet of floating gossamer already blocks the path.
They open Shànglín Park and compete to enter,
crowd Héqiáo and struggle to cross.
They emerge from Lìhuá's golden chamber,
descend from Fēiyàn's orchid palace.
Hairpins abundant, surprisingly heavy,
chignons high, fearing the wind.
Eyebrows rival willows in greenness,
faces compete with peaches in redness.
Reflections come upon the pond,
blossoms fall upon the gown.
Moss just turns green and hides fish, wheat barely greens and covers pheasants.
The terrace where Nòngyù played her flute,
the waters where pendants chime and steps grace the waves.
Move to Qīlǐ and the family grows rich,
enter Xīnfēng and the wine is fine.
Pomegranate wine briefly sipped,
grape brew newly fermented.
Lotus-patterned jade bowls,
lotus seed golden cups.
Fresh bamboo shoots, newly sprouted,
small-pitted bayberries, delicate.
Lǜzhū brings the lute forward,
Wénjūn sends the wine over.
The jade pipes are first tuned,
The singing strings are briefly plucked,
Playing the melodies of "Yángchūn" and "Lùshuǐ,"
Performing the dance of phoenixes and simurghs turning in flight.
The sheng reeds are warmed again,
The zheng bridges are shifted once more,
The moon enters the singer's fan,
Flowers adorn the rhythmic drum.
The Commandant of Harmony,
The Gentleman of Pheasant Shooting,
Park their carriages in the small garden,
Ride in a line to Chángyáng.
Golden saddles are newly draped,
Mulberry-wood bows are freshly strung.
Dust is brushed off as they gaze at the horse track,
Divided into teams, they enter the archery hall.
The horses are dragon breeds from the Heavenly Pool,
The belts are jade girdles from Jīngshān.
Gorgeous brocade bears heavenly deer,
New damask weaves phoenixes.
For three days, the winding stream flows toward the river ford,
By evening, many by the river release spirits.
Guests float cups beneath the trees,
People cross the water at the sandy shore.
Carved thin sleeves on narrow gowns,
Pearl-strung collars adorn scarves.
On the hundred-zhàng mountain peak, the sun begins to slant,
If not drunk by the third watch, do not return home.
The reflection in the pond outshines a mirror,
The scent of clothes indoors is not as sweet as flowers.

"Rhapsody on the Seventh Night"
The hare moon rises first,
The sheep lantern is next lit.
Behold the shining sight of the Ox Star,
Gaze at the Weaver Girl across the railing.
Then, the lovely concubines of Qín,

Graceful and famed as Yàn,
Elegant and surnamed Qín,
Disdain their morning makeup as half-worn,
Cherish their evening touch-up as wholly new.
At this time, they all leave their chambers,

Silk threads are taut to thread the square,

"Rhapsody on Elephant Chess"
Observe the creation at its inception,
The beginning of emperors and kings,
Modeling the congealing yin through profound virtue,
Looking up to the soaring qi in the clear void.
Then the green slips are opened,
The red board stands straight,
Principles deeply studied, subtleties explored,
Origins exhaustively sought to achieve sageliness,
Like striking a great bell,
Like hanging a bright mirror.
White phoenixes approach from afar,
Yellow clouds shine high above,
Able to transform customs and shift morals,
Able to govern offices and administer affairs.
Thus the board takes from the Qian hexagram,
Still depicting the profound heavens,
The moon disk newly full,
The solar halo just rounded,
Modeling the ornate canopy of the Imperial Guard,
Depicting the jade spring of the Mingtáng.
Kun serves as the chariot,
Hard and soft rolling and stretching,
Like a square mirror without reflection,
Like an empty city yet uninhabited.
Hastening the patterned lines,
Forgetting the chart of the divine turtle,
Horses as fine as thousand-gold steeds,
Tallies as clear as the six jiǎ talismans.
Then, holding tablets in order,
According to time, taking seats.
Turning earthly patterns on square jades,
Rotating heavenly patterns on round bi-disks;
Dividing the fine jade of Jīngshān,
Counting the min-stones of Lántián.
Southward goes the tally of Chìshuǐ,
Northward sends the strategy of Xuánshān;
Residing eastward, the blue dragon,
Exiting westward, the white horse.
Having displayed the dark symbols,
The golden board is settled for now.
Illuminating the light of sun and moon,
Riding the nature of wind and clouds;
Taking the true colors of the four directions,
Using the mutual generation of the five virtues.
Following the lunar mansions turning left,
Starting from Huángzhōng and proceeding orderly;
When yin flips, the gazing hare emerges first,
When yang changes, the spiritual crow shines alone.
Moreover, leisurely strolling in Rénshòu,
Enjoying music and fine sounds;
Water reflections shimmer in sunlight,
Flower radiance illuminates the woods.
Sometimes unfolding the chart for long study,
Or opening the classics for thorough search.
Though again accomplished by hand,
Ultimately must be grasped by heart.
Then there are dragon candles holding flowers,
Golden censers floating incense;
The moon sets, cassia droops,
Stars slant, willows fall.
Hesitating at the pivot,
Doubting the boundaries,
Looking back, perplexed,
Heart anxious and fearful,
Responding to Kǎn while charging Lí,
Suddenly at Shēn, taking Wèi.

"Rhapsody on Lamps"
As the nine dragons approach dusk,
Three cups are drunk, then rest.
Jade hooks half-risen,
Ruòmù trees fully lowered.
Windows hide brightness in whitewashed walls,
Willows deepen darkness in orchid chambers.
Kingfisher-feather pearl quilts,
Tasseled feather curtains.
Unfolding the knee-bending screen,
Covering the lotus-patterned traveling screen.
Rolling clothes on the bed of the Queen of Qín,
Sending pillows to the terrace of Jīng.
Then there are a hundred branches on one tree,
Four lamps linked on a single tray.
Fragrance enhanced with honey,
Scent mingled with burning orchids.
Embers long, nights enduring,
Light blue, nights cold.
Elegant splendor interplaying,
Salamander oil shining bright.
Moving scales and armor on whales,
Flames gleaming like calling cranes.
Moths flutter, scattering petals chaotically,
Wind rises, meteors falling finely.
Moreover, in Shànglán late at night,
At Zhōngshān, clear wine is poured.
The Chǔ consort retains guests,
Hán É harmonizes voices.
Low songs keep the rhythm,
"Wandering Strings" cease their sound.
Glowing red embers,
Blazing crimson blooms.
Suddenly nine lights connect in color,
Or twin flowers shine together.
Send word to Sū Jìzǐ,
He should know the feeling of remaining light.

"Rhapsody on Facing the Candle"
At Lóngshā and Yānsài, armor feels cold,

Before the lamp, sewing clothes seems dim,

Pluck the lampwick, hold the cassia candle,

Cast phoenixes holding lotuses,
Carved dragons sleeping side by side.
Embers high, as if trimmed many times,

Copper lotus holds tearful wax,
Iron snips catch floating smoke.
Once knew snowlight could reflect on paper,
Now marvel at lampflowers bringing coins.
Lotus curtains, cold stand, window brushed by dawn,
Bamboo cage,熏火, fragrance fills the floss.

Light clear, cold enters,

Fragrance follows.
Yùjīn garden,
Fúróng pond.
Qín Shǐhuáng's evil-warding not worth mention,
Hàn Wǔdì's foreign incense—what marvel is that?
Evening stars vanish,
Fragrant grasses rest,

Rhapsody on the Mirror
The River of Heaven gradually fades away,
The sun's wheel is about to rise.
Swallows chatter before the King of Wú,
Crows startle the Censor.
Upon the jade-flowered mat,
Inside the golden lotus curtain.
First folding the screen,
Then newly opening the door panels.
Morning light dazzles the eyes,
The early wind blows upon the face.
Approaching the rack below to pull on a gown,
Going to the chest's side to put on bracelets.
Last night's coiled hair still remains,
The fading makeup is already thin.
No longer are there pearl-like lips,
Only the eyebrow's calyx remains.
Stars grow sparse upon the dimples,
The moon falls from the forehead's yellow.
The mirror stand's silver belt,
Originally came from the Wèi palace.
It can hold the crescent moon horizontally,
And cleverly hang the returning wind.
A dragon hangs outside the case,
A phoenix leans amidst flowers.
The mirror reflects the gall and the heart,
Rare and hard to encounter.
Carved with a five-colored coiling dragon,
Engraved with ancient characters of a thousand years.
The pheasant sees it and dances alone,
The seabird beholds it and cries in solitude.
Facing water, the moon emerges in the pool;
Shining upon the sun, water caltrops grow on the wall.
Temporarily setting up the dressing case,
Then pulling out the mirror drawer.
Vying to learn life's sentiments,
Striving to cherish the present world.
Even hair at the temples is deliberately trimmed,
Even leveled eyebrows are still shaved.
Flying flower tiles,
Must be arranged in order.
Vermilion opens the brocade path,
Dark pigment mixes with oily sandalwood.
Rouge blended with shellac,
Moisture steeped in fragrant orchids.
Measuring the length of the coiled hair and temples,
Judging the distance for placing flowers.
Hanging charms upon the hairpins,
Wiping hairpin beams with powdered silk wadding.
After newly combing the hair, one looks at the clothing,
Then takes it from the dressing place to return.
Briefly observing the tied strings,
One already knows the patterned silk ribbons.
The gown is straight, the body long,
The skirt slanted, held by false loops.
Truly, this mirror is especially suitable,
It cannot be hidden in its case for even a moment,
Even when briefly going out into the garden, it follows of its own accord.
○From *Yìwén Lèijù*, scroll 70.
Rhapsody on the Mandarin Ducks
The concubine Yú Jī served King Wèi from youth,
Naturally possessing songs that could wind around the beams.
How could she ever have woven brocade?
Never willing to pick mulberry leaves.
In the end, she met a薄命 fate,
And lay upon an empty bed after dressing.
Seeing the mandarin ducks learning from each other,
She tilts her head and tears fall.
Nányáng powder is no longer looked upon,
The new eyebrows of Jīngzhào are lazily outlined.
Moreover, with two hearts and shared wings,
Tamed and familiar within the pond and cage,
Floating on waves, playing with reflections,
Preening feathers, riding the wind.
Flying together under the eaves and tiles,
Fully open to the Wèi palace;
Perching together on the catalpa tree,
Truly worthy of Hán Féng.
If Hán Shòu desires marriage,
Or Wēn Qiáo wishes for a wife,
The jade terrace does not send them,
The foreign fragrance is not yet present,
They must see these two flying together,
And feel the emptiness of the bed, hard to keep.

Rhapsody on the Wandering Man
The wandering man toils, pursuing the campaign march,
Guarding straight the thousand-mile wall of Chángchéng.
Lǒng River's ice is ever congealed,
The mountain passes are brightened only by the moon.
Moreover, rising from an empty bed with resentment,
The singing girl is parted from life.
Gauze windows shut alone,
Silken curtains long hang down.
The new zither is not played,
The long flute is羞吹.
In former years, the cassia garden,
In bygone days, the orchid chamber.
Luófū with hair just bound,
Nòngyù at first hairpin age,
New songs of "Zǐyè",
Old dances of "Qiánxī".
After parting, boudoir feelings are no more,
Before the mirror stand, the bright mirror need not be bright.
No message of union to send,
The palindrome weave is not yet finished.
Wandering dust fills the bed, no need to brush it away,
Fine grass grows横阶随意.
The other day, a Hàn envoy arrived at Zhāngtái,
Hearing that her husband must surely be returning.
The handkerchief still wishes to be dry,
The sorrowful brows then begin to open.
Imagining the traveler's arrival in reverse,
Going forth to meet him, coming with a含笑.

"Song of Joining the Army"
The "Hétú" discusses battle formations' energy,
The "Jīnguì" distinguishes astrological signs.

"Crows Crying at Night, Two Poems"
The cassia tree, knowing it is far away,
The wind-blown bamboo pole, how could it stoop low?
Alone I pity the bright moonlit night,
Solitary flight, still not yet roosting.
Who among the Tiger Guard shows pity?
How could the Censor accompany me?
Though said to be set to strings and pipes,
In the end, it's weeping within the tune.

"Song of Lament"
"Song of Lament"
My home is before Jīnlíng county,
Married to a young man from Cháng'ān.
Turning my head, gazing toward home, tears fall,
Not knowing where the edge of the sky is?
How many days until the Hú dust ends?
When will the Hàn moon become full again?
For you, I can sing this song,
Unaware, my heart follows the broken string.

"Charming Maiden"
In the morning, before the door, looking in the mirror,
Smiling radiantly, looking at myself.
Between the brows, thick black ink dots straight,
On the forehead corners, light yellow carefully placed.
Only suspect fallen flowers idly drift away,
Again say the spring breeze does not return.
In youth, there is only joy and pleasure,
Drinking wine, how can one leave leftovers?

"Song of Yān"
North of Dài, clouds and vapor darken day and night,
A thousand miles of flying tumbleweed, no more roots.
Cold geese honking cross the Liáo River,
Mulberry leaves scatter and fall at Jì Gate.
On Jìnyáng mountain peak, no arrow bamboo,
In Shūlè city, lacking water sources.
Vassal state conscripts long stationed far from home,
Yángguān news utterly cut off and sparse.
I wish to obtain Lǔ Lián's flying arrow,
To send a letter of longing for home to the Yān general.
Crossing the Liáo originally had its own general,
Cold wind soughing, ripples form on the water.
I, startled that Gānquán is full of beacon fires,
You, surprised that Yúyáng lacks battle clouds.
Ever since the general left Xìliǔ,
The wanderer's empty bed is hard to keep alone.
Coiling dragon bright mirror gifted to Qín Jiā,
Evil-warding fragrant incense sent to Hán Shòu.
Spring equinox, swallows come, how many days?
Second month, silkworms sleep, not long again.
Luòyáng drifting gossamer, a hundred zhang linked,
Huáng Hé spring ice, a thousand pieces pierced.
Peach blossom color lovely like horses,
Elm pods newly opened clever like coins.
One cup of grape wine, drunk for a thousand days,
With nothing to do, nine cycles learning to be immortals.
Surely take golden elixir, make several doses,
Able to make the ornamental pillar last a thousand years.

"Song of the Willow"
By the river, willow branches a hundred zhang long,
Especially long strands droop touching the ground.
River water rushes and strikes, roots and trunks endangered,
Suddenly on the river, wind and waves blow.
Pitiful the phoenix chicks in the nest,
Without reason, that year born to part.
Drifting raft once gone, ascends to the heavenly pool,
The Weaving Girl's shuttle-holder should follow along.
Who says it ever sheltered several states?
Merely using one small branch from the southeast.
In former days, the young lord left Nánpí,
Where to seek the Xuánwǔ slope?
Fine horses gallop northwest,
Left and right, bending bows aiming at the Yuèzhī.
Dappled horse, water-blocking trappings, crossing the stream rider,
White jade hand tablet, coiled dragon design falls.
You say a true man has no spirit?
I ask, how could the Yānshān get its stele?
Phoenix new pipe, Xiāo Shǐ plays it,
Vermilion Bird spring window, the Jade Maiden peeks.
Cloud-holding wine cup of red agate,
Sun-reflecting food plates of purple glass.
A hundred years of frost and dew suddenly scattered,
Once fame and achievement become unattainable.
Surely King Huái made mistaken plans,
For no reason, again and again used Zhāng Yí.
Better to drink wine at Gāoyáng Pond,
At sunset returning, cap worn backwards.
Under Wǔchāng city walls, who saw it transplanted?
Before Guāndù camp, how could one know?
Alone I recall flying catkins like goose down falling,
No longer green threads like horse tails hanging.
Wishing to leave a tune with the plum blossoms,
Together take the long flute and blow within the pipes.

River
"In Response to 'Sailing on the River'"
Spring river descends from Báidì,
Painted boat heads toward Huángniú.
Brocade cables turn back on sandy shoals,
Orchid oars avoid reed islets.
Damp flowers float along with the water,
Empty nests drift following the trees.
Jiànpíng boat rudders go downstream,
Jīngmén warships float.
Riverbank shrines have many tall trees,
Mountain city has enough lofty towers.
Sunset, river wind calms,
Dragon's chant echoes upstream.

"In Response to 'Mountain Pond'"
The pleasure palace has much leisure and ease,
Gazing at the park, the carriage temporarily turns back.
Sounding reed pipes ascend over extreme waves,
Flying canopy passes through connecting channels.
Cassia pavilion flowers not yet fallen,
Paulownia gate leaves half sparse.
Lotus breeze startles bathing birds,
Bridge shadows gather swimming fish.
Sunset holds mountain vapor,
Clouds return bringing leftover rain.

"Accompaging the Imperial Carriage to Zhōngnán Mountain, in Response to Yǔwén the Palace Secretary"
Accompanying the Imperial Carriage to Zhōngnán Mountain, in Response to Secretary Yǔwén
Jade Mountain borne by four conveyances,
At Jasper Pool feast the eight dragons.
Turtle Bridge floats on the Lesser Sea,
Crane-canopied carriage ascends the central peak.
Flying Fox Pass blocks the frontier road,
White Horse Ford confronts the river’s rush.
Waters settle the stones of three streams,
Mountains seal the pines of five trees.
Long rainbow, twin waterfalls,
Round towers, two lotus blooms.
Watchtower drums sound at dusk,
Mountain temple bells ring at dawn.
New rushes’ joints grow swiftly,
Short bamboo shoots, their sheaths still thick.
In trees dwell birds that hold cherries,
Flowers retain bees brewing honey.
Facing the wind, I descend Lièquē,
Sprinkle wine to summon Chāngróng.
Glad now to accompany the journey north,
I long to await the eastern fēng sacrifice.

In Response to Secretary Yǔwén’s Spring Mountain Outing
A traveler meets spring’s radiance,
Golden saddle ascends emerald heights.
Wind against, flowers strike the face,
Mountains deep, clouds dampen robes.
A wild goose leans on one foot,
A gibbon flies with both arms.
Watchtowers encroach on ridge paths,
Mountain villages encircle hunting grounds.
The Daoist Fēng Jūndá,
The immortal Dīng Lìngwēi.
Here they boiled elixirs,
Truly unwilling to return.

Mountain Outing
Mountain Outing
Casually I climb Xuánpǔ Palace,
Then ascend Zēngchéng Mountain.
Unaware how many miles high,
I bow my head to gaze upon the mortal world.
Singing, clouds gather as if to cluster;
Playing the qin, cranes dance as if to flutter.
At the ravine’s base, a hundred layers of flowers;
At the mountain’s foot, a sheet of rain.
Gracefully, vines hang inverted;
Tall and straight, pines stand upright.

In Response to Capital Official Yǔwén’s Hunting Excursion
The small park’s forbidden gate opens,
Hunters from Chángyáng arrive.
Knowing well the eyebrow-painting is done,
They gallop their horses toward Zhāngtái.
Ravine cold, the spring shrinks back;
Mountain clear, clouds drift in reverse.
Bears hungry, lick their own paws;
Geese startled, alone hold twigs in beak.
Fine wine from Yúháng intoxicates,
Lotus blooms promptly offer cups.

Reporting to Luòzhōu
Naval forces gather at Mèngjīn,
On the jiǎzǐ day, arrayed eastward.
Thunderous chariots startle war drums,
Sword chambers stir the metal deity.
Command tent’s aura of wind and clouds,
Army gate’s men of passes and frontiers.
Long banners adorned with bird plumes,
Joined armor embracing rhinoceros scales.
Starlight rays, flames a zhang long;
Lunar halo, seven layered wheels.
Líyáng’s waters gradually clear,
Guāndù’s willows should greet spring.
No merit to receive heaven’s regard,
Driving relays to govern southern Qín.
Prolix words weary documents,
Mixed customs mar the dusty world.
At Shàngluò I meet the commandant,
At Shāng Mountain I see the recluse.
Lingering south of Zhōngnán,
I am but a lone historian.

Reporting in Late Autumn, Sent to a Recluse
Reporting in Late Autumn, Sent to a Recluse
Wáng Ní encountered Nièquē,
Jiénì met Chángjǔ.
On a goosefoot-wood bed, they lie basking in the sun;
In wheat fields, they plow with classics in hand.
Naturally curved wooden table,
Nameless tadpole script books.
Gathering flowers to feed sparrows,
Digging ponds to try raising fish.
Small village mends rough paths,
Low fields repair broken ditches.
Autumn water pulls sand downward,
Cold vines cling sparsely to trees.
In vain the平原 rider comes,
Visiting Zhòng Wèi’s hut.

To Pillar of State Prince Zhào of Yìzhōu, Two Poems
Tóngliáng’s shadow on the pear tree,
Stone mirror reflects raised curtains.
Two rivers like dyed brocade,
Twin peaks like painted eyebrows.
Through lotuses, low evening canopies;
Withered willows hang remnant threads.
Elegance abundant, refined and scholarly,
Springs gush rich with literary phrases.
No chance to be like Zǐ Shū,
I briefly attend Línzī.

Desolate, the year’s end nears;
Vast and dim, cloud forms alike.
Crane feathers drift like scattered snow,
Chariot hubs spin flying tumbleweeds.
Wild geese return, knowing warmth’s direction;
Birds build nests, understanding to shelter from wind.
Cold sand on both banks turns white,
Hunting fires on one mountain glow red.
I wish to imagine the hanging quail’s tatters,
And sigh at times over the empty humble lane.

Respectfully Presented to the Minister of Justice, Duke of Huáinán
Respectfully Presented to the Minister of Justice, Duke of Huáinán
A perilous state long disrupted in virtue,
Heaven’s strategy at last seized the moment.
At Jiǔhé he heard the oath to the multitude,
For a thousand lǐ saw linked banners.
With Guó’s fall, the Chuíjí jade returned;
With Qí pacified, the precious tripod came back.
Long corrupted by worldly customs,
Greatly wearied by frontier garments.
A hobbled steed still runs a thousand lǐ,
A soaring roc takes flight ninefold more.
Still pitying the horse’s teeth advancing,
Should recall the banner tassels growing sparse.
Returning carriage enters the old hometown,
Garden willows begin to sway gently.
Old bamboos encroach on walking paths,
New paulownias add several arm-spans.
Cold valley pears should be heavy,
Autumn woods chestnuts even plumper.
Fine wine still partakes of the sage’s,
Carved texts originally enter the subtle.
Urgent songs welcome Zhào’s zither,
Playful strings summon Chǔ’s consort.
A petty man oversees recommendations,
Bright promotion—truly an unworthy reed.
Southern commandant governing capital guards,
Military strategy borrowing established authority.
Shāng Mountain recluse’s stone,
Dān River phoenix rock.
Country pavilion long tethers horses,
Mountain town early closes gates.
Heralds crowd with vermillion tallies,
Crossed halberds reflect crimson gates.
Thus making one forget Chǔ’s integrity,
How then merely eat Zhōu’s fern?
Thirty-six waters change,
Forty-nine articles err.
Alchemy furnace’s wind and smoke cease,
Years age, willow and rush decline.
Dare I not exhaust my duty as colleague?
Past days I fear are hard to reclaim.
○From the author’s collected works, juan 3.

〈New Year's Day at the Superior Judicial Office〉
〈New Year's Day at the Superior Judicial Office〉
At dawn I open the gate and threshold,
Complex phrases surge from the brush tip.
The grey hawk descends upon the prison clerk,
The xièzhì adorns the penal official.
At court, I hold the jade tally,
At the covenant, I bear the pearl tray.
The year's end sees stars shift their positions,
The intercalary month's law is not yet exhausted.
Snow piles three feet deep,
Ice forms a zhang thick with cold.
Short bamboo shoots still buried in the earth,
Fragrant hearts of orchids not yet risen.
At Mèngmén, long have I lost my way,
Suddenly borne aloft by the whirlwind.
The roosting crow returns to its mansion,
The abandoned horse comes back to its stall.
Glory and fame carry heavy weight,
My shallow virtue makes repaying kindness hard.
Méi Chéng returned to rise from illness,
Gòng Yǔ then brushed off his cap.
Just as the lotus-leaf sword hangs down,
The bamboo-root elixir remains unused.
Once I understand the laws of the hanging images,
Who would think of the fishing rod?
○From the original collection, volume three.

Farewell to Xué Wényuè in Response to His Gift
〈Farewell to Xué Wényuè in Response to His Gift, While in Luòzhōu〉
You dwell by the river's bend,
Where talented men have long gathered.
Salt forms may transform into tigers,
Tripod's aura suddenly becomes dragons.
If one bears virtue's legacy,
The palace walls surely rise layer upon layer.
Five roads open for debate,
Four illuminations kindle literary beacons.
I, unworthy, was recommended for office,
The people's wishes at last followed heaven's will.
Shàngluò divided the commandant's post,
Hóngnóng established a dependency.
Goat's Gut connects nine slopes,
Bear's Ear faces twin peaks.
White Stone Immortal's taro,
Green Woods Hermit's pine.
North Bridge sent off Sūn Chǔ,
West Embankment parted with Gě Gōng.
If old friends send letters,
Líyáng soil is enough to seal them.
○From the original collection, volume three.
From "The Collected Poems of Yǔ Kāifǔ," part one.

Zhèngyuán
〈Response to Zǔ Wáng Zhèngyuán Upon Mission to Yè〉
Our emperor rules the nine regions,
His influence and teachings reach boundless shores.
He promotes culture, enriches rites and music,
Lays down arms, gives rest to the common folk.
In my inadequacy, I drive fine steeds,
Bear banners and handle jade tablets.
Ancient steles, their inscriptions worn away,
Deserted cities, their ages lost to memory.
Melons ripen patterned on the ridges,
Fragrant grain heads bow low across the fields.
Your precious gift truly brings comfort,
To return your kindness, no path seems enough.

〈On Mission to Yè〉
A great state practices diplomatic rites,
Neighborly bonds grow stronger hence.
Unfurling banners over plains and marshes,
I report accomplished words before the screen.
Westward, braving wind and dew,
Northward, crossing Huányuán Pass.
Meeting in friendship with noble sons,
Performing rites before princely grandsons.
How to praise the fine trees?
Only joy in chanting "Gathering White Southernwood."
Four sets of sacrificial meats fill the carved stands,
Three offerings brim in the wine vessels.
A subject has no affairs beyond borders,
How then to delight in these words?
Customs differ, barriers arise,
Mountains and rivers no longer shared.
No chance to lodge in southern halls,
In vain I wish to sacrifice at the western gate.
With deep feeling, only this parting,
Hoping our early bond may long endure.

〈Entering Péngchéng Lodge〉
Lord of Xiāng earlier founded a state here,
Xiàng's clan once displayed awesome might.
The snipe's flight mourns the Chǔ battle,
The "Rooster Crows" laments the Hàn siege.
Ages change, customs differ,
Wind and clouds shift with rise and fall.
Water flows, floating chime-stones tremble,
Mountains echo with paired pheasants in flight.
Summer's remnant flowers soon fade,
Autumn nears, swallows grow sparse.
The locust court droops with green tassels,
Lotus shores shed crimson petals.
Only knowing the day grows late,
I see no return from the Rain Dance altar.

Red banks wind around the new village,
Green walls face the ornate gate.
Fàn Jū newly entered the ministry,
Ránghóu just left the fief.
Shànglín's hunting calls urge haste,
At the river bridge, crossing clamors loud.
Pheasants dart flying across the ravine,
Foxes hide entering broken plains.
The general's feast lasts into evening,
He comes to visit the green bamboo garden.

〈Observing Military Training with the Imperial Procession〉
Drilling troops beyond Chángyáng,
Entering the arena through the martial fence.
Formations spread like clouds rising sideways,
Camp opens like wild geese spreading wings.
Gates wary of magnetic stone hindrance,
Horses fear iron caltrop wounds.
Lóngyuān sword touches Ox and Dipper,
Fánruò bow startles the Heavenly Wolf.
Falling stars race like swift steeds,
Floating clouds mount Sùshuāng horses.
Fierce winds blow battle drums,
High dust envelops shell-adorned armor.
Terrified apes sometimes fall from trees,
Startled geese repeatedly break formation.
Trees cold, branches grow straighter,
Hills barren, chrysanthemums turn fragrant.
Leopard's strategy pushes for total victory,
Dragon's plan bows to each one's strength.
This humble servant delights in watching,

〈In Response to Prince Zhào's Poem Bestowed on the March〉
The supreme general marches from Dōngpíng,
First to pacify the Jiāng region's troops.
Bent bows make rocks tremble,
Shaken drums boil the sand with sound.
The Cross-Sea General's title,
The Long Wind swift horse's name.
Rain ceases, the broken rainbow fades,
Clouds return, a lone goose journeys on.
Dark cliffs, morning stones damp,
Empty mountains, night fires bright.
Low bridges cross ravine bottoms,
Narrow paths wind through flowers.
Brocade carriages share in establishing authority,
Fish-scale carriages differ in camping grounds.
Womanly spirit in the army,
Lady's city beyond the frontier.
I, petty man, neglect self-care,
Parted roads hinder our meeting.
How many months till the magic fields ripen?
What year will the golden furnace be complete?
Mournful reed pipes, frontier fortress tunes,
Neighing horses, parting's sounds.
The prince's person is a treasure,
Deeply thoughtful, not leaning on the chariot rail.

Matching the Poem by Prince Zhào on Sending Off the Army in the Gorge

White-feathered arrows test the command of troops.
The mountain city faces the waning moon;
The riverbank formations reach the level clouds.
Red serpents hang as crossbow shadows;
Shooting stars embrace sword patterns.
Barbarian flutes warn distantly through the night;
Frontier horses neigh darkly in herds.
The traveler passes through the Bright Moon Gorge;
Gibbon cries cannot be borne to hear.

Matching the Five-Rhyme Poem by Prince Zhào on the Journey
Fluttering, reflecting on carriage curtains;
Appearing and disappearing, gazing at linked banners.
Passing through clouds, they still flank the battle array;
Turning winds promptly send off the troops.
The gorge path's sand is like moonlight;
The mountain peaks' rocks resemble eyebrows.
Village peach blossoms brush with rouge powder;
Riverbank willows are clad in green threads.
The Brocade City is faintly visible in the distance;
Turning the saddle, I long for this moment.

Accompanying His Highness, Duke Xú, on a Military March
Eight winds foretell the battle's aura;
Six *jiǎ* cycles await the art of war.
Establishing headquarters, still spreading tents;
Commanding the army, immediately grasping the banner.
Long banners approach Guǎngwǔ;
Beacon fires illuminate Chénggāo.
Patrolling the cold, double-layered with padded garments;
Drinking water surpasses simple wine.
Behind the array, clouds grow ever straighter;
Deep in the troops, stars turn higher.
Lightning flames drive dragon-horses;
Mountain spirits engrave precious swords.
The distant frontier tosses elm leaves;
The cold pass sheds wild goose down.
Since I can follow the divine and martial;

“Listening to Clothes-Pounding at Night”
The sound of pounding clothes on an autumn night,
Flies over the Chángmén city’s height.
Tonight, the moon over Chángmén’s gate,
Should be as bright as the day’s light.
Small hairpins suit millet ear ornaments fine,
Round waists move in woven designs.
Autumn anvils adjust to urgent beats,
Random pestles change to new melodies sweet.
Dry stones make the anvil resonate more,
Hollow paulownia pestles cease to roar.
Sounding stones come from Huàyīn’s land,
Hollow paulownia from the phoenix forest grand.
In the north hall, slender-waisted pestles pound,
In the south market, maiden anvils resound.
Beating rhythm needs no drum’s aid,
Tuning melodies, no zither played.
Together tying linked-branch threads,
Doubly threading long-life needles’ spreads.
Singing towers startle parting’s lament,
Travelers’ hearts with sorrow are rent.
Hearts united, bamboo-leaf bowls in hand,
Doubly gone, doubly come, full and grand.
Skirts and robes cannot bear the length,
Blouse sleeves are better kept short in strength.
Dragon-patterned scissors engraved with care,
Phoenix-wing hairpins wrapped, beyond compare.
Graceful echoes harmonize in rhyme,
Sorrowful sounds break in mournful time.
New melodies wind through the night breeze,
Charming turns fill the air with ease.
Should be heard in Chánglè Palace’s hall,
Surely reaching Zhāoyáng Palace’s wall.
Flower hairpins, drunken eyes in patterned dye,
Dragon-sons with fine red lines lie.
Damp folds through the night’s dew pass,
Clothes blown by the wind all night, alas.
Jade steps, the wind turns swift and keen,
On the Great Wall, snow should darken the scene.
New ribbons just about to be sewn,
Fine brocade must be woven, soon shown.
Sounds bustling like “Guǎnglíng Sàn,”
Pestles urgent like “Yúyáng Càn.”
The new moon stirs golden waves’ light,
Autumn clouds drift past, vast in flight.
Who pities the garrisoned traveler’s plight,
Tonight at Jiāohé, in the lonely night?
Xǔyáng’s “Parting Rhapsody” in despair,
Línjiāng’s “Song of Sorrowful Thoughts” in the air.
Again making this tune filled with grief,
How much youth remains, how brief?

Desolate, I lean on the White Society,
Lonely, as if at Dōnggāo.
My learning differs from Nángōng Jìng’s,
My poverty matches Běiguō Sāo’s.
The Meng official observes autumn waters,
Lái’s wife spins fallen fur.
The traveler laments the year’s end,
The farmer wearies of toil.
Frosty skies dry the forest trees,
Autumn’s breath lifts winds and clouds high.
Restless and unsettled still,
I am about to let tears soak my robe.

“Chanting on Garden Flowers”
Briefly passing by the spring garden’s side,
Casually strolling to view the fruit trees.
Branches abundant like Jīngǔ,
Flowers mingling, reflecting Héyáng.
Naturally red, no need for dye,
Truly white, requiring no adornment.
Swallows send them back to the water chestnut well,
Bees carry them up to the honeycomb.
Not the scent of a golden censer,
Nor the fragrance of the Cypress Hall.
The scented robe is especially fine,
Should be presented to the King of Wèi.

“Xīmén Bào Temple”
The nobleman’s benefits are broad,
The wise man’s virtue deeply planted.
Duckweed and algae are offered here,
Firewood and grass fortunately untouched.
Reverently hearing of the upright minister’s sacrifice,
Truly understanding the heart that wears the leather strap.
His appearance and model, though from past ages,
His fine plans seem still traceable.
Chrysanthemums fragrant with wine,
Pagoda tree shadows approach the window.
Cranes flying as if chasing a dance,
Fish startled as if hearing a lute.
The Zhāng River flows over stepping stones,
The Bronze Sparrow Terrace casts shadows in autumn woods.

“In Response to Junior Guardian Wáng, Mourning Recluse Zhōu from Afar”
“In Response to Junior Guardian Wáng, Mourning Recluse Zhōu from Afar”
In the dark and silent, you wander to Dài,
Desolate and bleak, I head toward Qín.
Though we speak of differing life and death,
We are both men who do not return.
In the past, I served among officials,
While you avoided the dusty world.
Gazing at the aura, seeking true recluses,
Waiting at the pass for the free-spirited.
Suddenly I hear of a friend of springs and rocks,
Orchids and cassia could not protect his body.
Sadly, like Zhāng Zhòngwèi,
Mournfully, like Zhèng Zǐzhēn.
The Three Mountains still have cranes,
The Five Willows should greet spring again.
So I follow the Wèi River’s flow,
To cast my mourning by the riverbank.

Minister of Education Wáng Bāo
“Mourning Minister of Education Wáng Bāo”
In the past, I heard of Wángzǐ Jìn,
Lightly rising, pursuing immortals.
It was said you accumulated goodness,
And would succeed former worthies.
All under heaven are adrift,
Not alone in being displaced.
Who would have thought the central terrace would collapse,
You before the wind and candle.
Since your time, a bell-and-cauldron clan,
In Jiāngdōng for three hundred years.
Precious sabers still passed down through generations,
Carved spears originally from old transmissions.
Green ribbons winding around locust-tree seals,
Gold adorning the cicada attendants.
A land that established a loyal minister’s state,
A family that opened a filial son’s spring.
Naturally able to moisten withered wood,
Sufficient to make flowing water round.
With you inheriting ancestral deeds,
Among the lords, none could find fault.
The blue robe already faced the sun,
The child already discoursed on heaven.
Yǐngyīn’s pearls and jades were beautiful,
Héyáng’s rouge and powder were lovely.
Fame high, shared by the six states,
Value heavy, worth ten cities linked.
Eloquence sufficient to observe autumn waters,
Writing worthy of inscribing horsewhips.
Returning phoenixes embracing written characters,
Separated cranes winding around lute strings.
Holding the tasseled banner, governing the甸服,
Lowering the curtain, not being at the border.
Quiet pavilions only tether horses,
Idle beacon fires directly raise smoke.
Never neglecting to open the book desk,
Not hindering sitting in a fishing boat.
At Màolíng, suddenly many illnesses,
At Huáiyáng, truly not recovered.
Attending physicians beyond silence,
The divine principle then became continuous.
Forever parting with Zhāng Píngzǐ,
Long buried, Wáng Zhòngxuān.
At Bǎigǔ, moving pine trees,
At Yánglíng, buying burial fields.
On the Shǎn road, autumn winds rise,
The cold hall already rustles.
Hill poplars once shaken and fallen,
Mountain fires instantly blaze.
Once envied by others,
Now pitied by others.
The world’s path dawns and dawns again,
Human feelings mysterious and more mysterious.
Old friends grieve at this parting,
Leaving regrets filling the Qín plains.
Established name here established,
Complete virtue thus complete.
Only the Shānyáng flute remains,
Sadly, my “Remembering the Old” piece.

“Looking Up and Harmonizing with Vice Director Hé’s ‘Returning Home and Remembering the Past’”
At Purple Pavilion, morning court adjourned;
At Central Terrace, evening memorials grow sparse.
No more the thousand-golden smile remains,
In vain the five-day return home is made.
Steps and eaves, morning yet unswept,
Orchid chamber, daytime doors closed tight.
Moss grows where melodies were once composed,
Dust gathers on the loom of palindrome brocade.
Old zither’s lingering strings now broken,
Singing beams where autumn geese take flight.
Morning clouds though still in sight,
Night’s tent surely hard to rely on.
May I rely on sweet dew to enter,
And borrow wisdom-lamp’s radiant light.
Who knows the evening in Luòchéng,
Tears alone still soak my gown.

〈Seeing Off Master Jiǒng for Burial〉
Dragon Spring today is sealed,
Stone cave now is closed.
Jade case shatters the lecture-staff,
Suspended river halts the sharp debate.
Incense burner still bears cypress,
Deer-tail whisk turns to pine.
Outer gate not ten miles away,
Mountains wind, already many layers.
Still hear the incense hall’s chants,
Yet listen to Bamboo Grove’s bell.
Seeing off guests, wind and dust crowd,
Cold outskirts, frost and dew thick.
If the soul and spirit do not perish,
Where then shall divine principle abide?

〈Ancestral Emperor Dance〉
Metal conducts autumn's command,
White Emperor, Zhūxuān.
Regulating the five pheasants,
Singing praises to the nine rivers.
Holding the virtue of culture,
Facing and surpassing that heaven.
Blessed with fortune and happiness,
May the nobleman live ten thousand years.
○Same as above.
〈Black Emperor Yúnmén Dance〉
The North Star governs the Mystic Altar,
the sacrifices of the Northern Land are held at the Round Hall.
The dark jade tablet is prepared overnight, bathed in orchid water,
the virtue of the Kan trigram, with yin winds, wards off the cold.
The musical pitch is about to turn, ending the cycle,
the faint yang energy stirs the fine springs.
The pipes are still tuned to the yin bamboo,
the sound has not yet entered the spring strings.
Awaiting the remaining days to send off the calendar,
then we shall tread upon blessings in this year.
○ Same as above.
"Dance to Accompany the Emperor"
The earth begins to split,
the rainbow begins to hide.
Wearing dark jade,
residing in the dark hall.
Bathing in the fragrance of huì,
washing in orchid-scented water.
The gourd vessels are pure,
the spring water fragrant.
Ascend to accompany him,
blessings without end.
The lord is joyful,
this music brings peace.
○ Same as above.
"Songs of the Zhōu Ancestral Temple" Twelve Pieces
"Huángxià: The Emperor Enters the Temple Gate"
Solemn and pure is the ancestral temple,
lofty and steep are the inner doors.
The tilted vessel warns against fullness,
the golden man cautions against speech.
The yìngyìn drums hang,
the chóngyá stands adorned with feathers.
Steps change as songs ascend,
the courtyard teems with symbolic dances.
Tranquil and secure are the ritual settings,
bright and clear are the pure offerings.
The spring sturgeon first appears,
new duckweed is offered first.
Reverently entering the chamber,
solemnly taking position.
Treading with sorrow,
not due to cold.

Zhāoxià: Inviting the Deities
"Zhāoxià: Inviting the Deities"
Forever upholding the martial deeds of ancestors,
hidden blessings, spirits long-lasting.
The dragon chart heralds revolution,
the phoenix calendar returns to prosperity.
Merit shifts to the upper realms,
virtue shines in the central yang.
The pure temple is solemn,
the fierce tiger stands resplendent.
The melody lofty as the Great Xià,
the harmony matching the flourishing Táng.
The sacrificial animals cleansed,
the artemisia blend fragrant.
Harmonious bells arrive,
the egrets come soaring.
Forever spreading across ten thousand states,
thus setting an example for all directions.

"Huángxià: The Vessel Enters, the Emperor Ascends the Steps."
The auspicious year discerns the day,
aligning with the turtle's words above.
Presenting the wine, receiving the array,
coming to the court, swiftly rushing.
Carved grain adorns the jiǎ,
kingfisher feathers support the zūn.
Reverence exhausted thus,
respectfully performing the fanning.
