“Letter of Thanks to Prince Zhào for the Gift of Pheasants”
Summer pheasants fly in autumn,
river pheasants call in spring ravines.
The guest of Zhōngmóu County,
thus gets to sit and watch;
the wife of Minister Jiǎ,
must already be smiling.
I gratefully consume from the central kitchen,
served to this humble guest.
Mountains and rivers stretch far,
my mouth and belly know your kindness.
○From *Yìwén Lèijù*, scroll 90.
“Forty-Four Imitation Linked Pearls”
I have heard that the talent to order heaven and earth,
the strength to uproot mountains and span seas,
valor in battle swifter than gales,
strategies born from one’s own breast,
cutting the scales of giant whales,
severing the wings of flying tigers—
thus with one rage, the feudal lords fear,
and dwelling in peace, the world rests.
I have heard that Xiāo Hé and Cáo Shěn assisted governance,
relying on heroic plans;
Lǔ and Wèi charging ahead,
borrowing awe-inspiring might.
Thus at the Huángchí assembly,
they could contend for supremacy among lords;
with the Hónggōu covenant,
they could divide the world in half.
I have heard that to unravel the knot of the great boar,
and block the source of the long serpent,
one must make robes for a thousand miles,
and lick blood at the camp gate.
Thus to break a siege of a hundred miles,
one uses a single stratagem of Chén Píng;
to ally a state of a thousand chariots,
requires but one word from Jì Lù.
I have heard that gaining the worthy lies herein,
without wielding blades;
with excellent aides and limbs,
no need to discuss adaptation.
Thus with Qū Yuán as chariot companion,
the feudal lords lifted the siege of Fāngchéng;
with Gān Mù as minister,
the world saw no war in Xīhé.
I have heard that when Hándān was already in peril,
they only thought of Mǎ Fú;
when Jì City was lost,
they vainly employed Jīng Kē.
Thus a bamboo staff to support the crumbling,
cannot right the stone of Wǔdān;
reed ashes to shrink the waters,
cannot save the river at Xuānfáng.
I have heard that ants burrowing against a spring,
know not of distant plans;
swallows nesting on a tent,
how can they endure long?
Thus when a great hall is already ablaze,
one cannot douse it with tears;
when a long river bursts its banks,
one cannot stem it with hands.
I have heard that glib-tongued chatter,
marketplace bustle,
some advance with reed-like flattery,
some topple others with cunning deceit.
Thus when Zǐgòng was sent as envoy,
five capitals fell into turmoil;
when Zhāng Yí was employed,
the six states engaged in vertical and horizontal schemes.
I have heard that planning and counsel must be practiced,
flexibility and adaptation require skill,
sometimes adding stoves in Qí,
or lying beneath Yān’s walls.
Thus the troops at Jǐngxíng,
were like goose feathers meeting fire;
the soldiers at Chángpíng,
like autumn grass struck by frost.
I have heard that where the millet grows lush,
the nobleman feels the sorrow of collapse and chaos;
where the wheat sprouts tenderly,
the gentleman grieves leaving his state.
Thus when Jiànzhāng Palace sways low and high,
one can no longer gaze upon the Bà riverbank;
when Déyáng sinks into ruin,
one cannot again approach Yǎnshī.
I have heard that markets and courts shift and trade,
mountains and rivers stretch afar.
Thus where foxes and hares now dwell,
once stood Jiànshǐ Palace;
where thorns pierce the sky,
once lay the gardens of Chángzhōu.
I have heard that heaven repeatedly sends calamity,
collapse and chaos abound,
vainly thinking of discussing swords,
only hearing of sleeping on spear-shafts.
Thus even with Liú Kūn’s heroic plans,
he knew not how to save himself;
even with Zǔ Tì’s fervent spirit,
he barely managed to cross the river.
I have heard that Gǔlín stretches far,
Cāngwú does not follow,
only tung trees and kudzu vines,
no markers, no tombs.
Thus even pearls bright as sun and moon,
avail not against the fire of Lí Mountain;
the strings and pipes of Sparrow Terrace,
gaze emptily upon the pines of Xīlíng.
I have heard that thunder startles beasts and drives them to flee,
lightning flashes and fierce winds howl,
they traverse mountain passes and fortresses,
and sweep across rivers and lakes.
Thus the shape of the city walls lies like a crescent moon,
the formations of troops spread out like clouds—
these are not scattered soldiers of the Green Forest,
but rebels from Líshān.
I have heard of eternal partings at the Great Wall,
and separations in life at Hángǔ Pass,
the sorrow of the widow in Liáodōng,
the weeping of the bereaved wife in Dàijùn.
Thus moved by flowing grief,
the wall of Qǐliáng crumbled once more;
where tears were shed,
the bamboo of Xiānglíng eventually changed its hue.
I have heard that three generations of warfare
are not a legacy to bequeath;
scheming across generations
must end in misfortune.
Thus, Commandant Lǐ, weathered by frost and wind,
ascended Lánshān only to exhaust his arrows;
Lù Píngyuán, with his lofty spirit,
climbed Héqiáo only to find his path cut off.
I have heard that wandering souls do not return,
phosphorescent fires fly by night,
sometimes meeting soldiers on night hunts,
or ghosts perishing in empty pavilions.
Thus, in the wind and rain of the Shèshēng Barracks,
wronged souls often appear;
in the gloom and chill of Guǎnghàn Commandery,
nighttime weeping is especially common.
I have heard that on the borders of Jiāng and Huáng, where warhorses roam,
and in Yān and Yǐng, where storms rage,
some depart never to return,
others wander far with no set return.
Thus, beneath Zhānghuá Tower,
there must be a terrace for longing for a son;
beside Yúnmèng Marsh,
there should be many stones of wives gazing into the distance.
I have heard of separations in life without resentment,
affections severed midway,
vainly thinking of lotuses rising from the water,
never again the swirling snow in the returning wind.
Thus, while drinking in the tower,
Lǜzhū went forth and never returned;
singing sad songs within the tent,
Yújī bid an eternal farewell.
I have heard that those who govern as shepherds
hold the lives of the people in their hands;
and when they pass from this world,
they also sway the hearts of all under heaven.
Thus, when one horse gallops,
not a single hair remains unmoved;
when one boat capsizes,
not a single thing fails to sink.
I have heard that under severe frost’s descent,
nothing escapes its withering touch;
when tall forests fall,
nothing is left unshaken.
Thus, once the Chǔ moat is filled,
wandering fish have nowhere to rely;
when the Wú palace has burned,
where shall returning swallows nest?
I have heard that those famed among the Eight Paragons
were harmed by the faction of eunuchs;
those wise as the Three Heroes
perished by the schemes of women.
Thus, the flood-dragon of Hóngzé
could thwart the long-starved tiger;
the ants of Pínggāo
could bring down the dragon stranded out of water.
I have heard that Wú ships and Shǔ boats
cannot float without water;
bows painted red and green
cannot shoot without strings.
Thus, the crane in its cage
can never hope to spread its six wings;
the worn-out horse
no longer holds the value of a thousand gold.
I have heard that when the spirit is bent and oppressed,
depressed and unable to soar,
it may suddenly feel the world’s indifference,
or grieve for those unlike itself.
Thus, the waters of lamentation
uniquely form springs of resentment;
the clouds touched by sorrow
are especially filled with mournful air.
I have heard of exiles bearing white feathers,
banished to Fánglíng,
leaving home and parting from their villages,
clutching their chests in bitter regret.
Thus, when Wú Qǐ left Xīhé,
tears streamed down his face;
when Jīng Kē parted from Yān’s market,
he was overwhelmed with grief.
I have heard of General Lián’s guesthouse,
and Minister Zhái’s lofty gate—
fullness and emptiness shift in an instant,
how then speak of noble and base!
Thus, of lifelong friends,
only Guàn Fū did not depart;
of the guests at his gate,
only Rén Ān remained.
I have heard of holding the jade tablet to serve Chǔ,
and scholars detained in Qín;
the traveler from Jìnyáng longing to return home,
the minister stranded in Línzī.
Thus, even when kin and friends gather,
one cannot help but feel sorrowful longing;
even when separated by mountains and rivers,
one cannot help but be moved by wind and moon.
I have heard that by the age of fifty,
one’s youthful passions have long faded,
and sorrow can wound a person—
hence such grief.
Thus, like the jiāoràng tree,
it is half-dead yet said to live;
like the wútóng tree,
though remnants of life remain, it is as good as dead.
I have heard that autumn’s essence
brings melancholy and self-pity—
Gěng Gōng’s sorrow at Shūlè,
Bān Chāo’s longing for Jiǔquán.
Thus, Hán Fēi, a guest in Qín,
found no way to avoid slander;
Lord Xìnlíng, dwelling in Zhào,
yearned for home for many years.
I have heard that even in tattered clothes,
one who knows fate does not grieve;
eating but once in ten days,
if timeless, what shame is there?
Thus, the enterprise of the Unadorned King
belongs to the poor of the Eastern Gate;
the lords of Gūzhú
were truly starving scholars of the Western Hills.
I have heard that lacking learning in one’s heart
is like having no coin in hand;
the learning of today
rarely produces worthies.
Thus, Gāo Fèng of Fúfēng
abandoned his wheat without cause;
Nìng Yuè of Zhōngmóu
toiled in vain, sleepless.
I have heard that in a village of ten households,
loyalty and trustworthiness can be found;
within five paces,
fragrant virtue may be recorded.
Thus, the dried clam of Rìnán
still holds the bright moon pearl;
the dead tree at Lóngmén
yet embraces the melody of “Xiánchí.”
I have heard that a height of a hundred feet
is built upon nine layers of earth;
a weight of a thousand jūn
hangs from a single branch.
Thus, to cut a tiger’s tail is not perilous,
to wound a dragon’s scale is not yet dangerous.
I have heard that dwelling among orchids or in foul fish
depends on what one is accustomed to;
white feathers and plain silk
take on whatever dye they are dipped in.
Thus, though gold’s nature is solid,
when placed in a sword it becomes lethal;
though water’s virtue is calm,
when stirred by wind it turns treacherous.
I have heard that the yùzhāng tree, after seven years,
perishes amid lush grass;
fragrant orchids across nine wǎn
sink into secluded valleys.
Thus, to seek what is genuine,
in Jìnyáng there is artemisia that buries itself;
to appreciate its sound,
in Wú Pavilion there is bamboo long withered.
I have heard that using a bright mirror to steam food
is not its proper use;
using the Gānjiàng sword to mend shoes
is especially lamentable.
Thus, one with spirit enough to soar through clouds
should not end as a mere cavalry officer;
one with talent fit to assist a king
should not be exiled straight to Chángshā.
I have heard that where power converges,
and authority is borrowed,
one can surely catch the wind and seize shadows,
or confront tigers and cross rivers barehanded.
Thus, lightly as a goose feather sinks in water,
heavily as a boulder rides the waves.
I have heard that a resolute spirit is hard to oppose,
yet it does not rely on the strength to lift a cauldron;
a heroic bearing is naturally courageous,
and does not depend on raising the city gate bar.
Thus, when Cáo Guì ascended the altar,
the fields of Wènyáng were swiftly returned;
when Xiàng Rú glared at the pillar,
the jade of many cities was restored.
I have heard that the curled plant does not die,
so who must have a heart?
The banana plant grows on its own,
thus we know it has no joints.
Therefore, when snails and clams find a path,
they fear it differs from the Black Dragon’s abyss;
when sparrows and rats share the same end,
it should not be the Cinnabar Cave.
I have heard that the heights of Běimáng,
the ruler of Wèi could not level;
the struggle of the Gǔ and Luò rivers,
the king of Zhōu could not alter.
Thus, what virtue did the Foolish Old Man possess,
that he shouldered his shovel and moved the mountain?
What bird was the Jīngwèi,
that it wished to carry stones to fill the sea?
I have heard that if a noble man lacks the proper way,
he cannot possess wealth;
if he forgets his poverty,
he cannot be ashamed of his food.
Thus, Yán Huí with his gourd for drinking,
esteemed Qìng Fēng’s jade cup;
Zǐsī with his silver pendant,
admired Yú Gōng’s Chuíjí jade.
I have heard that when water is agitated,
its source becomes turbid;
when a tree is worm-eaten,
its roots will be uprooted.
Thus, in Yánnián’s household,
they anticipated sweeping the graves;
in the Yángshé clan,
they foresaw the extermination of the family.
I have heard of grinding the lips and mouth,
greasing the teeth,
spreading poison with the wind,
blowing sand toward shadows.
Therefore, respect them and keep your distance—
the jackal has five offspring;
alas, how fearsome—
the ghost has a whole cart.
I have heard that an empty boat does not provoke,
and virtuous conduct has no worries;
loyalty and trust are the zither and lute,
benevolence and righteousness are the kitchen.
Thus, following Zhuāngzǐ,
all things become minute of themselves;
returning to Lǎozǐ,
all existence becomes nonexistent.
I have heard of halting at the three passes,
the Great Wall with drooping wings,
both detained and wandering,
neither talent nor wisdom.
Thus, mooring the boat at Wūjiāng,
knowing there is no road to return;
the white goose carrying a letter,
certain there is no home to send it to.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 771.
“Letter from the Heir of the Marquis of Shànghuáng to His Wife”
“Letter from the Heir of the Marquis of Shànghuáng to His Wife”
In the past, even immortals practicing guidance exercises
still marked the three autumns;
the goddess about to comb her hair,
still awaited the ninth day.
Never has the dragon flown from the sword case,
or the crane parted from the lute terrace,
without bearing resentment and sorrow in heart,
hearing the ape and shedding tears.
I am not from Xīnshì,
where can I seek home?
Parting differs from Hándān,
how then should I know the way?
I imagine looking at my reflection in the mirror,
surely not without holding back tears;
outside the railing, about to pick flowers,
yet still smiling together.
Sharing the cup within the tent,
removing the fan before the bed,
these are indeed not to be thought of,
when can they be remembered?
You should learn from the sea god,
following the tide and wind to come and go;
do not be like the Weaving Maid,
waiting for the river to be filled to meet.
○From *Yìwén Lèijù*, volume 32.
“Preface to the Collected Works of the Duke of Zhào”
I have privately heard that when Píngyáng struck stones,
the valleys harmonized with it;
when the Great Yǔ blew the bamboo flute,
the wind and clouds were stirred by it.
Compared to those who contain and express spiritual nature,
modulate and elevate literary energy,
subtly transforming the “Spring Sunshine,”
reflecting light like the white sun,
how can they be spoken of in the same breath?
The Pillar of State, Duke of Zhào, when he speaks it becomes discourse,
when he takes up the brush it forms chapters,
unrestrained manner overflowing,
fresh sentiments stirring,
wind and clouds vying to fly,
fish and dragons each transforming.
Compared to jade tablets,
the assembly at Túshān is myriad-layered;
likened to clouds and mist,
the cliffs of Chìchéng are a thousand fathoms high.
His writing partakes of celestial phenomena,
immediately entering the books of the Office of Astronomy;
his rhythm involves silk and paulownia,
all returning to the observatory of the Director of Music.
Speaking of its grandeur,
it is like the roc rising halfway to the sky;
speaking of its fineness,
it is like the wren nesting on a mosquito’s eyelash.
How could it merely be like the blazing dawn,
where Zēngchéng embraces the light of sun and moon;
or the flaming flight at night,
where the Southern Dipper touches the aura of the dragon!
In the past, Qū Yuán and Sòng Yù
began with profound sorrow and lament;
Sū Wǔ and Lǐ Líng
were born in an age of separation.
From the end of the Jiàn’ān era of Wèi to the Tàikāng era of Jìn onward,
the carving of insects and seal script—
their style changed three times.
Everyone claimed to hold the pearl of the spiritual snake,
to embrace the jade of Jīngshān.
The Duke deliberated upon the *Elegantiae* and *Odes*,
harmonizing the pitch pipes.
If his words deviated from the proper sections,
then the Qūtái would not heed them;
if his sounds stopped at casual strumming,
then the National Academy would not accept them.
Thus he became the pillar and beam of the literary garden,
the crown and leader of the forest of letters,
the *Great Elegantiae* supporting the wheel,
the Lesser Mountain bearing the canopy.
○From *Yìwén Lèijù*, volume 55.
From *Chūxué Jì*, volume 21.
“Biography of Qiū Nǎidūn Chóng, Grand General with Imperial Credential, Duke of Guǎnghuà Commandery of Zhōu”
“Biography of Qiū Nǎidūn Chóng, Grand General with Imperial Credential, Duke of Guǎnghuà Commandery of Zhōu”
Chóng
was a man of Xiàoràng Village, Guǎngyì Township, Gǔchéng County, Dài Commandery, Héng Province.
In ancient times, when Shòuqiū established the state,
twelve people were granted surnames;
when Píngyáng promoted the worthy,
sixteen clans ascended the court.
How much more so when great lightning encircled the pivot,
and a shooting star entered the Pleiades,
branches divided and sources separated,
could the trunk not continue to flourish?
Emperor Dàowǔ of Wèi, with his epoch-making grand strategy,
watered his horses at the Hé and Luò rivers,
with ten brothers,
divided into ten surnames.
Distinguishing the winds and blowing the pitch pipes,
the Qiū clan was one of them.
His fifth-generation ancestor Miǎo
was General of Agile Cavalry, Palace Attendant with Equal Honors, Duke of Yíngqiū Commandery.
At that time, the heavenly way inclined to the northwest,
and he already possessed strategic planning;
the horse’s head turned southeast,
truly relying on his assistance and support.
Therefore, he was enfeoffed with the name,
and it became his granted clan.
Compared to the Elder of Nángōng,
there is indeed a connection.
The lineage is like the Music Master,
not without standards.
His great-grandfather Shuāngguǐ
was General with Imperial Credential, General of Agile Cavalry, Minister of Education, Governor of Qīng and Yǎn Provinces, Duke Wénzhāo of Fànyáng.
At the beginning of the Luò divination,
he mounted his horse to govern the state;
at the start of his promotion,
he ascended the locust tree to discuss the Way.
In life, he held a separate seat in the military palace;
in death, he was matched in sacrifice in the pure chamber.
His wife, née Wáng of Tàiyuán,
came from a family of generals for three generations,
and dukes for four generations,
a great lineage of the altars of soil and grain,
a noble clan of bells and tripods.
She was joined in marriage,
a match of Qín and Jìn.
He esteemed purity and tranquility in governance,
and integrity and clarity in law.
People could not bear to betray him,
nor could officials bear to deceive him.
By nature, he did not drink wine,
and had no particular cravings or desires.
Profound as a deep moat and high wall,
neither joy nor anger showed on his face.
His writings always used proper words,
and his music only elegant melodies.
Benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and moderation—
these were the things to which he devoted his heart.
For silk scrolls and fine texts,
he cherished and enjoyed them endlessly.
Nowadays, with fortifications rising on all sides,
there is still the humiliation of ministers and nobles;
with war drums never ceasing,
generals and commanders are still troubled with strategies.
Speaking of his hatred and shame,
he only wished to charge through deadly battlefields;
thinking of repaying his country,
he did not begrudge his body fattening the wilderness.
If only Heaven would grant him more years,
and the times bestow upon him peace and blessings,
then loyal and steadfast deeds—
these, sir, you may take from him.
Briefly recording the main points,
I present them to the upright historian.
○From Wényuàn Yīnghuá, volume 792.
“Reply on the Relocation of the Market”
In the past, even Zhāng Kǎi, a great Confucian scholar,
still moved the market of Hóngnóng;
and Yíguān, with his exquisite seal script,
still attracted guests to the wine shop.
How much more so for one whose virtue encompasses Xún and Zhōu,
and whose reputation surpasses Liáng and Chǔ.
Scholars who admire his style and righteousness
raise their sleeves to form a curtain;
those who lie before his carriage or turn back his wheels
jostle shoulder to shoulder.
Thus, the place where Wáng Chōng once browsed the market
has been moved far out to the desolate outskirts;
and the site where Shí Bāo once sold iron
now overlooks a cliff’s edge.
Our sage ruler’s virtue is humble and modest,
yet he has not forgotten the clamor and bustle.
He wishes for the flute players and dancing cranes
to return to their old marketplace;
and for the fortune-tellers and mutton butchers
to leave the new market gates.
But the trading crowds are fond of staying,
and the people of Bīn and Qí are hard to disperse.
○From Yìwén Lèijù, volume 65.
From Chūxué Jì, volume 24.
“Dispatch to the Officials of Héyáng in Qí”
On the twenty-seventh day of the fourth month in the fourth year of the Tiānhé era of Zhōu,

the Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Chariot and Horse General, Equal in Honor to the Three Ministers, Grand Governor, and Commander of Shǎnxī Prefecture dispatches to the officials of Héyáng in Qí:
Since the drums of war have fallen silent on the borders,
and beacon fires have been extinguished in the frontier regions,
the practice of righteousness and deference
has not lasted even a full month.
Sincerity in admonishing against theft
immediately encounters hidden schemes.
Therefore, the army with its wooden shields
must act when the time is right,
to secure its own territory,
not to seek confrontation or defense.
Although dust and turmoil briefly arose,
banners and drums did not encroach.
The five generals have already returned,
and the twin peaks of Xiáo are calm again.
Having just received the court’s decree,
we obtained your dispatch,
ordering us to accept the surrendered city
and have your troops return with their equipment.
We presume your border officials
have already received their instructions.
Since this return has been arranged,
we must promptly take possession.
We do not know on what day
the garrison troops may be sent away?
We entrust this to the envoy,
hoping for a swift reply.
The alliance remains unbroken,
and neighboring territories maintain good relations.
Looking out over the plains,
we feel greatly fortunate indeed.
Hence this dispatch.
○From Wényuàn Yīnghuá, volume 650.
On the tenth day of the eleventh month in the fourth year of the Tiānhé era of Zhōu,
Liáng Xīn, Chief Clerk of the Shǎnzhōu Commandery, dispatches to the officials of Héyáng in Qí:
Since exchanging jade tokens and continuing correspondence,
opening passes and removing barriers,
we truly thought that above, swords would be melted down,
and at Shānyáng, horses would rest.
Therefore, in receiving guests,
we may have been negligent with heavy gates.
But your former border officials,
secretly engaged in thievery,
with the ruler acting one way and ministers another,
the superiors harmonious but the subordinates discordant.
Our state, with the border regions unsettled,
must strengthen its defenses.
The Grand Marshal, Duke of Qí,
the emperor’s younger brother,
Commander of the Central Army,
skilled in the strategies of Sūn and Wú,
driving forth like tigers and leopards,
raised troops during the farming off-season,
different in principle from the city guards,
patrolled our borders,
but did not turn back to Yùn.
Just as the troops were packing up,
the vanguard banners had already turned back,
but your country’s soldiers, failing to guard,
with trailing dust from the rear,
caused an encounter.
Before the flags were fully raised on the ramparts,
and before five commands were given,
beside the city of Ānyè,
they were first startled by seven ambushes.
In the clash of blades at that time,
some fattened the wilderness.
The captured general from your side,
Xiàzhōu Governor Liáng Lǎo and his chieftains,
we now return to you.
Their homeland is not far,
do not let them remain long as guests.
Horses, donkeys, armor, and weapons—
we list them in detail,
and your border officials should receive them accordingly.
Lacking the will to fight from the start,
we did not engage in prolonged combat,
yet this dust of conflict arose—
who is to blame for it?
Hence this dispatch.
○From Wényuàn Yīnghuá, volume 650.
“Dispatch Detaining the Envoy”
On the first day of the month in such-and-such year,
such-and-such official informs the assigned prefecture or commandery:
Originally, we intended to send that envoy on his way,
but since his entry into our territory,
auspicious national events have been near,
and from autumn until winter,
we have not had the chance to extend proper hospitality.
Moreover, the Wolf Star marks the state,
and severe frost has already given warning;
crossing the turbulent rivers and Jì River,
the long journey is bitterly cold.
Now, as the year turns anew,
and the three beginnings herald celebration,
with jade tokens filling the court,
and Chinese and foreign envoys crowding the carriages,
we wish to observe the grand ceremonies,
and share in this joyous festivity.
With the warmth of spring already stirring,
and kindness spreading to all states,
we shall then send the envoy on his way, accompanied,
to forever strengthen neighborly amity.
Hence this dispatch.
○From Wényuàn Yīnghuá, volume 650.
“Eulogies on Paintings of Ancient Sage Emperors and Famous Worthies,” Twenty-Seven Pieces
“Huángdì Meets Guǎngchéngzǐ”
“Huángdì Meets Guǎngchéngzǐ”
Cultivating himself in the Purple Palace,
he inquired about governance at Qīngqiū.
The dragon lake submerged the tripod,
the cinnabar furnace let pearls flow.
Clouds rise and rain falls,
leaves wither before autumn.
The ultimate Way must be pursued to the limit,
and long life may be sought.

From Wényuàn Yīnghuá, volume 780.

“In Praise of the Crane”
“In Praise of the Crane”
In the second year of Wǔchéng, spring, second month,
A pair of white cranes flew and gathered in the Shànglín Garden.
General Zhèng Wěi set up bows and nets,
And captured them both.
Their six pinions already broken,
Their paired hearts both full of grief,
They looked at each other and cried mournfully.
The lone male died first,
The widowed wife faced his shadow,
And the Son of Heaven took pity.
I, Xìn, presented a memorial at the palace steps,
And was immediately commanded to compose this praise:
From distant Jiǔgāo they gathered,
From the Three Mountains they returned.
At Huátíng, a parting cry,
At Luòpǔ, an immortal’s flight.
Unaware of the parting arrow,
They first met with captivity.
The cage shatters moon-like feathers,
The arrow shreds frost-white robes.
At the frontier pass, their remaining calls,
At the mountain gate, bearing their old name.
Southward wandering to the Xiāng River,
Eastward entering Liáochéng.
Among clouds they fly, desiring to dance,
As dew falls, they cry out first.
Six pinions broken and shattered,
Nine gates tightly closed.
Looking at each other, crying mournfully,
Liver and heart severed.
On the pine, eternal sorrow,
In the qín, everlasting parting.
○From Yìwén Lèijù, scroll 90.

With Preface
“Inscription and Preface for the Buddhist Niche at Màijī Cliff in Tiānshuǐ Commandery, Qín Province”
Màijī Cliff is
A famous mountain at the base of Lǒng,
A numinous peak west of the river.
Its high peaks seek the clouds,
Its deep valleys are boundless.
Compared to Vulture Peak,
Its traces retreat through three dhyānas;
Likened to the Crane’s Cry,
It emptily flies through the six jiǎ.
Bird paths suddenly end,
Goat trails sometimes break.
Clouds like a roc’s wings,
Suddenly hang from the sky;
Trees like cassia blossoms,
Turn and can brush the sun.
Thus, flying monks’ staffs came from afar,
Alms-bowls crossed from distant lands,
They cleared the mountains and carved caves,
Lushly making a pure land.
Bowing to the Lamp King in the stone chamber,
They borrowed the driving wind;
Paying homage to the Flower-head in the mountain niche,
They relied on controlling cranes.
The Grand Governor Lǐ Yǔnxìn,
Rooted in past cultivation,
Deeply awakened to the Dharma-gate,
Then on the southern cliff of the wall,
Laddered clouds and carved a path,
Reverently made seven Buddha niches for his deceased father.
As if carving sandalwood,
As if working water-jade.
Serene as the full moon,
Shining like blue lotuses.
Shadows appear on Sumeru,
Fragrance is heard in Trāyastriṃśa.
In such a dusty wilderness,
Still opens a hall for preaching the Dharma;
Like that Fragrant Mountain,
Again faces the Buddha of peaceful abode.
In the past, the Tathāgata sought blessings,
There was the Sūtra of Repaying Kindness;
The Bodhisattva left home,
There were offerings of remembering kin.
Daring to follow this meaning,
I therefore compose the inscription, saying:
The land is anchored, lush and winding;
Its foundations reach the lofty zenith.
The stone pass ascends tenfold;
The bronze bridge rests nine times.
Cliffs stretch a hundred fathoms across;
Pines stand a thousand fathoms straight.
The moon borrows a path;
The sun turns its wings.
They hewed through mountains, clearing the way;
Pierced caves and spanned ridges.
Entangled like the starry river;
Swirling with light and shadow.
Cliffs are layered with sutra texts;
Grottoes repeat the Buddha’s image.
Carved wheels in moonlit halls;
Engraved mirrors in floral chambers.
Horizontal inscriptions on stone walls;
Hidden chiseling on mountain beams.
Thunder follows the Dharma drum;
Trees accumulate celestial fragrance.
Springs gurgle in jade valleys;
Dust is blown from stone beds.
Gathering numinous truth in lodges;
Hiding immortal records in libraries.
Fungal caves and autumn rooms;
Sandalwood groves and spring milk.
Water valleys with silver sand;
Mountain towers with stone pillars.
Different ridges share the same clouds;
The same peak parts the rain.
Remnants of Jìchéng customs;
Old traditions of Héxī.
Water sounds murmur softly;
Mountain forms loom grandly.
Dharma clouds abide forever;
Wisdom sun is endless.
When earthly realms are mustard-seed gone,
The celestial palace remains unchanged.
○From Wényuàn Yīnghuá, scroll 785.
“Inscription on the Righteous Valley of Zhōngnán Shān” with Preface
“Inscription on the Righteous Valley of Zhōngnán Shān” with Preface
In the second year of Bǎodìng of the Zhōu dynasty,
the cyclical year being Rénwǔ,
on the first day of the seventh month, Jǐsì,
the Grand Minister, the Duke of Jìn, ordered the valley of the stone pass to be excavated,
to bring down timber from the southern mountains.
The Duke, in rectifying human relations
and broadly achieving myriad merits,
amidst the leisure of harmonizing governance,
perused mountain classics,
considering that in Zhōngnán and Dūnwù,
where sun and moon are obscured,
there are chūn, gàn, guā, bǎi, yī, tóng, zǐ, and qī trees,
accumulated over ages—
what does it not possess?
Thus he consulted officers of mountains and marshes,
and summoned craftsmen of forests and game.
Eastward, emerging from Lántián,
it controls the Bà and rides the Chǎn;
westward, connecting to Zǐwǔ,
it holds the Jīng and floats the Wèi.
Tributaries branch into eight streams;
currents divide into nine valleys.
Bronze bridges with four pillars;
stone passes with twin openings.
Verdant splendor at spring gates,
canals reflecting each other.
Green locusts in autumn markets,
boats and oars interlinked.
Stored, it becomes massed clouds;
released, it becomes traveling rain.
Blue oxen and patterned zǐ trees,
white cranes and steadfast pines,
transported to build palaces,
raising these cloud-like dwellings.
Thousands of brackets support halls;
dragon heads touch the clouds.
Ten thousand qǐng of sparse seedlings,
cicadas sing for double harvests.
River deities yield virtue;
mountain spirits follow in reverence.
How could it compare to moving stones at Gānquán,
merely connecting to the palace of Yuèyáng;
or channeling water at Gǔshuǐ,
directly encircling the walls of Jīnyōng?
The task was not laborious,
yet the achievement is truly great.
The state rich, the people prosperous,
it shall be told for a thousand years.
Through merit, establishing deeds,
I dare inscribe on the mountain slope.
The inscription says:
Vast emptiness floats above;
towering peaks anchor below.
Cliffs stand a thousand zhàng;
peaks stretch ten thousand rèn.
Cassia moon perilously suspended;
wind and springs echo emptily.
Carriages climb ridge slopes;
spades lift at cloud roots.
Eight streams divide and flow;
nine valleys share a source.
Northward, embracing Tóngjǐng;
southward, floating to Shímén.
Modeled after the hexagram Dà Zhuàng,
measured by a hundred spans.
Vast and layered, ninefold;
winding and turning, a thousand pillars.
Cassia rafters surging over waves;
cypress beams dripping with rain.
Clearing streams, settling valleys;
felling fruits, breaking branches.
Deeds equal to clearing woods;
merit matching channeling rivers.
○From Chūxué Jì, scroll 5.
From Wényuàn Yīnghuá, scroll 787.

“Inscription on Yùzhàng Shān”
The jade tent is vast;
Kūnshān repels magpies.
Leaves gathered form curtains;
clouds joined rise as canopies.
Jade tablets hard to move;
golden flowers never fall.
Hermits play the qín;
immortals watch board games.
Cliffs retain ancient tripods;
hearths gather fresh thorns.
Boiling stones begin to soften;
refining elixirs nears completion.
Mulberry fields often change;
sea waters frequently fill.
Long have I heard phoenix melodies;
forever listen to xiāo sounds.

“Inscription on Chuītái Shān”

though mountains yield bamboo.
Qín xiāo summoned phoenixes;
this peak holds the truth.
Green locusts shun the sun;
vermilion grass heralds dawn.

“Inscription on Wàngměirén Shān”
Gāotáng blocked by stones;
Luòpǔ lacks a boat.
Where to gaze at each other?
A tower by the mountain side.
Peak named for five women;
stones called three lords.
More perilous than Dìfèi;
loftier than Tiānzhù.
Forbidden garden obliquely connects;

Songs heard among trees;
dances seen amid branches.
Perfectly facing the dressing table;

who comes not without autumn?

“Inscription on Zhìrén Shān”
Peaks span Crane Ridge;
waters learn from Dragon Ford.
Auspicious clouds, a single stretch;
immortal boys, a pair.
Third autumn, clouds thin;
ninth day, chill fresh.
True flowers briefly fall;
painted trees ever spring.
Horizontal stones by the steps;
flying eaves pillow the ridge.
Walls twined with vine sprouts;
windows frame bamboo shadows.
Chrysanthemums fall in autumn pools;
paulownias sparse by cold wells.
The benevolent find joy,
Inscription on the Bright Moon Mountain
The bamboo pavilion marks the peak,
Open on all sides to the void.
Precipitous cliffs, eaves soaring high,
Leaves fall, windows sparse and clear.
Looking at the rafters, a flute is there,
Facing the trees, no wind stirs.
Wind arises from the stone cave,
Clouds emerge from the mountain’s base.
Cranes cry on frosty mornings,
Gibbons call in autumn nights.
Dikes and bridges seem like weirs,
Wild paths resemble village lanes.
A boat lies moored beneath the dam,
Trees flank the ferry gate.
How different from the Huágài?
Who would recognize Táoyuán?

Inscription on the Walking Rain Mountain
Inscription on the Walking Rain Mountain
The mountain is named Walking Rain,
A land unlike the Yángtái Terrace.
Countless fair ladies are here,
Even goddesses would shy away.
Emerald curtains open at dawn,
Fresh makeup rises with the morn.
Trees reach into the bedside,
Flowers come before the mirror.
Grass green matches the gown’s hue,
Blossoms red rival the face.
As the new year chills depart,
In the first month, spring outings begin.
All shed their brocade cloaks,
And cast off crimson silks.
Heavenly threads vie with lotus roots,
Butterfly powder stirs the dust.
Creepers stretch across the path,
Willows bend low to greet passersby.
Who speaks of the Luò River’s shore,
With but a single river goddess?
○From Yìwén Lèijù, scroll 7.
From Wényuàn Yīnghuá, scroll 787.
Three Inscriptions on Blades
The Wind Earl blows the forge,
The Cloud Master refines the smelt.
Iron flames flow by day,
Golden essence descends by night.
Worth more than ten cities,
Fame surpassing a thousand steeds.
A thousand in gold for its tip,
Hundredfold tempering for its edge.
Light connects with the Dipper’s aura,
Flames stir the mountain spirits.
Patterns on its body ripple like water,
Its ancient blade gives birth to pearls.
The Dipper’s essence descends from afar,
Mountain spirits follow below.
Water patterns of a thousand curves,
Scales like a serpent, a hundred layers.
Whetstones from Yān gather its edge,
Waters from Shǔ open its锋芒.
Aura splits the light of day,
The ring forms a coiling dragon.
○From Wényuàn Yīnghuá, scroll 789.
Inscription in Remembrance of the Past, with Preface
In the year of Shètí,
When the stars dwell in Jiāndé,
Xiāo Yǒng, the late Marquis of Guānníng of Liáng, passed away.
Alas, how sorrowful!
When a man perishes,
It is not something metal or stone can alter;
When a scholar grieves,
Can there be a difference between spring and autumn?
The high tower has already crumbled,
At Jìxià, there are tears for the sound of the qin;
The brave man has departed once and for all,
South of Yān, there is sorrow for the striking of the zhù.
When Xiàng Yǔ rose at dawn in his tent,
When Lǐ Líng lingered at the crossroads,
When Hán Wángsūn was held hostage in Zhào,
When the Chǔ prince remained in Qín,
Even without the desolation of late autumn,
In those times, there was grief!
Moreover, when fish leaped in the armory,
It foretold the abandonment of armor;
When birds roosted at Díquán,
It presaged the omen of great floods.
When the stars marked Wú’s demise,
When Gēngchén saw Chǔ’s destruction.
When Marquis Jǐ departed forever,
And the Lord of Yǔ never returned.
Galloping across the plains and lowlands,
Parting forever at Huányuán.
Armor and robes were lost,
The royal vessel abandoned.
When the river overturned at Suānzǎo,
Catalpa and oak alike were swept away;
When the sea receded from Pénglái,
Fish, turtles, and dragons all perished.
Burning incense on the elevated road,
Could it summon the wandering soul?
Carrying wine in the imperial train,
Could it dispel the sorrowful air?
In autumn, orchids and foul weeds,
Though different in form, wither alike;
The lament of feathers, scales, and shells,
Though varied in sound, is equally mournful.
What is called Heaven?
It is but the azure ether;
What is called Earth?
It is merely clods of soil.
To resent such things,
How can it stir emotion?
A broken wing, maimed and torn,
Has no use for wind or storm;
Withered and fallen in spring,
It needs no frost or dew to hasten its end.
When the command tent was first opened,
Wise and talented men looked up with hope,
But after a year as a detainee,
Disciples took their leave.
As for bidding farewell to the east,
And departing forever for Xīlíng.
Carriages and horses of Shānyáng,
Gazed farewell at the suburban gate;
Guests of Yǐngchuān,
Mourned from afar along the pine-lined road.
At Jī Shūyè’s mountain courtyard,
Many willows still remain;
On Wáng Zǐyóu’s old path,
Only bamboo groves are left.
The burial ground of a noble scion,
Will become the palace of Chánglè;
The buried soul of a righteous man,
Is none other than a general’s tomb.
In the past, we shared joyful feasts,
Lingering amid breeze and moonlight,
Recalling a lifetime of memories,
Vividly before my eyes and heart.
And then, with wings drooping in Qínchuān,
A traveler stranded by passes and rivers,
Facing the sunset in the Valley of Sorrow,
Truly feeling the grief of existence.
Even while sipping fine wine,
I still think of the waters of Jiànyè;
Even with a qin in hand,
I long for the cranes of Huátíng.
To part again like this,
Alas, how profound the sorrow!
When the qilin dies, stars fall,
When the moon perishes, pearls grieve;
When the bottle is empty, the jar feels shame,
When the orchid burns, the iris sighs.
I only hope the bell sinks in the River of Virtue,
Yet its sound emerges from wind and clouds;
The sword lies buried in Fēngchéng,
Yet its aura remains between Ox and Dipper.
With tears, I remember the past,
And thus compose this inscription:
The wind and clouds above are somber,
the boat and ravine shift unseen.
Swiftly come the frost and dew,
the noble man is first imperiled.
Jì Hóu departed far,
Huái Wáng never returned.
The jade tree lies long buried,
its grace and charm now distant.
In Xún Bó’s old county,
Qìng Fēng’s remaining town,
a soul returns from ten thousand li,
but can it enter the Xiū Gate?
The tomb lies across the arsenal,
the mountain rests against Lúlóng.
Longing to return, the road is far,
no way to send the body back.
Only the geese that escort remain,
in vain the tall pines sway.
East of Pínglíng,
no more wútóng trees.
The sound of pines is soughing,
ever stirring the autumn wind.
In former times, noble and honored,
hand in hand, in speech and silence.
Entrusting feelings to Jī Kāng and Ruǎn Jí,
like wind and clouds, in harmony.
Wine flowed like the Shéng River,
warm to the end, yet restrained.
The morning sun sees the phoenix fall,
the great wilds mourn the qílín.
The fine city lies dense and still,
dwelling in exile in Qín.
At Shānyáng, seeing off,
only old friends remain.
The widow’s loom, the bereaved shuttle,
a lone phoenix, a solitary luán.
Deep in the chamber, night is still,
wind high, the moon cold.
This life is done,
when to cherish the past?
In the case, the strings are broken,
the neighbor’s flute is mournful.
Once it was the commander’s tent,
now it becomes a mourning curtain.
○From *Yìwén Lèijù*, scroll 34.
From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, scroll 790.
“Stele Inscription for the Scripture Repository of Wǔzhāng Temple in Hóngnóng Commandery, Shǎnzhōu”
I have heard that when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma,
it is like the sands of the Ganges, myriad upon myriad;
when the Bodhisattvas turn the wheel,
it is life after life, world after world.
How could it be limited to the Upadeśa,
the Geya, or the Sūtra alone!
Thus, the Hiraṇyavatī River,
the jīvitaputra tree,
the seven places and eight assemblies,
the three purities and four teachings,
leather and paper, bone and brush,
wooden leaves and mountain flowers—
what elephants could bear remains unborne,
what dragon treasuries hold remains inexhaustible.
Though silver caskets came east,
and golden banners turned south,
with Qín Jǐng distantly transmitting,
and Zhú Lán privately recording,
it is like obtaining a single pearl from the sea,
no less than a piece of jade from Kūnlún.
As for the Dharma cloud deeply stored,
the lion’s thunderous voice,
the Brahmin’s rebirth,
the Śrāvaka’s precepts,
the discourses of the arhats of the Snowy Mountains,
the Dharma of bodhi from Vulture Peak—
originally without limit,
how can it be fully expressed?
The Wǔzhāng Temple in Hóngnóng
is where Zhāng Yuángāo from Nányáng dwelled in this place.
In former times, families worth a thousand gold
were relocated to the five imperial tombs;
the great clans among the people
moved their households to the six commanderies—
such was their dispersal.
Yuángāo’s five sons
bore the legacy of his teachings.
Mastering the classics and discerning their aims,
all achieved renown;
entering the chamber, they shone with light,
each able to display virtue.
Moreover, they revered and upheld the wisdom tradition,
devoutly received the Dharma gate,
lived together as brothers,
and jointly donated their home to become a temple.
When the saṅghārāma was first established,
it was named “Wǔzhāng” after the five Zhāngs.
Thus we know that when a city was inhabited by Zhào Xìn,
it was still called Zhào Xìn’s city;
when a hall was entered by Xiāo Hé,
it was named Xiāo Hé’s hall.
Moreover, they spared no elephants or horses,
and gave away their robes and furs.
Spring gardens and willow paths
transformed into meditation groves;
the silkworm month and mulberry ferry
turned into waters of concentration.
Though Píngyú was prosperous,
how could it claim sole possession of the two dragons?
Though Fúfēng was most excellent,
it could not monopolize the fame of the five steeds.
The temple’s abbot, the Tripiṭaka Master Fǎyìng, and the village chief, Prefect of Luòzhōu Zhāng Lóng,
devoted wealth and practice as dāna,
exhausting body and mind.
They also transformed the villages and towns,
with several thousand monastics and lay followers,
reverently constructing all Dharma wheels,
completing over three hundred volumes.
Thunder-seal scripts and cloud-writings,
golden cords and jade labels,
they pared steamed chestnut tablets,
and bound sour jujube beads,
all entering the fragrant city,
sealed within the meditation pavilion.
Sitting in the hall, leaning on the railings—
this is no spirit of the Xiāng River;
green pods and purple calyxes—
enough to rival Prince Gōng’s hall.
With high palms gazing west,
the long river facing north,
tripod vapors ever float,
incense smoke always rises.
Windows and doors vast and open,
the wind of Lóngmén blows through all things;
beams and pillars lofty and towering,
bearing fruit like trees of the river’s source.
Monks gather like clouds,
not far from the city of Dūnhuáng;
fellow learners rush together,
converging more than the market of Huáyīn.
The two Shǎn regions once divided,
truly laid the foundation for royal transformation;
the two ridges now obstructed,
instead speed feathered dispatches.
Yú Gōng’s Qūchǎn horses,
mingle chaotically in the wind and dust;
Shào Bó’s sweet pear tree,
withers in the frost and dew.
Though capable of joint governance,
they have not sent the beast across the river;
beacon towers give warning,
truly disturbing the people moving through the pass.
Thus, when the Dharma King rules the world,
devas and humans discuss the Way,
drawing in the four streams,
encompassing the five fears,
so they can subdue resentment and hatred,
and dissolve the bonds of attachment.
The Dharma water as a bridge,
no longer faces the difficulty of Dǐzhù;
the tracks of the Fragrant Mountain,
are no longer the peril of Zhōngnán.
The Son of Heaven commanded me
to tentatively govern this region.
The ink stove not yet blackened,
Confucius’ mat not yet warm,
just as I arrived at the commandant’s domain,
the campaign of tower ships began.
Then, the southern wind not strong,
the northern route turned back;
the commander’s tent now opened,
the regional lord paused here.
The village elders and seniors,
still as before at this parting,
entrusted with this Dharma matter,
requested I compose this text.
Humbly, I exercise my emptiness,
to inscribe these words as follows:
In the land of Shèwèi,
in the garden of Qíhuán.
The ultimate realm of the Three Insights,
the profound source of the Eight Assemblies.
Debates compete along the river,
superior arguments contend in discourse.
Bōtí traversed eastward,
Qíyè translated southward.
Not emptiness but form,
transcending existence and non-existence, beyond words.
The enlightened rest here,
alone awakening from deep darkness.
Though the body is tethered like a horse,
the mind avoids leaping monkeys.
The meditation hall retreats from the moon,
the hall of righteousness soars with phoenixes.
Returning winds carry fragrant canopies,
reversed dew adorns pearl banners.
To the west, facing Dǐzhù,
to the east, backing Huányuán.
The river echoes at Yángxiá,
the mountains resound at Sūmén.
Soaring birds sing in melodies,
flowing streams strum with clamor.
Beasts remain after crossing the river,
old villages shift past the pass.
Once the capital’s domain,
now a frontier wall.
The city resembles Guǎngwǔ,
the land recalls Lóufán.
Beacon fires shine together,
elephants and horses flee singly.
Without bells, Jǔ is attacked,
with rain, Yuán is besieged.
Without support from all directions,
who resolves the three grievances?
Wind topples the earth’s pillars,
fire reaches heaven’s origin.
Silver hooks eternally firm,
golden records long preserved.
Sealing the lord’s horse-head,
attending to the southern frontier.
Following Yáng Pú’s words,
thanking Liú Kūn’s request.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, scroll 850.
“Stele Inscription for Prince Xiàn of Qí, Pillar of State of Zhōu”
In ancient times, Xuānyuán bestowed surnames,
upon fourteen individuals;
the Zhōu house first enfeoffed,
fifteen states.
Since then, inheriting foundations and continuing lineages,
preserving surnames and receiving clans,
though a sage arises but once in a millennium,
they remain of the same ancestral line for a hundred generations.
Thus we know that the former Eastern Capital,
was called the Yán-Hàn’s restoration;
the present Zhōu calendar,
is indeed Fēngdū’s revival.
The Duke, whose given name was Xiàn,
courtesy name Píhétū,
was from Wǔchuān in Héngzhōu.
In the Tàikāng era of Jìn,
he held Huánglóng;
at the beginning of Xiàochāng of Wèi,
he oversaw Xuāntú.
Tàizǔ, with the strength of a hundred and two lords,
divided the realm into three,
first ascending Hángǔ Pass,
greatly securing Hónggōu,
with achievements such as these,
he fulfilled his duty as a subject.
The Duke, endowed with heavenly grace,
was born to command the age,
descended from the spirit of Tàiyī,
under the constellation of Wénchāng.
With a pearl-like forehead, uniquely gifted,
a mountainous countenance displaying virtue,
his demeanor pure and cool,
his spirit lofty and transcendent,
he stirred the court,
illumined the palace gates.
Before reaching the age of losing baby teeth,
he already discussed affairs of the realm.
Some said:
“He is like a branch of the Ruòmù tree,
shading several states beside it;
like the long river’s straight course,
naturally flowing a thousand lǐ.
The windstorm seeks distance,
the light is about to rise.”
In the second year of Later Wèi,
he was enfeoffed as Duke of Fúchéng County,
at the age of five.
Rainbows filled the wilds,
overthrowing the lofty usurpers;
the yuèzhuó cried at Qí,
truly beginning the mandate of renewal.
The state, receiving the mandate and chart,
reverently upholding the calendar,
as the great wind first swept,
Chángshā was first enfeoffed.
In the first year of Zhōu,
he was advanced to Duke of Ānchéng Commandery,
with a fief of two thousand households,
and appointed Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, General of Agile Cavalry, and Excellency with Open Residence.
His open residence equaled Mǎ Jùn’s,
his rank matched the Six Ministers;
his agile cavalry equaled Liú Cāng’s,
his position surpassed the Three Excellencies.
The royal sons as walls of the city,
many among them felt ashamed.
In the second year of Wǔchéng,
he was appointed Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Great General, Commander of Military Affairs of Twenty-Four Provinces including Yì, Shòu, and Níng, and Governor of Yìzhōu,
changed enfeoffment to Duke of Qí,
with a fief of ten thousand households,
the Duke then being sixteen years old.
Wáng Wǔzǐ, as a senior general with open residence,
had not yet reached thirty;
Xún Zhōngláng, as commander of ten provinces,
was just past twenty.
Compared to the Duke,
they were already old.
Moreover, Yíngqiū faces the sea,
the city where Duke Huán of Qí received the sacrificial meat;
Mínshān guides the river,
the place where Emperor Wǔ of Hàn sought immortality.
If not like Zhàolíng and Gūzhú,
whose fame shook Chénlí,
how could one reach Mùlíng in the south,
or ascend Jīshí in the west?
Fortunately, there was no threat of the white tiger,
nor need for the covenant of the yellow dragon.
Qióngzuó trembled at his might,
Wēilú looked up to his virtue,
temples were built for him in life,
stones carved to extol his deeds.
Chéngdū had the sacrifices for Wén Wēng,
not during his lifetime;
Hànyáng had the stele for Zhūgě,
only after his death.
Compared to today,
how could they be spoken of in the same breath!
In the fourth year of the Bǎodìng era,
he joined the Grand Marshal, the Duke of Shǔ, in besieging the city of Jīnyōng.
When the army reached the banks of the Luò River,
the Guǎngwǔ camp fled in panic;
as the troops ascended Mount Máng,
the road to Héqiáo was severed.
The customs of the eight rivers,
the fame and profit of the five regions,
the iron markets and copper streets,
were all swept by wind and dust.
In the first year of the Tiānhé era,
he was summoned back
and appointed Acting Governor of Yōngzhōu.
With the brilliance of the sun and moon,
he wielded his authority to govern,
and the Qī and Jǔ rivers submitted,
while Jīng and Qí were pacified.
When the season of Shàoyáng prevailed,
oxen did not pant on the roads;
as Mid-Autumn arrived,
the people were unalarmed by floods.
In the second year,
he was appointed Grand Marshal,
while concurrently managing the duties of Junior Minister of Works and Supervisor of Palace Construction and Military Equipment.
The Ministry of State Affairs, with the state as its foundation,
oversaw the six codes;
the Ministry of War, with weapons as its focus,
specialized in planning the seven virtues.
Thus, military equipment was amassed in abundance,
already encompassing the achievements of Wú Hàn;
the palaces stood tall and majestic,
further strengthening the laws of Xiāo Hé.
At that time, with the cool winds of white dew,
and farming tasks idle during the agricultural lull,
he commanded thirty thousand troops,
setting out from Yíyáng,
capturing the city of Fúlóng,
and leveling the fortifications of Yáo Chǎng.
At Mǎlíng, where trees were stripped,
the Wèi general found his path blocked;
at Píngyīn, where crows were heard,
the Qí army fled in retreat.
As the emperor’s younger brother,
his status surpassed all other lords,
and wherever benevolence and righteousness led,
his actions were guided by virtue and morality.
In the first year of the Jiàndé era,
he was promoted to the rank of Prince,
and still appointed Grand Minister of Works.
Jī Dàn was enfeoffed at Qūfù,
yet did not neglect his duties at court;
Liú Jiāo was granted the state of Péngyáng,
yet remained a constant companion.
How could this be compared merely to Zhōu and Shào of the Two Souths,
who both served as tutors and mentors;
or the states of Jìn and Zhèng,
who were both ministers and officials?
The Xiōngnú surged into Wǔchuān,
and beacon fires lit up the area near Bàshàng.
He performed his duties, patrolling and inspecting,
and trained troops in Shuòfāng.
The stars flew over Mǎyì,
and the moon stirred at Lóngchéng.
Stirring the wine of Liúlí,
he planned strategies without advancing;
losing the Yānzhī Mountains,
he dismounted and departed.
The eastern neighbor defied orders,
acting against the Way and corrupting virtue,
imprisoning Jīzǐ in a frontier storehouse,
and confining King Wén at the Jade Gate.
The Son of Heaven prepared to lead an army to Mèngjīn,
and summoned him alone for counsel.
He responded by proclaiming the acceptance of Heaven’s Mandate,
and achieving his meritorious deeds.
In the past, King Zhāo of Qín raised an army in Shǔ,
and consulted only Zhāng Yí;
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn waged war against Wú,
and sought counsel solely from Yáng Hù.
Thus, when the central army lacked a commander,
all agreed that he was the one to lead.
In the fifth year,
he was appointed Grand Pillar of State.
The main army marched eastward to campaign,
and the king was provided with twenty thousand elite cavalry,
first attacking Tàiyuán.
The Dipper guided the troops,
and the heavens shifted in battle,
like tigers roaring and winds soaring,
clouds flying and lightning flashing.
Could the wild dates and chestnuts of the forest barbarians
ever satisfy hunger?
How could the reeds and wormwood of Jìnyáng
offer any defense?
He was then reinforced with sixty thousand elite troops,
laying a prolonged siege to Jìnzhōu.
Thereafter, the six armies deployed like stars,
and ten thousand cavalry thundered into action,
as the central command arrived,
the vanguard had already engaged in battle.
From then on, he served as the vanguard,
advancing unhindered into Yè.
Witnessing their chariots entangled in locust tree roots,
and horses startled by swirling mud,
armor piled as high as the walls of Kūnyáng,
corpses blocking the waters of Fùpíng,
all fell like tiles from a roof,
or bamboo split with ease,
and in a single command,
the six directions were pacified.
Thus, he glorified the martial prowess below,
and supported the brilliance of the central capital,
sufficient to vent the long-held grievances of the ancestors,
and dispel the resentment and suffering of the people.
Just as he was about to await the stone gate,
and arrange the jade drums,
to order heaven and earth,
and illuminate the sun and moon,
suddenly, red birds flanked the sun,
and a yellow bear entered the chamber,
Shíchén went without sacrifices,
and Sānglín received no offerings.
On the twenty-eighth day of the sixth month in the first year of the Xuānzhèng era, he passed away,
at the age of thirty-four.
With the death of Jì Yǒu,
Lǔ’s fate was known;
when Qí lost Zǐyǎ,
the state of Jiāng was in peril!
The Duke possessed a profound and expansive demeanor,
with a transcendent and far-reaching spirit.
Like a jade mirror illuminating the forest,
he embraced mountains and rivers.
He set out wine vessels awaiting the ladle,
hung bells awaiting the strike,
his reputation stirring the world,
his radiance illuminating the four neighbors.
Emperor Wǔ, as a close brother and beloved relative,
showed him special affection and friendship,
and regarding secret plans and extraordinary strategies,
treated him with added courtesy and respect.
He often said to his attendants:
"Confucius said:
'Since I have Yán Huí,
my disciples grow closer each day.'
This can be said of the Prince of Qí."
Employing him as a minister,
all regions harmonized in cooperation;
employing him to pacify the army,
the four borders were awed into submission.
How could it merely be like Gāo Yáo serving as Minister of Justice,
and the state having no unrighteousness;
or Suí Huì serving as a high minister,
and the people having no bands of robbers!
He cherished and delighted in books,
earnestly revered ritual and music.
When pipes and strings entered his ears,
streams and valleys all harmonized;
when elegance and refinement flowed in his heart,
mist and rosy clouds joined in melody.
Like Yǎng Yóu hitting a hundred bullseyes,
he could make geese fall and gibbons cry;
like Yìng Fèng mastering the five elements,
he was versed in silk scrolls and light-blue book covers.
His dignified and graceful bearing,
his modulated and expressive discourse,
were taken as a model by his contemporaries,
and as a standard by the gentry.
From youth he harbored lofty ambitions,
and diligently studied military texts.
The mysterious waters bestowed spirit,
Gǔchéng transmitted strategies;
the flying wind and long willows,
the moon-like forehead and star-like brows—
all were chanted and recited in his heart,
composed and written by his hand.
The military treatises he authored
amounted to five volumes in total.
The Six Secret Teachings and Nine Methods,
did not rely on Wú Qǐ's old writings;
the Three Commands and Five Instructions,
needed not the prior warnings of Sūn Wǔ.
It can be said he possessed loyalty and filial piety,
and also valor and martial prowess.
He was never arrogant or conceited,
but modestly deferred to others.
Like the man of Sòng who presented jade,
he considered not coveting as treasure;
like Bóchéng Zigāo,
he considered upholding benevolence as wealth.
It cannot be said that he used trust to invite deceit,
or that doing good brought him no joy.
He did not enjoy his natural lifespan,
Alas, how sorrowful!
On a certain year, month, and day, he was buried in the village of Hóngdúchuān, Shí'ān County.
The plains and lowlands are mournful,
having buried such abundant virtue for years;
the hills and mounds are desolate,
forever concealing such talent and goodness.
Thus the inscription says:
Remote indeed is the northern region,
distant is the extreme yin.
Mountains connect to bird paths,
the land ends at the Turtle Forest.
Great was the enterprise of Zhònglí,
deep were the merits of Bóyì.
Heirs who accumulate virtue,
are destined to rule.
The Grand Ancestor quelled chaos,
losing a lord, gaining a lord.
Merits turned the earth's axis,
strategies moved celestial patterns.
Still overlooking the Chìshuǐ,
again restoring the yellow clouds.
Eight hundred feudal lords,
the world divided into three.
The Duke's outstanding birth,
was truly Heaven's gift.
A divine descent from Cuìwēi,
the Wénchāng star descending.
Illuminating the four states,
filling the two altars.
Boat and oar for rivers,
pillar and beam for Huáxià.
Water flowed through his eloquent speech,
wind soared with his refined elegance.
A nature pure and deep,
righteousness reaching heaven's constants.
The way of loyalty and steadfastness,
moved the hundred spirits.
Sovereign and kin as one,
minister and son at peace.
Loyal springs issued from wells,
filial bamboo shoots grew in courtyards.
He then governed the Ministry of Officials,
as a pillar of the state.
He occupied the post of supreme general,
as a pillar of heaven.
He was sagely, he was divine,
cultured, he was martial.
Strategies lofty as creation,
might shifting clouds and rain.
Nine Palaces divine strategy,
three arts brilliant plans.
Celestial Li shifted formations,
Moon Virtue turned back troops.
Líyáng's waters trembled,
Guāndù's mountains startled.
Jìzhōu was thus settled,
Dōngyuán was pacified.
Ocean waves about to churn,
weak trees soon endangered.
The central peak, the mountain sundered,
half the sea, the roc hanging.
The phoenix sank in the Dānxuè,
the dragon perished at the black slope.
Línzī's market was abandoned,
Dōngwǔ's mountain moved.
A thousand ages, ten thousand years,
his heroic fame remains here.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, scroll 890.
〈Epitaph for Bù Lù, Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent of Zhōu〉
〈Epitaph for Bù Lù, Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent of Zhōu〉
The Duke, named Chěng,
courtesy name Jìmíng,
originally bore the surname Lù,
and was from Wújùn.
When the nobleman arrived,
he continued the line of the Yú guests;
the phoenix flying,
truly revived the state of Qí.
The envoy from Nányuè,
untied the Hàn emperor's robe;
the general of Xīlíng,
overturned the King of Wú's canopy.
His great-grandfather Zài
served as Marshal for the Prince of Sòng,
remaining to guard Guānzhōng.
During the rebellion of Hèlián,
he took up arms for the Wèi house.
At the Yellow River's high banks,
some lost the pursuit path;
at the Wūjiāng's moored boats,
there was no trace of return.
Thus he is now considered a man of Luòyáng, Hénán.
His great-great-grandfather
was Champion General and Governor of Yíngzhōu.
When men of Wú surrendered and submitted,
he led them all as a separate army.
From then on, officers and troops wielded bells,
becoming soldiers of Wú and Yuè;
gentlemen practiced naval warfare,
forming distinct tower-ship formations.
His father Zhèng
was General of Agile Cavalry, Grand General, Pillar of State with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies, Governor of Héngzhōu, and Duke Xiàn of Zhōngdū.
The Grand Ancestor supported the endangered and aided the falling,
managed and wove through obstacles,
avenged his lord's disgrace,
and campaigned far to Píngyuán.
Considering Gāopíng the foundation of his hegemonic enterprise,
he entrusted him with remaining to manage affairs.
The provisions supplied from Guānzhōng,
were not merely like the army at Xíngyáng;
the supplies provided by Hénèi for the army,
were not just the bamboo from Qíyuán.
The Duke, endowed with the spirit of Zhào Jìn,
descended with the virtue of a bright deity.
A fierce tiger shaking its cage,
for seven years it caused no alarm;
a ram butting against the fence,
at nine years old he could respond.
His elder brothers, because the Duke was the beloved son of their late father,
praised him as benevolent,
and pushed him to inherit the fief.
Although it was the end of an era,
his great, accomplished heart held fast to integrity.
Having already encountered a burning den,
he then turned to press the seal cord.
When Tàizǔ first enfeoffed Hángǔ,
and first assembled the feudal lords,
with the Duke’s eloquence,
he participated in planning confidential matters,
thus enabling military administration to be well proclaimed,
and strategic discussions to be without leakage,
and he was granted the surname Bùlùhú.
Entrusted with the deer-drawn carriage to discuss the capital,
entering Hóngmén to dance with a sword,
compared to those who harmonized with pitch-pipes,
he had abundant glory.
He began his career as Commander of the Forest of Plumes and General of Light Chariots,
and was appointed Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs.
His office was connected with accounting,
his duties involved the equitable standardization,
the water offices had accumulated rotting coins,
and the ever-normal granaries overflowed with red millet.
He was granted Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Pillar of State with Ceremonial Honours Equal to the Three Excellencies,
with an increase of a thousand households to his fief.
Soon he was promoted to Grand Master of the Imperial Stables,
concurrently holding the post of Grand Master of the Bureau of Personnel,
and served successively as Grand Master of the Bureau of Vassals and Grand Master of the Imperial Guard.
In the Eastern Capital’s tripod of talents,
he first added the merit of Dèng Zhì;
in the Western Jìn’s selection of officials,
they often used Shān Tāo’s recommendations.
How could it compare to the five princes attending court,
who surely oversaw the rites of host and guest;
the six dragons controlling the reins,
which determined the rhythm of the bells.
As Yùzhèng was an office that violated his father’s name,
he did not accept it.
Kuàijī had the fame of Wáng Huì,
whose son did not become its governor;
Bólíng had the enfeoffment of Wáng Chén,
whose son did not become its inspector.
He was promoted to General of Agile Cavalry and Palace Attendant.
He entered to oversee the reception of remonstrances,
and administered the Ministry of Rites.
He also served as Army Marshal.
His post was that of a constant attendant,
diligently inquiring in the Southern Palace;
his position involved the king’s words,
linking offices to the Northern Dipper.
Not only did he perform sacrifices to heaven and earth,
with the sounds of Lóngmén and Xiègǔ;
he also directed drums and distributed banners,
in the months of white dew and cool winds.
One night, someone offered him several dozen bolts of silk,
but the Duke closed his door and did not accept them.
The messenger insisted,
and he reported it fully to the throne,
earning praise from court and countryside.
Grand Commandant Yáng Zhèn,
directly refused gold from a former subordinate;
Liángzhōu’s Zhāng Huàn,
proudly declined horses from the Qiāng people.
Pure and fearing others’ knowledge,
I have no shameful virtue.
When the State of Qí sought peace,
the border officer received the mission.
Because the Duke had the talent for missions abroad,
he was ordered to perform the rites of displaying banners.
Having already sworn an oath with a pearl basin,
he secured the alliance of the State of Chǔ;
with a dagger ascending the altar,
he returned the invaded territory of the Qí people.
Is this not what is called an envoy?
Truly he brought glory to the state.
Among the dukes and marquises of the Three Adjuncts,
and the bell-cauldron families of the Five Mausoleums,
in the tóng streets and willow markets,
dust rose and wind flew,
so he was appointed Governor of the Capital District,
with his fief increased to a total of sixteen hundred households,
and his other offices remained as before.
The troops of the Shanglin Park rested,
and the bandits of Lánchí grew quiet.
He did not study Wáng Yáng’s lifelong art of casting gold,
nor was he like Zhāng Chǎng, who spent his days roaming Zhāngtái.
His household servant, returning at dusk,
found lost coins on the road,
along with ten bolts of white silk,
and the Duke sought out their owner,
and immediately returned them.
Seeing gold on the road,
he pointed it out to others;
finding coins on the path,
he hung them on a tree.
Compared to today,
different eras share the same ethos.
Soon he was promoted to Director of Finance,
and administered the Junior Minister of War.
He again oversaw the six armies,
and wielded the eight instruments of power.
His performance evaluations entered into the annual reports,
and his achievements were recorded in the “Annals.”
Soon he was appointed Commander of the Military Affairs of Yízhōu and Governor of Yízhōu.
Baring his cap to observe customs,
he halted his carriage to await rain.
A hundred cities surrendered their seals,
fearing the authority of Zhū Mù;
a thousand lǐ came to welcome him,
loving the virtue of Wáng Jī.
Before a full month had passed,
he was recalled by imperial decree.
The reluctant officials and people,
could not but make the plea of Hénèi;
the attached elders,
truly remembered the parting of Líyáng.
The Crown Prince cultivated virtue,
the front star guarded the vessel,
respecting teachers and yielding to elders,
necessarily awaited the worthy and capable.
Thus he was appointed Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
Compared to Liú Shí,
his Way was higher than that of a great state;
likened to Shān Tāo,
his glory was deeper than that of a small carriage.
He originally suffered from the illness of wasting thirst,
and often took mineral medicines to manage it.
His old illness slightly worsened,
and he suddenly departed from his official residence.
Below the Màolíng tomb,
no memorial on the fēng and shàn sacrifices remained;
in the camp of the Commandant of the Guards,
only the vessels for taking medicines remained.
Alas, how sorrowful!
He was forty-seven years old,
on the eleventh day of the fifth month of the second year of the Jiàndé era.
The Son of Heaven, due to the death of a great minister,
personally suspended hearing lawsuits;
the Eastern Palace, due to the dignity of a tutor,
personally attended the temporary burial sacrifice.
An edict posthumously granted him a certain office,
and the posthumous title of a certain duke,
according to ritual.
On the tenth day of the first month of the present third year,
he was buried at Gāoyáng Plain in the Capital District.
His wife, Yùjiǔlǘ,
was a royal princess from the west.
Respectful, solemn, and reverent,
her speech and appearance were virtuous and kind,
she was known for her admonitions and ablutions,
and never neglected the strings and tassels.
In her prime years,
she preceded him into the long night.
Now the chaste wife’s tomb is opened,
the pines and cypresses are already arm-span thick;
Jìsūn’s resting place completed,
the mound and hill are just beginning to be level.
Moreover, portraits of the virtuous consort,
are still in the Gānquán Palace;
while burying a talented man,
they used the Gāoyáng Plain.
His lordship's demeanor was outwardly bright,
his spirit and bearing inwardly radiant;
his capacity was deep and profound,
his foundation unfathomable.
In serving his sovereign, he was solely loyal;
in serving his parents, he was solely filial.
His words were a model for the age,
his conduct a standard for scholars.
He lingered over the ancient texts,
sorrowful and moved by literary compositions.
The Frost Office recorded his merits in the Department of State Affairs,
the Celestial Offices were overseen by the Controller of Accounts.
In and out of court, he assisted and advised,
often holding several positions concurrently.
His person bore the six tortoise tallies,
his waist constantly adorned with four silk ribbons.
Chén Píng's secret strategies
were not seen by the Son of Heaven;
Xún Yù's superior plans,
were not heard by the feudal lords.
When he governed a commandery,
he only took red earth to seal documents;
when he governed a province,
he only exchanged green salt for grain.
Leaving his household, he had no wealth in a thousand trees;
bequeathing to his son, it was merely one classic.
His eldest son, Cāo,
with utmost sincerity surpassing ritual,
pure filial piety leaving nothing undone.
The tree before the grave,
stained by tears, withered first;
the birds in the courtyard,
hearing sorrow, descended.
The inscription says:
Mountains link to the Rìguān Peak,
waters pillow against Diānjī.
Fùchūn's sands arise,
Kāiyáng's pillars fly.
The senior official yielded his integrity,
the general shook his might.
Nányuè received officials,
Xīlíng's siege was lifted.
In the past, our illustrious ancestor,
folded his wings in Qínzhōng.
The white horse had no path,
the Wū River was impassable.
Flutes lamented in the village,
zithers grieved the local customs.
Yíngzhōu, Héngzhōu,
bearing banners for generations.
Stout-hearted and dignified,
a hero among men at the frontier pass.
Straight rivers pierced Zhào,
level clouds approached Dài.
In life, he sought to achieve merit;
in death, he left behind love.
Descended from these mountains and rivers,
was born this steadfast and bright one.
Auspicious signs in clouds and vapor,
felicity joined with stellar essence.
Within palace curtains, strategies were settled;
on hall pillars, names were inscribed.
Loyal springs secretly seeped,
filial bamboo shoots grew in the cold.
The age belonged to Yīn and Zhōu,
the time met Chǔ and Hàn.
Under heaven divided in three,
the Hónggōu formed half.
With my clear strategy,
I came to participate in assistance.
The sun then shone again at noon,
heaven formed two dawns.
Successively joined the three highest offices,
served in turn as deputy to the six ministers.
Celestial Masters glorified their abode,
earth bore wise plans.
The Spring Offices fixed rites,
the Summer Offices governed troops.
Prophecies silently recognized,
warm trees bore no name.
Humble, respectful, meticulous,
words and actions without fault.
Loyal and public as a rhinoceros slain,
hidden virtue as a serpent buried.
Military and state affairs numerous and complex,
leading departments filled the steps.
Horses did not enter the stables,
gold did not enter his bosom.
All looked up to virtue alone,
high mountains alone were admired.
First ascended the Jiǎguān Hall,
first ascended the Dragon Tower.
In the eastern state, Huán Róng;
in the western capital, Shū Guǎng.
Years and age passed in a moment,
wind and lightning struck together.
The funeral banner twice vanished,
pond willows twice returned.
Lonely and forlorn, the heir,
bearing illness and containing grief.
His body illuminated by wild fire,
his heart fearing heaven's thunder.
Sun and moon pass by,
glory ends, sorrow begins.
Horses returned to the Director of Retainers,
books returned to the Grand Historian.
The calendar faced the celestial stars,
the grave joined the earthly market.
Mountain forms connect and fly,
pine shapes rise like canopies.
Virtuous words never cease,
the plain vanishes abruptly.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 900.
〈Epitaph for the Great General of Zhōu, Cuī Yuè〉
His lordship's given name was Yuè,
courtesy name unknown,
a man of Ānpíng County, Bólíng Commandery.
In ancient times, on the Huáyáng plain,
descended the spirit of the dragon's head;
in the capital of Lièshān,
opened the turtle-shell divination's prognostication.
Assisting Zhōu, then at Méngjīn there was a gathering;
aiding Xià, then at Lóngmén began the digging.
Traveling west, then rising to become Qín's chancellor;
entering east, then for generations serving as Qí's minister.
Fully recorded in historical texts,
can be spoken of.
Grandfather: Biàn,
General of Pacifying Distant Lands, Governor of Wǔyì Commandery.
Father: Kǎi,
Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments, Governor of Yīnzhōu.
Both endured wind and frost,
both displayed sharp brilliance,
messengers piled up tracks,
official departments stood in awe.
This is called Bào Huī of the Capital Officials,
a hundred cities trembled in fear;
Gě Fēng grasping the tally,
the capital folded its hands.
His lordship uniquely received heroic spirit,
particularly concentrated mountain grandeur,
majestic in appearance, outstanding and splendid,
brows and eyes clear and bright.
Viewing a tiger in a cage,
as a child, his hair unruffled, unafraid;
weighing an elephant on a boat,
able to respond while still in youth's garments.
As for pulling tigers and tethering bears,
crushing striped beasts and shattering paws,
forgetting to return with the Fánruò bow,
shooting down geese and making gibbons cry,
thus his vigor covered Guānzhōng,
his might extended beyond the river.
First appointed as Registrar in the Headquarters of the General of the Guards,
transferred to Advisory Army Counselor.
At that time, the ruling power lost control,
government rested with powerful families.
First discussing troops at Hángǔ Pass,
immediately arose the battle of Hánlíng.
Grand Tutor Hèbá Shèng served as Shepherd of Western Jīng,
his lordship acted as Acting Commissioner with Special Powers, Champion General, and Defense City Commander.
When Nányáng was lost,
he rolled up armor and fled to Liáng.
Yuè Yì, though a wanderer,
still thought of the road to Yān;
Chén Zhěn, sorrowful and distressed,
ultimately longed for Qín's sounds.
Fortunately, meeting with harmonious neighbors,
words of returning to the old state,
appointed General of the Guards, Commander,
enfeoffed as Open Country Viscount of Ānchāng County,
with a fief of three hundred households.
When Hóngnóng was recovered,
at Shāyuàn he wielded the blade,
advanced in rank to Marquis,
increased fief combined with previous to one thousand one hundred households.
The jade tablet of trust then again received the Director of Merit Titles,
the grain-patterned jade disc then returned to the Keeper of the Regalia.
Iron horses had the battle at Héqiáo,
spear-armed ships had the troops at Fénshuǐ.
Appointed Governor of Jīngzhào.
Moving people to a lesser town,
he did not study like Biān Sháo;
galloping on horseback through Zhāngtái,
he differed from Zhāng Chǎng.
Promoted to Commander-in-Chief, Commissioner with Special Powers, Army Pacifying General, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Ad Hoc, Grand Commander.

He was soon promoted to Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry, Commandant with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies, President of the Board of Personnel, and Grand Impartial and Just of Dìngzhōu.
In handling memorials from the five ministries,
he possessed the loyalty of Zhū Mù;
in evaluating men for the nine-rank system,
he displayed the integrity of Yáng Qiáo.
His fief was changed to the Marquis of Ānguó County,
with his estate increased to a total of fourteen hundred households.
He was granted the surname Yǔwén,
and his personal name was changed to Yuè.
When the Prince of Hàn altered the clan name of Lóu Jìng,
the matter concerned weighty discussions on the capital;
when the Empress of Wèi changed Chéng Yù's name,
the favor ran deep as holding up the sun.
He was promoted to Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry and Commandant with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies with the right to establish a personal administrative staff,
and was additionally appointed Palace Attendant.
When Dòu Xiàn held successive offices,
he could obtain the precious tripod of the Chányú;
when Zhāng Kuān secured his position,
he could recognize the shooting star at the Wèi Bridge.
The seven crafts of the Director of Wood,
already managed the taxes from the hills and mounds;
the six statutes of the Director of Accounts,
then balanced the talents for governing the state.
In appointing officials with capable men,
this was a time of great flourishing.
He was advanced in rank to Duke,
with his fief changed to Wànnián County,
totaling twenty-four hundred households.
He was appointed Regional Inspector of Lǒngzhōu and Commander of the Military Affairs of Lǒngzhōu.
The road to the Lǒng Ridge was distant,
the view of the Qín Plains far-reaching,
yet like Dèng Zhònghuá, he would not leave;
like Mǎ Wényuān, he desired to return.
