He was soon appointed Regional Inspector of Liángzhōu and Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Héxī, Gānzhōu, and Guāzhōu.
The land resembled a crouching dragon,
the city was like a flying bird.
The true records of Dūnhuáng,
were as if held in his bosom;
the outposts of the Yùmén Pass,
required no laborious mapping.
If there were horses like sheep,
he would not bring them into the stable;
if there were gold like millet,
he would not take it into his bosom.
The Pillar of State, Prince of Qí,
is the full younger brother of the present emperor.
He reverently undertook a punitive expedition,
to call to account at Héyáng,
and appointed the Duke as his Senior Administrator of the Campaign Army,
to participate in planning within the command tent.
For the commander of the central army,
Wèi Jiàng was already employed;
for the assistant of the senior minister,
Xún Lín was indeed used.
Comparing the Duke to them,
he was hardly ashamed in virtue.

He was appointed Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Grand General, Grand Commander of the Military Affairs of the thirteen defenses of Chóngdé, Ānyì, Jiànzhōng, Jiǔqū, Ānlè, Sānquán, Fúliú, Zhōuzhāng, Píngquán, Gù'ān, Mán, Tōng, and Gǔ; the three prefectures of Xióng, Hé, and Zhōng; and the ten garrisons of Huánglú, Qǐgǔ, Wángyàn, Gòngchāo, Qiānyáng, Wēnhú, Jiāohé, Dàlǐng, Bìyǔ, and Mùzhàsì; and as Commander of the Chóngdé Defense.
At Yíyáng, the superior land,
there were again Qín troops;
before Mount Xióng'ěr,
they still encountered hidden ambushes.
Thus they linked camps at Hángǔ,
hunted on horseback at Líyáng,
their might shook both rivers,
their fame towered over the Three Jìn.
His fief was changed to Duke of Ānpíng County.
Huáiyīn, a single state,
was the hometown of Hán Xìn;
Hùyǒu, with ten thousand households,
was the native place of Chén Píng.
The Duke, in this brocade return,
is fully worthy of being classed with them.
On the tenth day of the first month of the fourth year of Jiàndé,
he passed away at his private residence in Yǒngguì Ward of Cháng'ān,
at the age of sixty-four.
An edict posthumously awarded him Commander of the Military Affairs of Fū, Yán, Dān, Suí, and Héngzhōu, and Regional Inspector of Fūzhōu.
He was given the posthumous title Duke Zhuāng,
in accordance with ritual.
On the twenty-fourth day of the second month of the same year,
he was buried at Jíqiān Ward of Píngyuán Township in Jīngzhào.
At the northern mound, remembering the distant past,
the Grand Marshal had the grace of bestowing burial insignia;
in the Western Capital, bestowing honors for the journey,
the Marquis of Guànjūn had the ritual of an edict burial.
Alas, sorrowful indeed!
His eldest son, Commandant with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies Yǎn,
served him in life with ritual,
and buried him in death with ritual,
in loving his parents he had the filial piety of Wáng Xiáng,
in harmony with his siblings he had the concord of Jiāng Gōng.
The foundation of all conduct,
was fully present in him.
Moreover, the pines and catalpas are deep and dense,
already sealing the tomb of blue stone;
the mound and hill bear the marker,
and must be engraved with a golden stele.
Thus the inscription says:
The spirit of Huáyáng,
the ancestor of Lìshān.
At Phoenix Wilds he aided Zhōu,
at Dragon Gate he assisted Yǔ.
The sun bathed in the dark pool,
mountains floated on the sea shore.
Fǔ and Mù's hegemon state,
Yíngqiū, the land of joy.
His descendants in this ancestral town,
inherited this land's kingship.
The fief was moved to Dōngwǔ,
and he was enfeoffed as lord of Ānyáng.
The central army's critical points,
the northern garrison's sharp edge.
The autumn wind hunts the grass,
lightning fire drives the frost.
The Duke's splendid form,
inherited the steadfast stem.
His bearing was a model for the hills,
his spirit and manner, a lofty bank.
In filial piety he had perfect virtue,
in loyalty he could aid and support.
He did not neglect the laid-aside lute,
nor hinder the leaning desk.
Already ranked among the Three Excellencies,
he also assisted in the Six Ministries.
Wèi Qīng received the edict,
Hán Xìn ascended the altar.
The Great Wall's horse caves,
Guǎngwǔ's weapon racks.
The army's officers committed no offense,
the camp's people suffered no cold.
He thus employed the six stratagems,
he thus discussed the three policies.
The city walls' orientation,
the stars' roles as host and guest.
The sword drawn from the sunken rhinoceros,
the bow drawn on the crouching stone.
The Chǔ ruler yielded in the alliance,
the Qín lord returned the jade disc.
A hundred years are fragile and perilous,
a thousand fathoms are shattered and hidden.
The feudal lords' lands were torn asunder,
the border general's star fell.
Light chariots and mounted knights,
black armor and yellowed cypress.
The altar like the land of Qí,
the temple like Tóngxiāng.
Inscribing the merit, praising the virtue,
stele and tower gaze upon each other.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 904.
〈Epitaph for the Great General of Zhōu, Sīmǎ Yì〉
〈Epitaph for the Great General of Zhōu, Sīmǎ Yì〉
The Duke, taboo name Yì,
courtesy name Zūnyìn,
was a man of Wēn in Hénèi.
In the past, at the command of Zhuānxū,
first Nánzhèng was appointed to govern the heavens;
among the descendants of Zhòng and Lí,
again Xī and Hé were made to oversee the calendar.
Xiàyáng went to Jìn,
and he followed Suí Huì in fleeing together;
the Eastern Sea avoided Qín,
and he went into seclusion with Máo Gōng.
Afterwards, when the Metal Virtue received the mandate,
the jade box moved south,
the imperial lineage reached its limit on the maps,
and the central court arrived at the region south of the Yangtze.
His great-grandfather, Chǔzhī,
was the second son of the Grand Tutor of Jin, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, and the Governor of Yángzhōu,
Prince Wénxiào of Kuàijī,
and the youngest brother of Yuánxiǎn.
After Yuánxiǎn was murdered,
at the beginning of Huán Xuán's usurpation and rebellion,
from his childhood,
he concealed himself among butchers and fishermen.
On the roadside in Hénèi,
he embraced his sword and wailed long;
before the walls of Dàijùn,
he mourned grievously with a spiritual sacrifice.
Men of purpose and integrity from the Jiāng-Huái region,
and wanderers from the dust of Rǔ and Yǐng,
moved by a single word,
all largely attached themselves to him.
Subsequently, clouds arose over Fúguī,
stars emerged from the whale-fish,
the Great White Star crossed the heavens,
and the Chīyóu banner illuminated the wilds.
The Duke then gathered the remaining embers,
ascended the parapet with tears of blood,
faced the pass of Wǔláo,
and held the slopes of Chénggāo,
rallying a multitude of ten thousand households,
and submitted to the Wèi court.
Emperor Míngyuán of Wèi,
remotely appointed him General-in-Chief Who Pacifies the South and Governor of Jīngzhōu.
He inherited the title of Prince of Lángyá Commandery,
married the Princess of Hénèi,
was commanded by the Prince to uphold the imperial regulations,
and followed the rituals of a guest state.
At that time, Sòng troops were encroaching,
their banners and drums invading and pressing close,
the Tiger's Lair was unsealed,
and Jīnyōng had no reinforcements.

Emperor Tàiwǔ of Wèi appointed the Prince as Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Palace Attendant, General-in-Chief Who Pacifies the South, and Pillar of State with the Privilege of Establishing a Personal Secretariat,
granting him the ceremonial music of the front and rear sections.
The great army set forth,
determined to wash away the grievance and shame,
ascending the altar with fervor,
the three armies wept covering their faces.
Grain transported on the Yellow River,
had already exited Shímén,
white horses with connected banners,
were about to reach the wild slopes.
Then, the alarm arose in Yúnzhōng,
beacons were lit in Dàijùn,
the banners turned southward,
and the northern campaign reached its end on the road.

He was posthumously granted the titles of General-in-Chief Who Conquers the West, Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Ten Provinces: Liáng, Yì, Qín, Níng, Jīng, Yǎn, Qīng, Yù, Yǐng, and Luò, Governor of Yángzhōu, and Minister of Education.
He was posthumously named Prince Zhēn.
His grandfather, Jīnlóng,
was enfeoffed as General-in-Chief Who Guards the West of Lángyá, Pillar of State, and Minister of Personnel,
posthumously granted the title of Minister of Works,
and named Prince Kāng.
His father, Yuè,
was General Who Guards the South, Governor of Yùzhōu, and Marquis Zhuāng of Yúyáng.
While overseeing Jīng and Hé,
the times were marked by chaos and separation,
strife arose within the household,
and thus he met an untimely death.
The Duke was born posthumously,
wandering amidst bandits and rebels,
carried in swaddling clothes within double walls,
embraced by trees in the deep mountains.
Like Chéng Yīng hiding Zhào Wǔ,
he was attended by household servants;
like Wáng Chéng concealing Lǐ Xiè,
he worked as a laborer in the wine market.
When the grief of the Grand Lady befell him,
he stayed by the grave mound with a grass mat,
until the end of the mourning fire,
his body emaciated and haggard,
exceeding the rites of mourning.
At the age of fifteen,
he began to manage family affairs.
Before the pillars, he chiseled the column,
immediately retrieving the left books;
on the stone, he opened the pine,
still seeking the old sword.
He began his career as an Army Consultant in the Ministry of Education,
and was appointed General of the Resolute Army and Extraordinary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
At a time when the Wèi court faced many difficulties,
uprisings erupted everywhere,
north of Mèngjīn,
there were no more royal domains,
south of Sōngshān,
it immediately became a battlefield.
The Duke proposed to repair Wǔ,
and established a stockade at Wēn City,
the Hángǔ Pass was sealed to the west,
the Héqiáo Bridge was cut off to the north.
Horses registered at the long pavilions,
were all brought into Wǔ City;
rental carts from a hundred *li*,
were all delivered to Wēn County.
Emperor Wén, the Grand Ancestor, established the capital in Guān,
managed the barbarian obstacles,
recruited with propriety,
and cherished the distant with virtue.
Like Mǎ Wényuān choosing his lord,
he left Lǒngdǐ and submitted himself;
like Dòu Zhōugōng entering the court,
he was in Héxī and received the imperial decree.
In the seventh year of Dàtǒng,
he was granted the titles of General Who Pacifies the East and Governor of Běixúzhōu.
In the tenth year,
over four thousand households of old adherents in Hénèi,
wishing to establish loyalty,
awaited the Duke's glorious return,
and he was appointed Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, concurrently Governor of Hénèi,
with the additional title of Former General.
Huáizhōu expanded its territory,
two towns were in turmoil;
at Liǔquán, the battle turned,
three cities surrendered their leaders.
In the thirteenth year,
the Grand Ancestor summoned the generals from east of the mountains who had established righteousness,
those who could lead their followers into the passes,
would receive increased rewards.
The Duke was the first to arrive,
leading a thousand households,
which were to be his fief,
but he firmly declined to accept.
The gifts of beans and grain,
were sometimes like pointing to a full granary;
the rewards of horses and cattle,
were to be measured like grain.
The court considered Huáyáng to be the western extremity,
the Hàn River flowing eastward,
lamenting Mèng Dá's fleeing troops,
and marveling at Liú Fēng's mistaken strategy.
In the first year of the former Wèi era,
he was transferred to garrison Hànzhōng,
appointed as the commander of Báimǎ City,
concurrently Governor of Huáyáng Commandery.
Formerly known as Dǎoyàng,
now heard as Shàngzhū,
smoke settled over the ice well,
rain ceased at the cloud gate.
That year,
he was appointed Grand Commander,
with the additional title of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
The Pillar of State, Duke of Shǔ,
opened the road of Jīnniú,
and cleared the pass of Mùmǎ.
The Duke rolled up his armor and headed north to the frontier,
suspended his carriage and bound his horses,
thus gaining the opportunity to strategize at Jiāméng,
and achieve merit at Miánzhú.
He was enfeoffed as Viscount of Lóngmén County, Founder of the State, and Governor of Púzhōu,
still concurrently governing Xīnzhōu.
Soon he was appointed Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Chariot and Horse General-in-Chief, Pillar of State, and Grand Impartial and Just.
The prosperous Zhōu received the mandate,
Heaven's protection greatly settled,
due to the Duke's talent and reputation,
he remained as an old minister.
Thus, righteousness deepened in remembering the distant,
favor flourished in continuing the cut-off,
and he was re-enfeoffed as Duke of Lángyá County,
with a fief of five hundred households.

He was further promoted to General-in-Chief of Agile Cavalry, Pillar of State with the Privilege of Establishing a Personal Secretariat, Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Bāzhōu, and Governor of Bāzhōu.
In the second year of Wǔchéng,
he was ordered to rush to the aid of Xìnzhōu.
The Yúfù road was blocked,
repeatedly repelling Cén Péng;
the Jīngmén waters were swift,
nearly drowning Wú Hàn.
The Duke then was the first to ascend Yuèxiá,
and went straight up Qútáng.
The Son of Heaven, considering the Duke's conduct loyal and diligent,
and his demeanor upright and honest,
summoned him to be the Grand Master of the Imperial Clan,
and soon transferred him to be the Grand Master of Correctness,
with a fief of one thousand one hundred households.
As a close attendant in the pivotal office,
he issued and received the silken words,
truly one who knew much of the old statutes,
and was peerless in the palace.
Reverently observing the celestial phenomena,
harmoniously ordering the welcoming of dawn.
Shǎoliáng fled to Huà,
the land entered Xiánqín.
The clan was subdued, horses rose,
the records ceased with the capture of the qilin.
The jade mirror began to form,
the metal phase then took shape.
Xiàngpǔ opened its passes,
Lóngshā established its outposts.
Shàngsǎn’s stones arose,
Héyáng’s waters clashed.
Five horses drifted south,
three stars lodged in the east.
The Grand Tutor became a governor,
encompassing the Jiāngtuó region.
The Minister of Education fled the chaos,
upholding authority in Jīnghé.
Pushed southward by the carriage,
still longing to rest on spears.
Dragon steeds filled the plains,
gray rhinoceroses crossed the waves.
In the later years of Lord Zhuāng,
calamities followed one another.
The noble lord left behind heirs,
who traversed rugged paths with cherished hopes.
Zhào Wǔ hid in the mountains,
Lǐ Xiè concealed himself at home.
Wǔ Yuán’s path was blocked,
Yān Dān’s road was distant.
Fleeing south to the Chǔ frontier,
evading north to the Qín bridge.
Water flowed over the ridges,
cold winds crossed Liáo.
The meritorious Protector-General,
was as esteemed as Piáo Yáo.
Carrying books while mounting horses,
learning rites while joining the army.
Deploying formations of the six Jia,
divining troops with the eight winds.
Concealing pine-wood swords,
shooting willows with carved bows.
Sincerely emulating Jiǎ Fù,
humbly yielding like Lián Gōng.
Eight wings frequently soaring,
six cycles repeatedly grasped.
Courageous in this benevolence and righteousness,
practicing this blend of leniency and severity.
Holding the seal, mountains opened,
Chénlí’s bandits quieted.
Taking armor without mounds,
equalizing fields without wells.
Rewarding achievements with titles,
bestowing high ranks upon generals.
Receiving edicts in the army,
ascending altars beyond the frontier.
Just as Cānhé was slaughtered,
again fiercely fought at Gāolán.
Yúchuān’s poisonous waters,
Bódào’s calamitous aura.
The land lost its Commandant,
the rapids mourned the Envoy.
Valleys cold without sunlight,
mountains empty, filled with clouds.
Northern winds blew the funeral banners,
autumn rains wept for the army.
Double offerings sent forth,
two funeral banners displayed.
Qìnshuǐ shared the grave,
Píngyáng united the tombs.
Grieving the heir,
climbing and wailing without solace.
Sorrowful as the wind-tossed branches,
deeper than frost and dew.
From this, what era begins?
From now, how many years?
Qílín desire to battle,
Huábiǎo pillars burn within.
The terrain rose like towers,
pine hearts formed canopies.
Vast are the burial mounds,
generation after generation of heroes and sages.
○ From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, scroll 904.
“Stele Inscription for Tuòbá Jiǎn, Pillar of State and Great General of the Zhōu Dynasty”
“Stele Inscription for Tuòbá Jiǎn, Pillar of State and Great General of the Zhōu Dynasty”
It is heard that when Fàngxūn established rule, Xīhé ascended;
when Chónghuā rose, Yuánkǎi were employed.
Thinking of the many talented men,
they accomplished the merits of the Western Earl;
with brilliant virtue and clarity,
they settled the campaign against Náncháo.
Thus it is known that without a ruler, the worthy are not sustained,
and without the worthy, the ruler cannot govern.
As for the ruler and ministers sharing one virtue,
opening hearts and enriching minds,
this was seen in Chāngníng Wéngōng.
The lord, named Jiǎn,
styled Qìngmíng,
was from Gāolù in Héngzhōu.
The Northern Peak, star of the celestial grandson,
the land of Yānhé, realm of the emperor’s sons,
thus produced many extraordinary integrity,
and flourished with splendid customs.
Gāoquè looked south,
two kings shared the same carriage;
the Great Wall uprooted,
ten clans divided their origins.
His great-grandfather,
Grand Commandant and Prince of Běipíng.
Assisted five rulers with brilliance,
properly managed all affairs;
Héng and Wèi were pacified,
Huái and Yí were governed.
His grandfather, Bào,
Dragon-Soaring General and Governor of Héngzhōu.
In Chángshān’s administration,
there was no lack of signs to replace;
as Dragon-Soaring Commander,
his title resembled that of the pacifier of Wú.
His father, Yù,
whose life ended at the capping age,
honorably concluded by returning the seal.
The lord, endowed with the five constants’ wisdom,
and the six climatic energies’ virtue,
riding heaven’s mandate, he spurred his horse with divine inspiration;
descending as a spirit, he responded to the images of Qiān and Láng.
Upright in heart towards all things,
water and fire were tranquil;
without failing heaven,
thunder and lightning held no fear.
Wealth and honor he attained himself,
needing no words from Táng Jǔ;
his fame was widely known,
requiring no recognition from Lǐ Yīng.
At age eighteen,
he began his career as an Attendant Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat.
Soon appointed Light-Chariot General and Commander of the Imperial Guard.
The Great Ancestor, Emperor Wén, steered the celestial net,
encompassing heroes and talents,
selecting the lord for his ability and virtue,
gloriously assisting the Central Secretariat.
Like Zhūgě Liàng’s return west,
Yùlěi established the tripartite realm;
like Guǎn Yíwú’s entry into service,
Kuíqiū achieved the feat of unifying.
The cunning Qiāng of Tiānshuǐ,
the bandit hordes of Yúyáng,
thus he was transferred as Chief Clerk of Qínzhōu and Grand Commander of the City Defense,
enfeoffed as Earl of Xìndū County.
In the third year,
Huàzhōu swarmed like ants,
defending the stronghold, risking lives,
banners fallen, chariot tracks disordered,
crossing the river on ice.
The Chancellor and Grand Mobile Headquarters appointed him Acting Jiedushi and Army-Pacifying General,
acting as Governor of Huàzhōu.
In the first year of Dàtǒng,
appointed Jiedushi and Governor of Xīxiàzhōu,
with additional title of Regular Attendant.
The Zhìzhī clung to horses,
as if hearing of Gěng Bǐng’s battles;
the Chányú wished to recognize him,
seeming to fear Wáng Shāng’s authority.
In the fifth year,
promoted to Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Eastern-Pacifying General, Commander of Military Affairs of the Three Xīxiàzhōu in the Northeast, and Governor of Xīxiàzhōu,
with increased fief of a thousand households,
changing his title from Earl to Duke.
Thereafter, the Jiāng and Hàn were distant,
chariots and writings fell silent.
The Lord of Shǔ’s skull,
had not yet emerged from the waters of Tánxī;
the King of Qín’s flying pheasant,
still headed towards the city of Nányáng.
In the sixth year,

he was appointed as Envoy with Credentials, Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of the Twelve Provinces of Sānjīng, Èrxiāng, Nányōng, Píngxìn, Jiāng, Suí, Yǐng, and Zhè, Governor of Jīng Province, and Vice Director of the Southeast Circuit Branch Department of State Affairs.
Though Chǔchéng bordered neighboring territories,
he truly yielded fields;
though Wú people faced his camp,
it did not hinder the exchange of medicines.
When a subordinate city within his jurisdiction
was accused by others,
he gathered civil and military officials,
bared his upper body, and imposed punishment upon himself.
When brothers refused to yield,
Yánshòu blamed himself;
when officials or people erred,
Wēngguī took the blame.
The Son of Heaven found this remarkable,
issuing an imperial edict to commend and inquire,
bestowing gifts and increasing rewards,
with imperial envoys arriving one after another.
The Grand Chancellor wrote in a letter:
"Such virtuous deeds
are unheard of and unseen.
I admire and praise them endlessly,
hence I have dispatched a special envoy."
He excelled at pacifying and governing,
and was adept at receiving and guiding others.
No talent in the mountains or marshes was neglected,
bribery did not prevail,
he showed people his sincere heart,
and treated others with kindness.
Thieves dared not act,
and the people could not bear to deceive him.
At this time, military officers and elders in the southern part of the provincial capital
erected the Tower of Pure Virtue,
and inscribed a eulogy for the worthy minister.
When Dù Zhènnán governed,
a stele was erected in his time;
when Dòu Chēqí commanded the army,
a stone was carved during his lifetime.
Compared to today,
who were they alone!
At that time, the population increased daily,
barren lands were fully cultivated,
flowers and fruits flourished abundantly,
and the black-haired people prospered in peace.
Yet it was feared that the duties of the imperial court were deficient,
awaiting him to remedy them;
the cauldron of governance was not harmonious,
requiring him to rectify it.
Therefore, the hopes of the people of Hànyīn,
the talents of Jīngnán,
all submitted petitions to the imperial court,
jointly pleading for him to remain.
When Hénèi sought to borrow Kòu Xún,
they were ashamed to petition the emperor again;
when Jiāozhōu requested Shì Xiè,
they still submitted memorials.
In the ninth year,
he was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry, and given the rank of Yìtóng Sānsī.
In the twelfth year,
he was appointed Grand Secretary of the Branch Department of State Affairs,
and concurrently served as Marshal to the Grand Chancellor.
Because of his strict and clear judgment and bearing,
and his pure and frugal will and integrity,
his name was changed to Jiǎn,
with the courtesy name Qìngmíng.
It was not about recording the months,
nor awaiting the viewing of steles;
fortunately, a thousand acres differed,
and two mountains were not abandoned.
In the thirteenth year,
he was granted the title of Kāifǔ,
with other offices remaining unchanged.
In the fourteenth year,
he was appointed Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs,
granted the title of Shìzhōng,
and promoted to General of Agile Cavalry.
Residing in the position of the star of enforcement above,
and in the seat of Wénchāng,
with his talent and reputation,
he possessed both.
In the fifteenth year,

he was further appointed Vice Director of the Southeast Circuit Branch Department of State Affairs, Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Fifteen Provinces, and Administrator of Jīng Province Affairs.
In the sixteenth year,
the Grand Chancellor commanded sixteen armies,
conquering Qīnghé and Luòyáng.
He again divided his forces,
participating in planning within the tent.
When selecting outstanding aides for the hegemon,
he served as Chief Clerk.
That year,
he was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Thirty-Six Provinces of the Southern Circuit,
with other offices remaining unchanged.
The literary scholars of Nányáng
again encountered Wáng Jī;
the embroidered robes of Zhānghuá
once more welcomed Guō Hè.
In the past, regarding the strategy to attack Shǔ,
Zhāng Yí's plans aligned with King Zhāo of Qín;
concerning the benefits of pacifying Wú,
Yáng Hù's intentions matched those of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn.
When Tàizǔ first secured Chéngdū,
he already harbored ambitions for Jiānglíng.
He secretly presented his strategy,
which perfectly matched the profound intent,
grain supplies had long been accumulated,
scaling ladders and assault vehicles were promptly prepared,
with one battle capturing Yān and Yǐng,
and a second battle burning Yílíng,
thus sweeping through Sānjīng.
This was another achievement of his.
An imperial decree rewarded him with three hundred male and female slaves.
Tàizǔ wrote to him:
"Thanks to your planning,
it indeed turned out as strategized."
He then personally garrisoned Jiānglíng,
to pacify the Shǔ region.
In the second year of the Later Wèi,
he was enfeoffed as Duke of Wǔchuān Chāngníng Commandery.
The residents of Lìyáng
were not only those enfiefed to Jǐng Dān;
the households of Qūnì
were not merely those of Chén Píng's fief.
That year,
he was appointed Grand General.
During the Tàihé period,
Cáo Zhēn received his appointment within the headquarters;
at the end of Yuánfēng,
Wèi Qīng was appointed in the army.
His comparison to these
is abundantly honorable.
An imperial decree stated:
"The Wú people have not yet been subdued,
requiring assistance in planning and strategy.
Now, the troops of Prince Liáng
shall be under your command."
In the third year,
he was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Fifty-Three Provinces of the Southeast Circuit,
with an additional ten thousand households added to his fief.
When the Zhōu dynasty initiated its revolution,
it brilliantly established its enlightened rule;
serving as the secondary official of the Ministry of Personnel,
he harmoniously assisted in governing the state.
In the first year,
he was appointed Junior Minister of Personnel.
In the second year of Bǎodìng,
he governed as Prefect of Pú Province and Inspector of the Six Frontier Defenses Military Affairs.
In the fourth year,
he governed Xiāng Province,
and was appointed Pillar of State Grand General,
with other offices remaining unchanged.
His rank reached that of the Four Peaks,
and his status equaled the Six Ministries.
Was his merit not greater than Zhāoyáng's,
and his reputation higher than Cài Cì's?
Controlling and governing fifty provinces,
his influence spread over several thousand li.
He removed garden mallows and dismissed weaving women,
free from three delusions and断绝 the four forms of knowledge.
Within his household,
it was inevitably empty and plain;
his daily meals
consisted of merely three cups.
An imperial decree then bestowed one thousand bolts of silk and colored fabrics,
and two thousand hu of grain and wheat.
In the first year of Tiānhé,
he served as Prefect of Shǎn Province and Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Eight Provinces and Twenty Frontier Defenses,
relinquishing the overall command of Jīng Province,
with all else remaining unchanged.
His route passed through Wángguān,
and the city overlooked the river bend;
garrisons were cleared west of Shǎn,
and he gazed loftily from the shade of the pear tree.
Managing numerous and繁杂 affairs,
exhaustion from dawn till dusk led to illness.
In the fourth year of Tiānhé,
he retired due to illness in the old capital,
and passed away at his private residence,
at the age of seventy-eight.
The imperial carriage descended,
music ceased in the suspended chimes,
he was bestowed with the nine-tasseled dragon banner,
and escorted by knights from the three rivers.

An imperial decree posthumously appointed him Grand Guardian and Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of the Ten Provinces of Liáng, Xià, Líng, Yín, Chángyuán, Hé, Shàn, Gān, and Guā, and Governor of Liáng Province.
His posthumous title was Wén.
The Duke's appearance was lofty as a hill,
his spirit and bearing were open and magnificent.
Like a beautiful jade mountain standing tall,
or a towering pine soaring straight upward,
the edges of his misty aura were unfathomable,
the waves of his vast depth were immeasurable.
In youth he suffered bitter hardships,
observing mourning in the mountains until its end.
He clung to withered cypress trees,
and wild beasts died among the pines he tended.
He served the state with utmost loyalty,
exerted all effort in governance.
His gate was as bustling as a marketplace,
yet his heart was as tranquil as still water.
With ingenious strategies and secret plans,
all officials looked up to him;
with loyalty, steadfastness, and integrity,
the enlightened ruler held him in high esteem.
As for the divinations of wind and yin-yang by Fēnghòu,
the measurements of stars and constellations by Lìmù,
the military treatises of Lord Wèi,
the archery methods of General Lǐ,
there was none he did not memorize by heart,
applying them for timely use.
In daily life, his attire and pastimes
were sometimes coarse blankets and pinewood beds;
on his trays and tables,
there was nothing beyond mulberry-wood cups and stone tripods.
His final command regarding his tomb
was that nothing be used at all;
public and private funeral gifts
were all not to be accepted.
He was to be buried only beside the mausoleum of the Great Ancestor,
never forgetting his service to the sovereign.
Dūn and his brothers all possessed the utmost filial nature,
excelling in observing mourning rites.
They wailed and longed at the grave mound,
faithfully following his last instructions.
Thus, just as Wèi Qīng's tomb
still accompanies Hàn Wǔdì's mausoleum,
and Guǎn Zhòng's grave
immediately adjoins Duke Huán of Qí's tomb,
in the sixth year of Tiānhé,
the Son of Heaven, because the realm was not yet at peace,
and three powers stood in tripartite stalemate,
cherished thoughts of commanders and generals,
and spoke of ministers guarding the frontiers.
Having already depicted the Cloud Terrace,
he then inscribed the Unicorn Pavilion,
and further posthumously enfeoffed the Duke as Duke of Kuài,
with a fief of five thousand households.
Honoring him among the ranks of rulers,
the affair reached the utmost of spirit and soul;
changing again the funeral banner,
the grace enriched the sealing of the tomb.
The Duke left affection among the people while alive,
and after his passing, he is remembered with longing.
On auspicious days and fine hours,
they offer suburban and wild sacrifices.
Yítóng Zhào Chāo and six hundred ninety-seven others
petitioned to establish a temple,
requesting a statue at the palace gate.
An edict granted permission.
With cassia pillars and apricot beams,
green steps and blue-painted doors,
songs are arranged and dances gathered,
with phoenix canopies and rainbow robes.
The southern bank sends off departing clouds,
the east wind scatters drizzling rain.
Thus we know that before Hànyáng Commandery,
it was not only the temple of the Military Marquis;
below Línzī city walls,
surely it is not solely the altar of Duke Luán.
Alas, sorrowful indeed!
Thus the inscription says:
The Way gathered in "Difficulty" and "Peeling,"
the age belonged to clouds and thunder.
The earth's axis turned leftward,
heaven's gate opened northward.
Carriages accommodated the Zhōu house,
horses tethered at the Qín terrace.
Then he harmonized the seven regulators,
and responded to the three powers.
The illustrious ancestor harmonized,
the ninefold support, beams and pillars.
Seeking talent, he encountered the hunt,
searching for worthies, he entered dreams.
Assisting officials like clouds,
planning strategies, recording phoenixes.
Regulations fixed the ducal clan,
jade tablets divided duties and tributes.
Then came the inheritor of virtue,
truly holding heroic spirit.
His body mapped the Dipper's lodgings,
his face encircled the Pivot Star.
In blue collars, he revered his tasks,
as a youth, he mastered the classics.
Like Lord Xìnlíng leaving the left seat empty,
like Gānmù dividing the courtyard.
Loyalty and filial piety pure and deep,
pivotal mechanisms precise and thorough.
Like Kǒng Guāng speaking not,
like Cáo Shēn missing nothing.
Warming the mat, fanning the pillow,
pleasing with expression, delighting at the knee.
Fish startled in frozen streams,
bamboo shoots emerging in cold forests.
Solemn were his governance and customs,
profound his capacity and bearing.
Upright like firm bamboo,
gentle like auspicious jade.
Pure without needing water,
bright without raising a torch.
Horses wished to be like sheep,
gold must resemble millet.
The supreme general ascended,
the chief commander was arrayed.
Three victories at Xiàyáng,
one campaign at Yílíng.
Leaning on the chariot rail, he subdued Qí,
crossing the river, he entered Chǔ.
The tripod returned to the calendar chamber,
the bell rejoined the great pitch.
The six ministers all served,
heavenly offices were managed.
The two southern regions he governed as lord,
the shade of the pear tree truly brought order.
Pure winds had their ode,
green bamboo heard the poems.
The scrolls presented at his departure,
transcended, an imperial teacher.
Once he served in the orchid garden,
now he accompanies the apricot grove.
Life and death, partings and meetings,
never straying from a single heart.
Wind and clouds gather gloom,
mountain barriers link shadows,
mound fields and wilderness lie silent,
pine paths cold and deep.
The mound of Xià Yīng,
the tomb of Qiáo Xuán.
Horses see a thousand years,
carriages turn back three steps.
To the left, no Chánglè Palace,
before, no armory.
Gazing straight at the tall stele,
increasing sorrow for the passing way.
○ From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 905.
〈Stele Inscription for Pillar of State Grand General Hégàn Hóng〉
〈Stele Inscription for Pillar of State Grand General Hégàn Hóng〉
The Duke, named Hóng,
courtesy name Guǎnglüè,
was from Chángchéng County, Yuánzhōu.
His original surname was Tián.
When Yúbīn was on the throne,
it was based on the custom of yielding;
when the phoenix flew about,
it succeeded in the state of kin and worthies.
Speaking of his successive generations' merits,
then Díchéng had its temple;
narrating the beginning of his family's relocation,
then Chánglíng had its stele.
Moreover, again, at the high temple presenting a memorial,
in a small carriage facing the Hàn king;
at Liáochéng sacrificing to birds,
on the long mountain driving away the Yān general.
The Duke, in the month of prenatal education,
the year's virtue was in yín;
on the day of his birth,
the stellar essence emerged from the Pleiades.
Thus, a tree grew in the moon,
the youth knew speech;
a melon floated on water,
the blue-collared did not play.
And receiving books from the Yellow Stone,
his intent lay in the plans of a king;
brandishing the sword like the white ape,
his mind held the use for a hegemonic state.
During the Yong'ān era of the Wei dynasty,
he served as a Zidu Dudu,
defended the city of Yuánzhōu,
and received orders from the Prince of Lǒngxī.
At that time, Luòyì was in chaos and disorder,
the ruling power was endangered and threatened,
rites, music, and military campaigns
did not emanate from the Son of Heaven;
the promotion of the worthy and punishment of the cruel
truly lay with the powerful ministers.
The Great Ancestor, Emperor Wén, first established his hegemonic achievements,
initially toiling for the royal house,
grooming horses and inspecting chariots,
pledging his troops at Tàiyuán,
the Duke, with sword in hand at the camp gate,
boldly strategized for the age.
Like Suí Hé arriving from afar,
he truly relieved the worries of the Hàn Emperor;
like Xǔ Yōu coming by night,
he immediately secured the enterprise of King Cáo.
During the Yǒngxī era,
he first welcomed Emperor Wǔ of Wei into the pass,
and was enfeoffed as Kāiguó Zǐ of Chúnyīn County,
with a fief of five hundred households.
The Great Ancestor bestowed upon the Duke the iron armor he himself wore,
saying:
"If the realm is pacified,
bring this armor back to show me."
The fine sword of Báishuǐ,
presented to Chén Chǒng after court was dismissed;
the excellent black steed,
bestowed upon Lǐ Zhōng upon the army's return.
Both were gifts of carriage and attire,
sufficient to form a parallel.
In the third year of Dàtǒng,
he was transferred to Shuài Dudu,
and advanced in rank to Duke.
In the fourteenth year,
he was appointed Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Commander of All Military Affairs of Yuánzhōu, and Governor of Yuánzhōu.
Like an immortal returning,
re-entering the city of Guìyáng;
like a dragon seed coming back,
again seeking the road of Báishā.
The Duke, in this brocade return,
brought honor to his hometown.
Attending the Great Ancestor,
he fought at Héqiáo,
recovered Hóngnóng,
lifted the siege of Huàshān,
and pacified the battle array of Shāyuàn,
always achieving principal merit,
and often receiving special rewards.
When the Great Ancestor was in Tóngzhōu,
with civil and military officials gathered,
he issued the command:
"If everyone were as devoted as Hégàn Hóng,
would the realm not have been pacified long ago?"
He was then appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry, Commandant with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies.
In the first year of the Former Wei,
he was transferred to General of Agile Cavalry with the authority to establish a personal staff.
While Qílián was still distant,
he already received the marquisate of Guànjūn;
before the desert frontier was opened,
he was first appointed to the office of Chángpíng.
Xiāo Sháo, Governor of Xìnzhōu of Liáng, and Qiáo Yān, Governor of Níngzhōu, among others,
still occupied Yǒng'ān,
raising troops in Yúyáng.
The Duke received orders at the central army,
swiftly flowing down the rapids,
thus managing to depart from Báidì at dawn,
and lodge at Jiānglíng by dusk,
unperturbed by the cries of gibbons,
settling matters by the crowing of cocks.
The rebelling Qiāng of Xīpíng,
originally possessed the valor of Yúyáng;
the rebelling Dī of Fèngzhōu,
were also accustomed to the spirit of Chóuchí.
The Duke pushed the vanguard straight forward,
with naked blades crossing before him,
risking death in a decisive fight,
causing the fierce mob to largely crumble.
His body was struck by over a hundred arrows,
with nine wounds piercing flesh and breaking bone;
his horse was hit by ten lances,
the battle report displayed on his armor,
the court admired his valor.
The hempen sandals tightly bound,
Wei had the song of leaving the old;
the falling dew heavy,
Zhōu received the mandate for renewal.
He was then advanced in rank and enfeoffed as Duke of Yànmén Commandery,
with a fief, combined with previous grants, totaling two thousand seven hundred households.
In the first year of Bǎodìng,
he was appointed Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Commander of All Military Affairs of Mínzhōu, and Governor of Mínzhōu.
The flowing water at Lǒngtóu,
gazing afar towards the Qín passes;
the lofty brows upon the river,
still connecting to the Shǔ roads.
The Duke did not send private letters,
nor light official candles.
Beasts carried each other across the river,
insects passed each other out of the border.
In the fourth year,
he was appointed Grand General,
his other offices remaining as before.
When Wèi Qīng received his commission,
he had not yet entered the gate of Yùmén;
when Dòu Xiàn held office,
he was still below Yānshān.
Compared to these, his present appointment,
left little room for shame.
The Hún king rebelled and defied,
obstructing our western frontier,
the Qiāng chieftains of Dàng fled and hid,
the fences and barriers became disloyal,
the Duke received the sacrificial meat at the altar,
leading a flanking army on a distant raid,
raising banners at Lónghé,
tethering horses at Gānsōng.
Twenty-five kings,
their banners drooping, their tracks chaotic;
seventy-six stockades,
like quails fleeing, pheasants scattering.
Having received the reward for fulfilling his duty,
he then presented the music of the returning army.
In the second year of Tiānhé,
he was sent on a southern campaign,
with armored troops a million strong,
ships stretching for a thousand li,
the river's source swelling with water,
the sea god riding the currents.
At the city of Chuánguān,
they ascended nests and hung cooking pots,
the Wú soldiers, skilled in navigation,
drove their warships far forward,
with wind-borne ashes and fiery arrows,
suddenly assailing the city.
The Duke, with white-feathered fan commanding the army,
and red silk measuring the water,
for over seventy days,
only then could he loosen his garments.
The court, considering that Jìn, by capturing Xiàyáng,
first opened the way for the policy of destroying Guó;
that Qín, by opening Wǔsuì,
first inquired into the plan for annexing Hán,
therefore sent a relay carriage to summon the Duke,
appointing him as commander of Rénshòu Fortress.
The Qí generals Duàn Xiàoxiān and Húlǜ Míngyuè,
deployed troops to secure Lǒng,
intending to aid Yíyáng.
The Duke, with his back to the Luò River and facing Xióng Mountain,
arrayed the central army and spread out the vanguard,
seizing the moment in one battle,
caused Yíyáng to surrender.
His fief was increased by five hundred households,
he was advanced to Pillar of State Grand General,
this being the record of the Ministry of Merit.
In the first year of Jiàndé,
he was appointed Grand Minister of Works.
In the second year,
he was transferred to Junior Guardian.
In the three ranks of the Jī court,
the Junior Guardian came first;
among the five offices of the Yán rectification,
the Winter Office was in the north.
Frequently honored with appointments,
this is called worthy and capable.
In the third year,
he was appointed Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Commander of All Military Affairs of the Six Provinces of Xiāng, Yǐng, Chāng, Fēng, Táng, and Cài, and Governor of Xiāngzhōu.
Between the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
not even chickens or dogs were startled;
below Fán and Xiāng,
there were even more officials and carriages.
Then, as the Three Xiāng were remote and distant,
times encountered the entry of owls;
the Five Streams were low and damp,
sometimes one saw kites flying.
His old illness increased,
and he passed away at the provincial garrison.
The Son of Heaven painted the Pavilion of Ascending Mist,
speaking in remembrance of old ministers;
leaving the Palace of Peaceful Joy,
truly longing for a worthy mentor.
There was an edict posthumously granting him certain offices,
according to ritual.
On the twenty-fifth day of the fourth month of the fourth year, he was returned for burial at the mountain of the garrison of Gāopíng in Yuánzhōu.
The dependent state's black-armored troops,
light chariots and armored warriors,
all followed the rites of General of Agile Cavalry Huò,
and the burial of General Wèi.
Alas, how magnificent!
The Duke entered official service for forty-five years,
personally experienced one hundred battles.
Wounds pierced through his body,
his suffering surpassed Cáo Shēn;
scraping the bone to apply medicine,
his deeds exceeded Guān Yǔ.
Yet his demeanor was resolute and brave,
his bearing deep and majestic,
serving his parents without concealment or offense.
His learning was not confined to the classics,
but broadly surveyed books and records;
in military matters he did not solely follow antiquity,
yet naturally mastered strategies of alliance and confrontation.
The divinations of "Qīng Wū" and "Jiǎ Yǐ,"
the astrological changes of "Bái Mǎ,"
the calculations of the Nine Palaces,
the ambushes and rises of the Three Gates,
the archery methods of the Celestial Bow,
the camp diagrams of Tài Yǐ,
all were memorized by heart,
as if pointing to his palm.
Capturing the Qīng Dú troops,
he indeed had secret plans;
burning the grain at Wū Cháo,
he originally left no flawed strategy.
The retreat of the Xī Líng bandits,
could be known by counting on fingers;
the return of the Nánjùn army,
awaited with markers planted.
He often wished to grasp the golden drum and question the King of Wú,
to wield the carved spear and reclaim the land of Qí,
but his ambition was unfulfilled,
and his loyalty ended in death.
His heir, Gōng, and others,
filial piety pure and deep,
observed mourning beyond ritual norms.
Facing his thatched mourning hut,
the catalpa trees grew cold;
hearing his sorrowful weeping,
nesting birds descended at night.
Alas, how grievous!
Thus the inscription says:
Tiān Qí's waters merge,
Rì Guān's mountains connect.
Soldiers strong in Eastern Chǔ,
lands distant from Western Yān.
The five ministers all upright,
the three kings equally worthy.
Divine dragons rise again,
flaming elephants reignite.
Virtue from Heaven,
your ancestors, your father.
The sacred mountain sent down its spirit,
giving birth to Shēn and Fǔ.
Northern gate's beam and pillar,
western region's clouds and rain.
Courage awed Yān city,
name inscribed on Hàn's pillar.
The Duke began as a youth,
bearing his demeanor through generations.
Fierce beasts did not startle him,
domestic fowl could respond.
Studied swordsmanship from a thousand schools,
read books of six dynasties.
Exhausted in loyalty,
never violated reverence and love.
He counted military provisions,
he held military tallies.
Poured sand to form ramparts,
gathered stones to create diagrams.
Winds and clouds, favorable or adverse,
camp formations, isolated or void.
Spirit rain, gongs resounding,
beacon fires, flying foxes.
Huái Yīn received the mandate,
the Chariot and Cavalry General ascended the altar.
The Duke as senior general,
shared office with these.
Burned Chǔ on the Xiàjiāng,
devoured Hán on the Shàngdì.
Merits pushed onto the jade table,
strategies settled on the pearl tray.
Heaven has three steps,
the Duke received its command.
The state has six ministers,
the Duke followed its governance.
Terrace stars shone together,
scholar's court doubly reflected.
Assisted in cultivating the seven virtues,
planned with the eight instruments of power.
Belly full of spirit and energy,
heart open like a bright mirror.
Fú Bō received the sacrificial meat,
Lóu Chuán pushed the carriage wheel.
The eastern road not followed,
the southern campaign not returned.
A well where cinnabar was drunk,
springs watered, no chrysanthemums.
Merits preserved in Liǔlín,
body lies in Mánmù.
Moved the mat, returned for burial,
carried the coffin over mountains.
Straw figures at Lǒng's waters,
mournful dirges at the long wall.
Mountains like Běi Máng,
trees like Dōng Píng.
Pine gates, stones rise,
stele characters, gold born.
Vast, vast rivers and mountains,
lonely, lonely descendants.
Weeping blood, walking on foot,
rushing and toiling a thousand miles.
The Filial Waters dried first,
sorrowful clouds then arose.
Generations count the living and dead,
grief and honor from start to end.
○From "Wényuàn Yīnghuá" 905.
Also briefly seen in "Yìwén Lèijù" 46.
〈Stele Inscription for Ěr Mián Yǒng, Pillar of State Grand General, Grand Governor, and Governor of Tóngzhōu of the Zhōu Dynasty〉
〈Stele Inscription for Ěr Mián Yǒng, Pillar of State Grand General, Grand Governor, and Governor of Tóngzhōu of the Zhōu Dynasty〉
The Duke, named Yǒng,
courtesy name Yǒng Bīn,
was from Língquán Village, Shíchéng County, Liáodōng Commandery, Dōng Yān.
His original surname was Duàn.
In ancient times, Chāng Yì dwelled on high ground,
first dividing the surname from Ruò Shuǐ;
Gòng Shū fled into exile,
beginning the clan of the capital city.
The recluse of Xī Hé,
defended Wèi and repelled Qín;
the general of Běi Yuè,
awed the Hú and served Jìn.
Thereafter residing in Běi Dài,
they were first enfeoffed at Liáo Shuǐ,
recorded in historical texts,
can be briefly stated.
Grandfather Yuán,
General Who Guards the West, Governor of Féng Yì.
Father Rú,
General Who Pacifies the East, Credential Bearer, Commander of Military Affairs of Héng, Yān, and Shuò Three Provinces, Governor of Héng Province.
The Duke, just reaching adulthood,
encountered chaos and displacement,
galloping between passes and frontiers,
early harboring ambitions of alliance and confrontation.
Military formations, square or round,
needed no labor of gathering rice;
mountains and rivers, their shape and situation,
required no unrolling of maps.
In the fifth year of Zhèng Guāng of Wèi, he entered service,
beginning as Palace Guard General.
In the third year of Xiào Chāng,
added General Soaring Dragon.
In the second year of Yǒng Píng,
appointed General Who Pacifies the East, Military Commissioner.
At Zhōng Yān establishing righteousness,
meritorious planning came first,
rewarded as Founding Baron of Cāngquán County,
with a fief of one hundred households.
That year, the Huái and Féi encroached aggressively,
the southern borders levied troops,
the Duke received the sacrificial meat leading a flank army,
achieving three victories in one month.
In the past, Zhāng Liáo suddenly arrived.
◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇County Founding Earl,
with a fief of five hundred households,
advanced to the rank of Marquis.
In the first year of Yǒngxī,
he was appointed as Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Left Radiance and Prosperity.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi specially summoned him to serve as Grand Governor of the Inner Palace.
Mǎ Wǔ was cautious,
serving King Xiāo within the bedchamber;
Diǎn Wéi was loyal and brave,
accompanying Empress Wèi in the palace.
At that time, the rebel commander Yuán Bó
plundered cities and towns,
stretching west from Tóng and Hán,
and east to Gǒng and Luò.
The Grand Governor of the Capital Region requested seven thousand cavalry,
but the Duke said:
"This rebel has no other strategy,
and will soon scatter like birds.
I only request five hundred cavalry,
and I will capture him alive with ease."
The court praised his strategy,
and the people rejoiced at the removal of this scourge.
Soon, chaos and turmoil multiplied,
the people were uprooted and displaced,
the imperial carriage fled west,
and the ancestral temples moved north.
The Duke, with profound insight into celestial phenomena,
deeply understood the cycles of fate,
and together with his brothers planned for self-preservation,
beheaded the Western Central General,
sent his head to the Guān region,
and was rewarded with the title of Kāiguó Zǐ of Chāngpíng County,
with a fief of three hundred households.
In the first year of Dàtǒng,
he was appointed as Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Governor, and Prefect of Běixú Province.
He pacified the Dòu army,
recaptured Hóngnóng,
fought at Shāyuàn and Héqiáo,
and in all these battles, the Duke was among the first to ascend,
personally facing the enemy's vanguard.
His strategies and adaptability
are fully recorded in the Bureau of Merits.
His fief was increased by eight hundred households,
bringing the total to two thousand households,
and he was promoted to the rank of Kāiguó Gōng of Wòyáng County,
appointed to oversee military affairs in Nánfén Province and serve as Prefect of Nánfén Province.
In the fourteenth year,
his fief was increased by three hundred households,
and he was transferred to the position of Grand Governor.
That same year, he was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry, and given the rank of Yítóng Sānsī,
with the additional title of Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant.
In the sixteenth year,
he was appointed General of Agile Cavalry, granted the authority to establish a personal administration,
and given the additional title of Palace Attendant.
Soon after, he was appointed to oversee military affairs in Héng Province and serve as Prefect of Héng Province.
Later, he was transferred to serve as Prefect of Yún Province.
In ancient times, when the Xuānqiū clan divided,
there were fourteen people of different surnames;
when Fēngyì established its lords,
there were forty states in the alliance.
Emperor Wén, the Great Ancestor, swept across the Guān and Hé regions,
dividing the world into three parts.
Those from Yǐngchuān who followed him
shared the bond of hometown kinship;
old friends from Xīnfēng
were not without the ties of humble origins.
Ninety-nine new surnames were established,
and thirty-six states were preserved.
The old lineage was restored to the surname Ěrmián.
His fief was increased by one thousand households,
and he was promoted to the rank of Kāiguó Gōng of Guǎngchéng Commandery.
Soon after, he was appointed to oversee military affairs in Wén Province and serve as Prefect of Wén Province.
The state, with Yùmén blocking the west,
had long toiled at its outposts;
with Yángguān pasturing to the north,
it was often troubled by wind and dust.
In the second year of Wǔchéng,
an imperial edict promoted the Duke to oversee military affairs in Guā Province and serve as Prefect of Guā Province.
Thus, his fame spread to Zǐ Ridge,
and his reputation shook Yú Pass.
Wúléi trembled at his might,
and Guìshuāng cherished his kindness.
In the third year of Bǎodìng,
he returned to court,
and was appointed as Grand Master of the Ministry of Works,
soon transferred to Military Commander.
The Ministry of War,
awaited the white dew to train troops;
the Ministry of Works,
recorded the dark clouds to assign duties.
In the fourth year,
his fief was increased by three hundred households,
bringing the total to three thousand nine hundred households.
That year, he was appointed Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Grand General, and Governor,
commanding the Left Eighth Army,
overseeing military affairs.
In the morning, he ascended as a senior general,
in the evening, he met with common soldiers.
In matters of interaction,
he observed the situation and withdrew.
In the second year of Tiānhé,
he concurrently served as Junior Minister of Justice.
Among the three degrees, there is a star named Celestial Prison;
among the eight trigrams, the Kǎn trigram symbolizes penal law.
The Duke's severity was not as harsh as autumn thistles,
nor was his strictness as scorching as summer sun.
The people understood the law,
and did not regard prison officials as supreme;
the officials knew the penal code,
and dared not intimidate with the ashes of the dead.
He also served as Commander of the Third Army of the Left Wing,
and was ordered to lead troops
to the north for training.
When Hán Xìn entered the passes,
he immediately enforced military discipline;
when Chén Nóng received the edict,
he still studied military texts.
How could it be only the fine families of the six commanderies,
or the knights of the five camps,
who recognized the orderly banners from afar,
and discerned the towering spirit from a distance?
Braving frost and dew,
drums and banners galloped.
Suddenly, he fell ill,
and his condition worsened severely.
On the sixteenth day of the sixth month in the fifth year,
he passed away in Hègé City,
at the age of sixty-eight.
The general died in retreat,
and the three armies marched in mourning;
the Protector-General's remains returned,
and border regions held memorial ceremonies.
On the twenty-third day of the ninth month,
his coffin arrived in the capital.
The emperor attended the funeral,
and all officials came to pay their respects.
An edict dispatched Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Yítóng Sānsī Hèbá Guǐ to oversee the funeral arrangements.

Another edict dispatched Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Yítóng Sānsī Hédòulíng Liàng to confer posthumously the titles of Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Pillar of State Grand General, overseeing military affairs in Tóng, Huá, Yí, Fū, and Dān Provinces, and Prefect of Tóng Province.
He was posthumously honored as Duke Gōng.
On the fifth day of the eleventh month of that year,
he was buried in Gāosī Village, Gāoyáng Plain, south of the capital.
His wife, née Hèlián,
was the daughter of Yuè, Prefect of Yǎn Province.
At the age of fourteen,
she married into the Ěrmián family.
She was enfeoffed as Lady of Lǔchéng County,
later promoted to Lady of Qīngyīn Commandery,
and further promoted to Lady of Guǎngchéng State.
Respectful, virtuous, and graceful,
a model of talent and virtue,
her four virtues shone brightly,
and the three stars glowed even brighter.
The wives of the Three Dukes
are seen in her.
She passed away in the twelfth month of the first year of Jiàndé,
at the age of fifty-eight.
In the first month of the second year,
she was laid to rest in the Gāosī tomb.
The tomb of Liú, Prefect of Jīng Province,
was jointly buried on the southern bank of the Xiāng River;
the tomb of General Wèi,
shared the same grave at the foot of Lú Mountain.
Alas, how sorrowful!
The eldest son, Jí,
Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, General of Yítóng,
concurrently served as Grand Master of the Ministry of War.
Pure in filial piety, he served his parents;
loyal and steadfast, he served the state.
He upheld propriety and righteousness,
and his reputation was well-known.
The inscription reads:
The Xuāntái received the clan name,
and Ruòshuǐ descended to dwell.
Xīchéng had Zhòngyìn,
Běilù had Zhìyú.
Mountains and rivers were majestic and fierce,
customs were flourishing and sparse.
In the past, our frontier passes,
followed the ways of war.
Times encountered uprooting,
the world faced turbulent waves.
To the north, sealed in Dàijùn,
to the east, holding Liáohé.
The land was not yet unified,
heaven still sent calamities.
Our lord restored glory,
succeeding in culture and following in martial steps.
He governed three frontiers,
and concurrently administered six auxiliary regions.
Elegant and common observed the customs,
the capital pavilion awaited rain.
No interrogating officials were encountered,
no sound of alarm drums was heard.
The lord, carrying the age,
stood out with this fine reputation.
In filial piety, he had three virtues,
in loyalty, he served only one lord.
At Mǎlíng, he resolved peril,
at Liáochéng, he settled disputes.
Military defenses were full as the moon,
battles avoided welcoming clouds.
The commander of Chángsōng,
the general of Xìliǔ.
Having governed Huáihǎi,
and also guarded Héng and Dài.
High walls leaned against the passes,
long pavilions pierced the frontiers.
The drum of covenant oversaw alliances,
Officials could not deceive,
soldiers dared not betray.
At Yùguān, he left his rule,
at Fénhǎi, he left his love.
When the great general received the edict,
the lord ascended his altar.
The six ministers all attended to affairs,
the lord assisted their offices.
Yílíng burned Chǔ,
Shàngdǎng divided Hán.
The army camped at Cānhé,
battles were fought at Gāolán.
As years deepened, hardships arose,
when fortune passed, disasters were born.
The high platform cracked the mountains,
the secondary general’s star fell.
Barren land wept in sorrow,
the white tiger mourned and cried.
Bows hung in the spirit tent,
horses tethered at the frontier wilds.
Smoke congealed, unmoving,
springs froze, soundless.
The Son of Heaven grieved deeply,
pursuing with posthumous honors.
The ritual officials bestowed the edict,
burial near the imperial tomb, receiving land.
Seals and ribbons were called the decree,
clothes and coverings were called the burial garments.
The dark burial was arranged in order,
the yellow cypress was in place.
From this, what age is it?
From now, how many springs?
Trees became the stable shrine,
mounds became valley spirits.
Who would know the Cloud Pavilion,
where his name rests among the meritorious officials.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 905.
“Stele Inscription for Duke Hélóu, Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry of the Zhōu Dynasty”
“Stele Inscription for Duke Hélóu, Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry of the Zhōu Dynasty”
In ancient times, Xuānqiū bestowed the clan name,
initially dividing the surnames of brothers;
Ruòshuǐ descended to dwell,
first establishing the states of feudal lords.
From then on, they took office as clan,
and took land as lineage,
like water branching and dividing,
this can be known.
The lord’s given name was Cí,
courtesy name Yuándá,
originally surnamed Zhāng,
from Dōngwǔchéng in Qīnghé.
Serving in the Zhōu,
Zhāng Zhòng was known for filial piety and friendship;
advising in the Jìn,
Zhāng Yàn was a worthy minister.
In Hán, there was Kāidì,
then for five generations the state was strong;
in Zhào, there was Mèngtán,
then the three ministers did not wage war.
Grandfather Qìng,
in youth practiced as a frontier general,
relying on wisdom and courage.
Although he again had five cartloads of bamboo slips,
he did not seek the title of Erudite;
with one volume of military texts,
he deemed himself a general.
With the horn-tipped bow in hand,
there would surely be no invasion from Qí or Lǔ;
with the lotus inserted at his waist,
he greatly possessed the aura of the dragon.
He served as Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry, Commandant with Equal Honor to the Three Ministers, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, and Founding Baron of Bàchéng County,
and was posthumously awarded as Prefect of Hézhōu.
Father Càn,
a son of lords and grandsons of dukes,
had foundations under heaven;
skilled bowyers and skilled smiths,
had hereditary crafts in family tradition.
In books, he knew the Hundred Schools;
in swords, he could match a thousand men.
The Three Locusts used the tripod to depict things,
knowing their divine deceit;
the Five Ranks used the jade tablet as a banner of auspice,
guarding their palaces.
The lord, with talent and reputation,
possessed both.

He ended as Commissioner with Discretionary Powers, Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry, Commandant with Equal Honor to the Three Ministers, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, and Founding Duke of Wǔdìng County,
and was posthumously awarded as Prefect of Hézhōu.
The lord alone received the essence of mountains and peaks,
imbibed the energy of stars and constellations,
in his childhood years,
just able to wear clothes.
Bamboo horses came to welcome him,
already known by name to Guō Jí;
goat carts on the road,
immediately appreciated by Wáng Chéng.
How could it be merely a child understanding the classics,
a scholar discussing the hexagrams?
As for the clear discourse of the Dhyāna river,
the lofty talk of autumn waters,
thus with debate he broke the turtle forest,
his voice sped through the deer wilds.
In the state’s official clans,
the lord was the foremost surname.
He began his career as Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry, Commandant with Equal Honor to the Three Ministers,
inherited the title as duke,
with a fief totaling one thousand six hundred households.
At the age of twenty, he entered the court,
his summons and reception were highly favored.
The high ministers of Hàn and Wèi,
truly had no such comparison;
the regional lords of the central court,
rarely had such years.
The Grand Steward, bearing the responsibility of the pivot,
was diligent in royal strategy,
cherishing the lord’s loyalty and stoutness,
entrusting him with claws and teeth.
He garrisoned the left wing’s trusted troops,
and went out as defense commander of Liángzhōu.
Huáyáng to the western extreme,
the Hànshuǐ flowing east,
Bā and Pú already pacified,
Chénlí then quieted.
In the fourth year of Bǎodìng,
the royal army campaigned north,
because of the lord’s valor,
he was summoned to lead troops.
The army descended to Yíyáng,
he personally ascended Hángǔ,
intending to burn the city of White Horse,
to overturn the ramparts of Blackbird’s Nest.
Then midway there was heavy rain,
and they did not succeed in besieging Yuán;
the army commander heard of mourning,
and did not complete the invasion of Sòng.
The Pillar of State, Prince of Zhào,
is the ninth younger brother of the present sovereign.
In civil affairs, he submitted memorials like the Prince of Héjiān;
in military matters, he deployed formations like the Prince of Rènchéng.
He governed the strategic post at Mínqiū,
and unfurled his banners over the Jǐn River.
The customs of the White Tiger tribes were difficult to pacify,
and the alliances with the Yellow Dragon people were unstable.
With your wisdom and strategy,
you entered the court to assist the central authority.
In the first year of the Tiānhé era,
you were appointed Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Grand Governor, and Administrator of the Office of the Pillar of State Commander-in-Chief,
and subsequently transferred to the position of Military Marshal,
while your other official titles and fiefs remained unchanged.
When Xiàngrú journeyed west,
he carved inscriptions upon the sacred mountains;
when Marquis Wǔ campaigned south,
he floated boats upon the Lú River.
Compared to the present day,
how could they alone be considered exceptional?
In the nine-rank assessment of merit,
he was placed in the upper-middle grade.
In the fourth year,
he entered the court,
and returned to serve the ministerial ranks.
He then received the post of Grand Master of the Ministry of Transport,
and was dispatched on a mission to the State of Qí.
Seeking alliances beyond the borders,
he employed the rituals of peaceful neighborliness;
entering the state and hearing of mourning,
he still observed the rites of attending a funeral.
"He may be set to face south [i.e., rule a state]" —
is this not said of him?
Soon after, in his original office,
he entered to administer military justice.
As for military texts like those of the Wèi River,
he kept them in mind as his aspiration;
the battle formations of Xuānqiū,
where stones were gathered to form encirclements.
Since he obtained troops who were not wearied,
and soldiers harbored no resentment or slander,
he entered to attend within the imperial precincts,
and further held the title of Commandant with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies.
The guesthouses and city walls,
the gates, barriers, and household registries,
all relied on his patrols and vigilance,
and were jointly managed by his office.
The close ministers of the imperial city,
the intimate relatives of the ducal house,
when encountering him, felt as if meeting the Director of Retainers,
or feared him like the Metropolitan Official.
Subsequently, the solitary city's old woman of Zhèng,
could not divine his years;
the old man of Fú on the Bā River,
could not cure his illness.
At the age of thirty-three,
he suddenly departed from the official residence.
When Lǚ Zǐmíng's illness grew severe,
the King of Wú sighed with grief;
when Ruǎn Yuányú long departed,
the Lord of Wèi was deeply sorrowful.
There was an edict bestowing upon him the posthumous title of such-and-such official,
in accordance with ritual.
On a day in the third month of the fourth year of the Jiàndé era, he was returned for burial at Jìn Mountain in Yuànchuān Commandery of Hézhōu.
The Duke was from a fine family of the six commanderies,
a prominent clan of Xīhé,
the land vigorous with the Metal Phase,
the people heroic with frontier spirit.
The seven scrolls of *Military Texts*,
floated down the river;
the three chapters of *Archery Methods*,
descended by night from the celestial bow.
Banners and pennants never rested,
alarm gongs constantly startled,
yet he still managed to read books on horseback,
and practice rites within the army.
Tàishǐ Zǐyì excelled in planning and strategy,
Zhūgě Gōngxiū was adept at comforting and commanding.
For four generations, Commandants with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies,
for seven generations, Governors of Hézhōu,
bells and tripods formed rows,
official caps and canopies cast continuous shade,
truly what is called "living as a noble minister,
dying as a noble spirit."
But because his wandering soul long sojourned abroad,
the return for burial was a distant journey,
the road obstructed, the mountains long,
wife widowed, children young,
mournful sounds filled the wilds,
sorrowful airs connected with the clouds.
Moreover, the pines and catalpas swayed in the wind,
just facing the garrison of Wǔwēi;
the hills and mounds winding far,
directly opposite the city of Líntáo.
Mǎ Yuán died at Wǔxī,
his coffin returned to Huáilǐ;
Liáng Hóng died in Kuàijì,
his wife and children returned to Pínglíng.
Alas, sorrowful indeed!
Distant and rugged is the way.
In former times, before the shrine at Fánchāng,
there was already a stele of yellow gold;
beneath the tomb at Déyáng,
still passed down a stone tablet of blue-green.
This is called inscribing merit,
thus the inscription reads:
For seven leaves they assisted Hàn,
for five generations they served as ministers of Hán.
Loyal ministers entered service,
filial and fraternal held office.
The immortal cavern of Qīngchéng,
the altar of the Yellow Stone shrine.
The terrace fit for running horses,
the writings sufficient to turn back phoenixes.
Martial determination like wind and storm,
the frosty city stern and solemn.
Together galloping two relays,
both sharing twin bamboo staffs.
Generations of inspectors and recommenders,
riding abreast in dragon-embroidered robes.
Grass bending on the green hills,
wind speeding through the red valley.
The age does not lack worthies,
among them stood this noble heir.
In filial piety, he possessed the three virtues,
in loyalty, he had not a second thought.
With sword sufficient to stand firm in person,
with writings fit to be tested face-to-face.
Having grasped the commander's tally,
the high cicada [ornament] moreover adorned his cap.
The tortoise turns on the seal box,
the serpent coils on the ribbon case.
General of the Left and Right,
Regular Attendant before and after.
Following in the steps of the five marquises,
continuing the practices of the three affairs.
Banners over the nine slopes,
prows and stems on the twin streams.
Returning to drive the wooden horses,
again leading the golden oxen.
River waves where brocade falls,
fire wells where stars float.
Libation wine gazes upon the emperor,
peaceful songs for the Marquis of Shǔ.
Receiving the sacrificial meat at Héyáng,
a flank army at Luòpǔ.
Deploying formations at Chénggāo,
connecting banners at Guǎngwǔ.
Day troops reducing cookfires,
night camps with many drums.
Arrows bring down six elk,
spearpoints crush nine tigers.
Swiftly passing from the human world,
suddenly now is ancient times.
Malign stars arose in pairs,
physicians startled by the two demons.
The wandering soul communicated in dreams,
speaking of returning to the old grave mound.
Purple clay bestowed cinnabar,
yellow heartwood granted for the journey.
The road ascends Shíniǔ,
the path enters Jīnchéng.
Cold passes with trees straight,
autumn frontier with clouds level.
Sword buried with joined pillars,
writings stored in carved pillars.
Marquis Wǔ became a temple,
Luán Duke became an altar.
Cloud canopies lowly approach,
rainbow garments descend in profusion.
The stele pillows on a golden tortoise,
pines stretch across stone horses.
Eternal is his person and age,
his name remains in Huáxià.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 906.
〈Inscription for the Spirit Way Stele of Pǔtún Wēi, Duke of Sù State, Pillar of State of Zhōu, and Governor of Hézhōu〉 with Preface
〈Inscription for the Spirit Way Stele of Pǔtún Wēi, Duke of Sù State, Pillar of State of Zhōu, and Governor of Hézhōu〉 with Preface
The Duke, named Wēi,
style Mǒu,
was a man of Luòyáng in Hénán.
His original surname was Xīn,
and he was from Lǒngxī.
His foundation was like the source of a river;
he descended from the lineage of Shāngqiū.
Settled in Dà Bó,
he indeed established his dwelling;
enfeoffed at Xiǎo Xīn,
thus forming his surname.
Therefore, when the Three Rivers loosened their hair,
Xīn Yǒu grasped the opportunity to serve;
when the Eight Trigrams divined the lines,
Xīn Liào possessed the insight to know men.
Assisting in governance as the supreme general of the Eastern Capital,
he caused the Wèi Emperor to disrobe;
as a meritorious minister of the Western Kingdom like Wǔxián,
he made the Hàn King push the carriage.
His grandfather, Dàhàn,
was Governor of Wèi Prefecture.
His father, Shēng,
was the Four-Sides Commander-in-Chief and Grand Governor of Hé Prefecture.
Noble ministers of Lǒngyòu,
prominent clans of Héxī,
dukes and marquises following in succession,
governors and shepherds riding abreast.
Together they gained renown that shook Chángyú,
and fame that dominated Gāoliǔ.
The Duke, endowed with the essence of mountains and rivers,
born under the stars,
with hair bound in youth, dignified and firm,
by childhood had perfected his virtue.
Like a vast expanse of clear waves,
or a marker raised a thousand ren high,
his sharpness already lofty,
his brilliance far-reaching.
As a youth in blue collar learning swordsmanship,
he was already praised by his lord;
as a boy discussing military affairs,
he immediately assisted in the strategies of the central army.
In the first year of Yǒngxī,
he entered official service,
and was granted the post of Direct Assault Commander-in-Chief.
When Emperor Wén of Tàizǔ washed away the shame of the former ruler,
and achieved the merit of the Earl of the West,
first dividing the Hónggōu,
and initially ascending the Hángǔ Pass,
the Duke lifted his robes and washed his hair,
grasped his sword at the camp gate,
was welcomed with the washing of feet abandoned,
and descended the guest steps to be consulted.
From then on, he resided within the tent,
and still served as Direct Attendant,
appointed as General of Pacifying Distant Lands, Supervisor of the Forest of Plumes, and Founding Earl of Báitǔ County,
with a fief of five hundred households.
In the first year of Dàtǒng,
following the welcoming of the imperial carriage,
he was advanced in rank to Marquis,
with an increased fief of three hundred households,
and additionally appointed as Champion General and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
then transferred to Grand Commander-in-Chief.
The Duke excelled in employing troops,
and was adept at comforting and controlling them.
From attacking Luòyáng,
pacifying Hóngnóng,
fighting at Héqiáo,
to leveling Shāyuàn,
he braved blades and charged the front,
facing no enemy formation that could withstand him.
Moreover, with a bow of six jun strength,
and armor of seven layers of rhinoceros hide,
his gate often hung with helmets,
his arrows always hitting the saddle.
Weapons piled up like mountains,
cattle and horses filled the valleys,
military officials calculated merits,
the Ministry of Honors rewarded with strategies,
appointing him Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Silver and Blue Glorious Grand Master,
advancing his rank to Duke,
with an increased fief of eight hundred households.
In ancient times, receiving the mandate with the red tally,
Hán Xìn matched a thousand li;
training troops at Báidì,
Zhāng Fēi rivaled ten thousand men.
Comparing to today,
this refers to the Duke.
In the fifth year,
he was appointed Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs of Yáng Prefecture, and Governor of Yáng Prefecture.
Sailing on the rivers and seas,
reaching the Huái and Sì rivers,
where bamboos and reeds spread,
and precious stones were arranged in order.
In the thirteenth year,
he was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry, Commandant with Equal Honors to the Three Excellencies,
soon promoted to General of Agile Cavalry with Separate Headquarters,
and additionally granted the surname Pǔtún,
thus becoming an official clan.
Entering to attend in the military tent,
going out to command military strategies,
he established headquarters at Yángguān,
and raised banners in the Vast Sea.
Thus he could submit memorials to Hàn,
and be employed as of the same clan;
contending for precedence in Zhōu,
still without differing surnames.
In the sixteenth year,
he was appointed to All Military Affairs of Fū Prefecture and Governor of Fū Prefecture.
The Duke frequently governed two regions,
his administration enlightened and divine,
tigers left Xīhé,
owls moved from the Eastern Commandery.
Auspicious airs by the river's edge,
specially manifested his integrity and fairness;
divine light in the sacrifices of Fū,
everywhere illuminated his uprightness.
When Wèi ended its heavenly mandate,
and Zhōu received the renewal,
the clear mandate had shifted,
and the constant principles were sometimes changed.
In the first year of Zhōu,
he was reappointed as Grand General, Founding Duke of Fúhǎn Commandery,
with an increased fief of one thousand households.
Receiving edicts in the army,
not merely discussing the merits of northern campaigns;
the great general ascending the altar,
needing no strategy for eastern return.
Deploying formations at Tàipíng,
he opened the road to Yīnjìn;
linking troops at Guǎngwǔ,
he received the city of Xíngyáng.
Fighting at Dānshān,
moving camp to Báibì,
in all these, his courage topped the three armies,
his fame surpassed the five generals.
In the fourth year of Bǎodìng,
he was appointed Commander-in-Chief of Níng Prefecture.
Guarding its northern gate,
he was already entrusted by the State of Zhèng;
defending its western border,
he feared no pressure from the Qín outpost.
Thus building the walls of Pínggāng,
the men of Wèi folded their hands;
garrisoning the marshes of Xíngbō,
the Liáng clan trembled with fear.
The court had inner and outer kinship with the Duke,
ordering the Duke to follow the nobility of the imperial relatives' quarter,
and thus gave the daughter of Emperor Wén of Wèi to be the Duke's wife.
Thereby, to the left of Chángmén,
a separate garden for the princess was opened;
beside Zhuólóng,
a residence for the royal princess was established.
In the fifth year,
he was summoned to the capital,
and appointed Junior Minister of War.
Expecting him in charge of military affairs,
they regarded the Duke as Wèi Jiàng;
assisting in the central army,
they regarded the Duke as Xún Shǒu.
How could one merely call him the Quail Fire,
or refer to him as Jìnyún?
That year,
he was sent to lead troops out to Xīliáng Prefecture,
to respectfully welcome the Tūjué Empress.
Jì Lièrú came,
the minister acting on behalf of the ruler to meet her;
traveling with his clan named,
honoring the ruler's command.
In the first year of the Tiānhé era,
he was appointed Pillar of State,
and made Grand Minister of Justice.
The Pillar of State of Chǔ,
was likened to the southern fire;
the Minister of Justice of Xuān,
was compared to the western clouds.
All these appointments were conferred upon the Duke,
truly capable of appointing worthy officials.
In the second year of the Jiàndé era,
he was appointed Junior Tutor.
In the fourth year,
he was appointed Commander-in-Chief of Hézhōu and Military Governor of the Seven Provinces,
and concurrently became the Grand Impartial and Just of Hézhōu.
The Duke’s ancestral home
was originally in this region;
serving again as its governor,
he frequently returned in glory.
Like the dragon offspring of Xiāngchéng,
he returned once more to his ponds and terraces;
like the immortal of Guìyáng,
he came back to his native village.
The elders and close guests,
celebrated with joyous songs;
carriages drawn by four horses,
were admired throughout the realm.
In the first year of the Xuānzhèng era,
he was appointed Supreme Pillar of State,
and additionally made Junior Tutor.
Paired with the highest ministers,
he assisted in the strategic plans at Xuánhù;
residing in the capital,
he truly possessed strategies like those at Yíqiáo.
His title was changed to Duke of Sù,
with a combined estate of five thousand five hundred households.
Shooting geese in the old park,
dancing cranes in the remaining city,
he once crossed the Suānzǎo River,
and faced the bamboo groves of Qíyuán.
When he came to court at Jiànzhāng,
the Son of Heaven would rise from his mat;
when he visited the imperial relatives’ quarter,
all the nobles would descend the steps.
Thus his deeds filled heaven and earth,
and his name was known throughout the four seas.
Just as he was about to brilliantly assist five sovereigns,
and participate in planning the seven administrative affairs,
heaven’s pestilence gave no warning,
