and he passed away at his residence,
at the age of sixty-nine.
When Liǔ Zhuāng announced the funeral,
it grieved the pillars of the state;
when Zhèng Qiáo was said to be gone,
he received the rites due to a feudal lord.
An imperial edict posthumously awarded him the office of
and the posthumous title of Duke,
in accordance with ritual.
On a certain day in the seventh month of the first year of the present Kāihuáng era,
he was returned for burial at Yuànchuān Township, Jīnchéng Commandery, Hézhōu.
The mountain path leads to the foot of Lǒng,
the land enters the frontier plains;
gazing at Jīshí Mountain along the river,
facing Kōngtóng Mountain as one descends the slope.
Black armor and yellow-hearted cypress,
winding through watchtowers and barriers;
when the cloud-offerings were cleared away,
only then were the elm-carriages wearied.
As for planting trees on the returned soil,
and raising the great mound,
in the end, a stele like that of Yǐngchuān is needed,
to manifest the monument of Huàyīn.
His eldest son, Yítóng Yǒngdá,
renowned for his filial nature,
observed mourning with proper ritual.
Lamenting the sea’s change into fields,
fearing the mountains’ flight and earth’s severance,
he engraved stone in the burial field,
and thus composed this inscription:
Descendant of Shǎodiǎn,
son of Xuánwáng.
A rainbow pierced the moon,
metal succeeded water.
Descending to the Zhōu,
dukes and marquises began anew.
Customs and climates,
mountains, rivers, inside and out.
The river connects to Jīshí,
the mountains are girded by Kōngtóng.
Qín pavilions northward,
Hàn envoys westward.
The metal phase’s vigor strong,
the land’s force breeds heroic men.
Towering high integrity,
awe-inspiring, forthright demeanor.
Ancestors shielded the realm,
the turbid Hé, the clear Wèi.
Two lands of wise counsel,
twin radiances shining bright.
Water without other hues,
clouds without different breaths.
As official, as commoner,
only mindful, only reverent.
The Duke succeeding his age,
truly possessed heroic spirit.
Descending deity of Central Peak,
revolving stars arrayed in script.
Phoenixes soared and glanced,
pearl-like forehead, mountain-like brow.
As minister, profound in righteousness’ root;
as son, utmost in heaven’s constant way.
Battle arrays at Luòchéng,
flags and drums at Héqiáo.
Arrows drank from the stone bridge,
swords kindled the bronze pillar.
Together splendid as six elk,
both drawing twin tigers.
Yùmén established as commandery,
Yángguān set up as prefecture.
Twice serving as high minister,
twice as Junior Tutor.
Model for the imperial teacher,
organizer of the state’s course.
Sincerely inheriting lofty virtue,
reverently wise, discerning in counsel.
Not sparing the carriage mat,
who speaks of the warm tree?
Heaven’s way obscure and dim,
years and age swift and fleeting.
The general’s star opened,
the meritorious minister’s tripod sank.
Nine plains, hills and mounds,
mountains, rivers, armored troops.
Precipitous terrain, tortoise woods,
perilous camps, horse caves.
Eternal parting from Xīzhōu,
long farewell to the northern gate.
Mountains spread empty canopies,
wilderness sacrifices, vacant curtains.
Mound-plains, earth remote,
pine-lined path, wind sorrowful.
Inscribed on the stele stone,
engraved with the faithful tortoise.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 911.
“Spirit Way Stele of Duke Mùróng, Pillar of State and Duke of Chǔ of Zhōu, Governor of Qízhōu”
“Spirit Way Stele of Duke Mùróng, Pillar of State and Duke of Chǔ of Zhōu, Governor of Qízhōu”
In ancient times, the Yīn writings praised rewards,
the *Zhōu Lǐ* deliberated on merit,
feudal lords tallied achievements,
great officers proclaimed their deeds.
Only the Grand Tutor Shàngfǔ
and Kūnwú bore inscriptions on precious tripods;
the king’s command to his minister,
at Xúnyì transmitted the gift of an engraved dagger-axe.
Thus it is known that the highest virtue is to establish virtue,
and clearly test it with merit;
in life, there is the honor of illustrious rank,
in death, the nobility of a great name.
Heaven, unkind,
is it not the Duke of Chǔ?
Worthy to have his virtue displayed on the resonant bell,
his merit engraved on sacrificial vessels,
to manifest his splendid beauty,
and proclaim his grand achievements.
The Duke, named Níng,
courtesy name Yǒng’ān,
was from Túhé in Chānglí.
The Commandant governed the ministers of six counties,
the famous mountain was called assistant of the five peaks.
Yān’s Grand Ancestor, Emperor Wén, Mùróng Huàng,
as a hero of his age,
possessed all north of the Hé.
To the southern borders of Zhào,
he moreover built a royal city;
in the northern lands of Jì,
it still became a rising state.
The Duke, being a descendant of Huàng,
his family for generations dwelled on Yān’s frontier.
The High Ancestor (Gāozǔ),
Palace Attendant, Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Commander of All Military Affairs Within and Beyond the Capital, Grand Guardian, and Recorder of the Imperial Secretariat.
During the era of the Prince of Běidì, Mùróng Chāo,
he served as a protective screen for the royal house.
This is detailed in the *Yān Record*,
and he can indeed be praised for it.
The Great-Grandfather,
the Prefect of the Imperial Secretariat,
due to the troubles of the Wei court,
changed the family surname to Dòulú,
and they remained an official clan.
The Grandfather served Emperor Wénchéng of Wei.
The Father died early.
The court, considering his meritorious service and lineage,
bestowed deep favor in remembrance of the distant past.
In the third year of the Bǎodìng era,
an imperial edict posthumously granted him the titles of Pillar of State General, Junior Mentor, and Duke Who Established the State of Fúlíng Commandery,
with a fief of two thousand households.
The Duke possessed a harmonious and balanced disposition,
and auspicious signs descended from the mountains and rivers.
His exceptional intelligence was evident in his childhood years,
and his mastery of ritual was praised in his youth.
From an early age, he displayed remarkable integrity,
and in childhood, he showed signs of great accomplishment.
When sharing fruit with his brothers,
he was fully aware of yielding and deferring;
when guests untied bells (as gifts),
he never showed a grudging expression.
In the first year of the Yǒng'ān era,
the Grand Tutor, Ěrzhū Tiānguāng,
chief supporter of the Wei court,
held military power west of the Huái River,
and opposed authority south of the Yangtze.
The Duke, then serving as a Separate General,
immediately followed him on campaigns.
From then on, at the Great Wall and Xiáshí,
he was always at the forefront of battle formations;
south of Qín and west of Lǒng,
he constantly faced arrows and stones.
In crushing strongholds and riding the momentum of victory,
none did not charge ahead;
when merits were recorded and rewards distributed,
he was always ranked first.
In the first year of the Yǒngxī era,
he was appointed as a Junior Commander,
and additionally granted drum insignia and military honors,
appointed as Prefect of Sānggān,
and then transferred and promoted to Commander.
That year,
due to the King of Wei's westward journey,
he welcomed the imperial carriage,
and was enfeoffed as Count Who Established the State of Héyáng County,
with an increased fief of three hundred households.
He was soon promoted to Grand Master of the Palace,
his title changed from Count to Marquis,
with the fief increased to a total of nine hundred households.
He was then appointed Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Commander of All Military Affairs in Xiǎn Prefecture, and Governor of Xiǎn Prefecture.
In the fourth year,
he was promoted to General Who Guards the East and Grand Master of the Palace with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon.
That autumn,
during the battle at Héqiáo,
he was first to ascend and break the enemy formation,
and was promoted to General of Chariots and Cavalry and Pillar of State.
In the fifth year,
for his merit at Shāyuàn,
he received additional enfeoffment,
bringing the total to two thousand households.
He was soon appointed Governor of Fū Prefecture,
with the additional title of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
externally deeply entrusted with military command,
and internally serving in the Secretariat.
In the fifteenth year,
he was appointed General of the Right Guard.
In the sixteenth year,
he was appointed Great General.
In the first year of the Later Wei,
he was reappointed Governor of Fū Prefecture.
The Duke, having previously governed there,
firmly declined and did not take up the post.
In the third year,
he was re-enfeoffed as Duke Who Established the State of Wǔyáng Commandery,
appointed Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
his duty being to assist with memorials,
his responsibility encompassing sealing and handling documents,
sharing the duties of the left and right officials,
and concurrently overseeing the selection of candidates.
At that time, due to armed resistance south of the Yangtze,
and the Zhǔgōng Palace facing enemy borders,
military affairs were urgent and alarming,
with arrows and blades crisscrossing.
The Duke received orders and set off at dawn,
the main army opening the way.
He commanded the elite troops of Qín,
combined with the numerous soldiers of Jīng.
Naval forces vied with the power of twin blades,
infantry and cavalry displayed the might of four divisions.
After Yílíng was burned,
and Qiánzhōng was pacified,
he turned the army around, reversed the banners,
laid down armor, and rested the troops.
Later, when Fèng Prefecture rebelled internally,
and Chéngdū was cut off externally,
the Duke again commanded all armies,
mustered chariots and immediately marched,
without shedding blood in battle,
captured them all,
relocated their chieftains,
and accepted their surrender.
The imperial court received the mandate,
and Emperor Wénzǔ carried out the revolution.
The Divine Ancestor selected the worthy and capable,
changed policies and established new institutions.
He then issued a patent,
appointing the Duke as Pillar of State,
with an increased fief of four thousand households.
In the second year,
he was appointed Governor of Tóng Prefecture.
It was the strategic key to the Guānfǔ region,
the lips and teeth of Qín and Jìn.
Registered households were numerous and prosperous,
storehouses and granaries were amply stocked.
This was a responsibility for defending the borders,
not a position for relatives and the worthy to reside in idly.
The Duke raised his banner and served as regional governor,
lifted the carriage curtain and toured his jurisdiction,
implementing the six guidelines of inspection,
and all cities were encouraged.
In the third year,
he was appointed Grand Minister of Justice.
Again, due to his particularly outstanding merit and service,
he was enfeoffed by patent as Duke of Chǔ,
with a fief of ten thousand households,
because he had defeated Hóu Fāngrén and others in Jīng and Shǎn,
and was enfeoffed with that land.
He investigated and rectified royal wrongdoing,
relaxed and tightened punishments and administration.
To suppress violence and cruelty,
he governed with a combination of leniency and severity;
to pacify the distant and be capable with the near,
he then balanced them with harmony and moderation.
When Shùn appointed Gāoyáo,
the unrighteous were kept at a distance;
when Jìn promoted Suí Huì,
all bandits fled.
In the fourth year of the Bǎodìng era,
he was appointed Commander of All Military Affairs in Qí Prefecture and Governor of Qí Prefecture.
A severe and lingering illness persisted.
On the fourth day of the third month in the fifth year of Bǎodìng,
he passed away at his private residence,
at the age of sixty-two.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him a certain office,
and conferred the posthumous title of Duke of [a certain name],
according to ritual.
On the Gēngshēn day of the tenth month,
he was buried at the river of Hóngdú.
Horses were dispatched, the ancestral temple was mourned,
funeral carriages had the right of way on the road,
black armor covered the soldiers of the dependent state,
armored warriors formed the cavalry of light chariots.
He achieved a good end,
honored in life and mourned in death.
Alas, how sorrowful!
The Duke, upholding virtue and embracing wisdom,
embodied the Way and resided in steadfastness,
though honored, he contemplated humility;
though prosperous, he reflected on restraint.
A thousand acres of clear waves
could not alter his purity or turbidity;
a wall a hundred fathoms high
could not measure his depth or shallowness.
In establishing himself and conducting his life,
he dwelled in safety as if on the brink of a fall;
sacrificing himself for righteousness,
he viewed peril as level ground.
As for military strategy and adapting to change,
employing surprises and setting ambushes,
the divinations of Tàiyī and wind angles,
the observations of constant stars and celestial phenomena,
the records of naval battles and formations,
the manuals of powerful crossbows and swift archery—
in all these, he moved in harmony with the subtle and divine,
issuing commands like thunder and lightning.
Where his scaling ladders and assault vehicles advanced,
no city with a hundred towers could stand;
where his long halberds reached,
the fields were cleared of triple-gate formations.
Thus, in beheading generals and capturing banners,
he fought forty-three battles;
in holding high office and receiving generous emoluments,
he served for thirty-seven years.
His martial prowess displayed the righteousness of the seven virtues,
his songs extolled the achievements of the nine merits;
his deeds were recorded in the inscriptions of vessels,
his conduct illuminated the canon of posthumous names.
In the past, when Zāng Wénzhòng passed away,
Mù Shū praised his establishment of words;
when Zhèng Qiáo departed,
Xuānní wept for his enduring love.
The tomb at Déyáng with its blue stone
remains unleveled for a thousand years;
the white tiger stele at Zhījiāng
stands undestroyed for a hundred generations.
Daring to follow this principle,
I thus compose an inscription, saying:
East of the Liáo River,
north of Jìzhōu.
He was called a commandant,
and also named a dependent state.
Gathering courage and remaining valiant,
he left a model for defending the frontiers.
Filial piety was truly the constant of heaven,
loyalty was the virtuous conduct.
Crowned with hereditary honors,
he was a model for his descendants.
Customs were influenced by Yān Dān,
yet his demeanor put Yīng and Lìn to shame.
Toiling in service and travel,
enduring hardship in battle formations.
His bravery surpassed drowning steeds,
his spirit exceeded shattering tiles.
The royal state could produce such a man,
thinking of the many outstanding scholars.
Gentle and respectful,
modest and noble.
Holding the banner and scepter,
he served abroad and in court.
□□ through five reigns,
he established his standard over a thousand li.
In times of change and upheaval,
his name was recorded for meritorious service.
Summoned and appointed at Huáiyīn,
he broke the army at Zhāoyáng.
In charge of penal administration,
he was cautious in legal intricacies.
No sheep were drowned in wine,
no bandits heard of in the reeds.
Campaigning against Bā and Yōng,
he led expeditions across the Jiāng and Hàn.
Commanding six regiments,
his troops comprised seven camps.
Using long-range to strike short,
substantial in the rear, his reputation preceded.
Increasing fortifications to awe the enemy,
reducing cooking fires to conceal troops.
Bells tolled in the night's water-clock,
dew dried under the morning sun.
The villages desolate,
the dwellings and curtains bleak.
A grand stele lowered with the coffin,
the inscribed pall transported in mourning.
The palace overlooked Chǔlǐ,
the terrace tilted like Mèng Cháng's.
Divining the burial date,
distant stars foretold the oracle.
Virtue left behind after death,
fame illuminated the departed world.
The lodge long abandoned,
the spring gate forever closed.
Yàn Yīng mourned for Qí,
Liǔ Zhuāng grieved for Wèi.
Windy autumn on the northern plain,
sunset as the river flows away.
Burial fields of old acres,
new mounds of foreign soil.
Tears fall on a stone slab,
a sword hangs on a lone pine.
Pure eminence and noble example,
a trace remaining for a thousand years.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, juan 919.
〈Epitaph for Duke Yǔwén, Governor of Yǎnzhōu and Duke of Guǎngráo of the Zhōu Dynasty〉
〈Epitaph for Duke Yǔwén, Governor of Yǎnzhōu and Duke of Guǎngráo of the Zhōu Dynasty〉
The Táng dynasty advanced Yuán and Kǎi together,
sixteen in number;
the Zhōu house enfeoffed by Zhāo and Mù precedence,
fifteen states.
Originating from ancestral lines,
branches and leaves divided;
founding states and continuing families,
pearls joined and jades matched.
Thus, they could illuminate lofty virtue,
thinking of the many outstanding scholars;
great virtue has its descendants,
and the Duke was indeed prosperous!
The Duke, named Cháng,
styled Zǐyuán,
was from Yíngyáng in Yùzhōu.
With the Zhōu Xuān king's restoration,
then were worthies established and relatives appointed;
with Zhèng Wǔ's possession of a state,
then were surnames preserved and clans received.
The tribute of Jīng and Héng of a thousand chariots
dared not add troops;
the fiefs of Guó and Kuài of ten cities
were instead offered as territories.
Moreover, at the suburban gate, riders were sent
first to welcome the guests of the Neishi;
at the southern court's morning audience,
he alone recognized the shoes of the Shàngshū.
His grandfather, Sīqìng,
was General of Establishing Might and Governor of Shānyáng.
The title "Establishing Might" taken from Cáo Rén's designation
can define a name;
Shānyáng had the worthiness of Wáng Chàng,
sufficient to observe customs.
His father, Xū,
with silver-blue and gold-purple ranks,
compared to Wēn Xiàn and Fù Zhī;
as General Pacifying the South and Conquering the East,
he matched Liú Hóng and Xún Yǐ.
The register of rewarding merit
was modeled on the Huái Road;
the canon of posthumous honors
appointed him shepherd of the Jīng River.
The Duke was precociously intelligent from a tender age,
his youthful aspirations early formed;
he stood always square and upright,
spoke without plagiarizing others' words.
In his blue-collared youth, wise and brave,
he already buried the cloud-dreaming snake;
with a child's benevolent heart,
he already cherished the pheasant of Zhōngmóu.
Beginning his studies in the village school,
he did not lack a Confucian's honor;
sometimes reading military texts,
he then harbored ambitions of wind and clouds.
Outwardly loyal, inwardly filial,
he devoted himself wholeheartedly to affairs;
cultivating his person and establishing his name,
he exhausted principle in his nature.
In the third year of Dàtǒng,
he raised an army at Huáyáng,
first ascending Guǎngwǔ,
crossing the Qián and Miǎn rivers by raft,
entering the Wèi and disturbing the Hé,
and was granted the titles of Founding Baron of Yǒng'ān County and Auxiliary General.
From then on, long following Tàizǔ,
he entered service as a Commandant within the tent.
In the battle joined at Héqiáo,
the autumn waters did not flow for three months;
wielding blades at Luòchéng,
the Jīnyōng was cut off for a month.
When Xījīng was unsubmissive,
and Qiāng and Róng tribes encroached,
the city like a flying bird,
the land harboring a hidden dragon.
The Duke, with golden arrows freshly drawn,
and divine axes briefly raised,
the bee-eyed already fled,
the wolf-hearted then reformed.
He was promoted to General Pacifying the East and Commander-in-Chief.
In the fifteenth year,
he inherited his father's enfeoffment as Founding Earl of Wèichāng County,
and transferred to Grand Commander.
In the second year after the Wei,
he was appointed as Envoy with Credentials, General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Commandant with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies.
Huáng Quán received the imperial edict,
praising his achievements in entering Wei;
Dòu Xiàn assumed office,
rewarding his strategy for pacifying the barbarians.
This appointment of the Duke,
marked his illustrious merit.
He was advanced to the rank of Duke of Guǎngráo County,
with a fief of five hundred households.
In the third year of the Bǎodìng era,
he was appointed as Military Governor of Luó Prefecture and Prefect of Luó Prefecture,
while concurrently commanding the troops of Jīn Prefecture,
to rendezvous with the Duke of Shàngyōng on the Wéngǔ Road.
The streams were rugged,
the cliffs perilous and steep,
where mountains ended and rivers ceased,
horses were tethered and bridges soared.
Once the central fortress was opened,
the twin cities surrendered.
In the past, Shēn and Xī were completely overrun,
and Jiāng and Huáng had no aid.
At the farthest shores of Cényáng,
they were repeatedly assailed by wind and dust;
westward floating from Xiàshǒu,
they frequently encountered arrows and blades.
The Duke, like the General Who Calms the Waves receiving the sacrificial meat,
and the Towered Ship Commander rallying the troops,
entered the battle array at Héngjiāng,
and advanced the troops at Xiàlài.
The Yuè guests with tattooed bodies,
eventually departed with the Chánlú sword;
the Wú men with long beards,
sailed far away on their yúhuáng ships.
In the fourth year of the Jiàndé era,
he was appointed as Envoy with Credentials and General with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies.
Gōngsūn Áo descended from the Guānglù Pass,
and Zhūgě Dàn fortified the Wāndū Mountain.
In the Duke's position,
he was not ashamed in virtue.
With diverse customs from all directions,
and different practices across the land,
due to his integrity and capability,
he was made an inspector.
Riding post-horses with credentials,
raising banners and holding axes.
Mounted on a piebald horse,
and clad in embroidered robes,
the bandits stood in awe,
and the nobles restrained themselves.
Staying overnight in village pavilions,
fortunately without suspicion of returning on an inauspicious day;
presenting memorials at the public carriage station,
how could there be days of reversed branches?
Thus, even Yáng Qiú as the Director of Retainers,
could not exert his authority;
and Bào Huī as the Capital Official,
relied on others to accomplish tasks.
Emperor Wǔ, the High Ancestor, rallied the troops in mid-spring,
and crossed the river on the jiǎzǐ day.
The Duke, with sword in hand among the six armies,
deployed the eight battle formations as per the diagrams.
Like Zhāng Liáo of old,
who as vanguard reported to the Wei ruler;
comparable to Gěng Yǎn,
who fought first and awaited King Xiāo.
When the nine provinces were unified,
and the four corners settled,
he then achieved merit worthy of the brave ranks,
and his name entered the Office of Merits.
He was appointed as Senior General with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies,
and his fief was increased by five hundred households.
Moreover, rewards were given for his achievements,
and grace was extended to divide his fief.
Returning with double carriages,
shining upon the city of Qiáo Commandery;
bearing treasures back,
illuminating the waters of Línzhāng.
On that day, he was granted the surname Yǔwén,
becoming of the same clan as the state.
Lóu Jìng presented his memorial from the deer-drawn carriage,
and Xiàng Bó danced with his sword at Hóngmén.
This honor of the Duke,
is worthy of such comparisons.
Due to the Duke's achievements in perilous times,
and his sincerity enduring wind and frost,
that year he was appointed as Envoy with Credentials, Military Governor of Dōngxú Prefecture, and Prefect of Xú Prefecture.
In the first year of the Xuānzhèng era,
he was appointed as Military Governor of Nányǎn Prefecture and Prefect of Nányǎn Prefecture.
Governing across the Jì River,
his influence spread like wind over Léizé;
raising banners between the sea and Tài Mountain,
his transformation reached Huái and Yí.
As his carriage curtains entered the territory,
the greedy and cruel officials resigned their seals;
as he governed with the imperial crown,
the benevolent and righteous welcomed him in the suburbs.
How could it be merely about opening channels at Báishí,
exchanging green salt for grain,
auspicious clouds entering the territory,
and rain following his carriage?
While in office, he fell ill,
and passed away at the frontier command.
Huángfǔ Sōng oversaw this region,
a worthy and capable prefect;
Xún, the Palace Attendant, governed this area,
a regional lord of the restoration.
In glorious reputation and abundant virtue,
the Duke possessed these.
An imperial edict posthumously awarded him a certain office,
and conferred the posthumous title of a certain duke,
as was ritually proper.
On the tenth day of the eleventh month in the second year of the Dàxiàng era,
he was returned for burial at the old tomb on a certain mountain in Xíngyáng.
The Nine Plains are desolate and sorrowful,
what could Zhào Wénzǐ say?
The four horses neigh in grief,
as Téng Chénggōng has gone far away.
As for inscribing tripods and engraving steles,
recording merits and extolling virtues,
displaying his noble example,
must be done while alive.
Alas!
This erected stele,
differs from the waters of Zhū and Sì;
this engraved stone,
differs from the Yānrán Mountain.
Woe and alas!
Thus the inscription says:
Descendant of Gāoyáng,
grandson of Shǎodiǎn.
From distant Cānglín,
and remote source of Ruòshuǐ.
Dukes and marquises revived,
bells and tripods multiplied.
Inheriting the foundation and continuing the lineage,
establishing the state and opening the fief.
Our might, our valor,
both duke and marquis.
Black robes emerged from Zhèng,
high officials returned to Zhōu.
Fish Hill ascended northward,
Yíngzé flowed eastward.
The river shifted at Suānzǎo,
grain rained at Chénliú.
Ancestor guarded the southern lands,
father secured the eastern capital.
Two turtles as seals,
twin serpents knotted ribbons.
Observing shadows by day,
divining stars by the Long Willow.
Thus is the legacy passed down,
his name immortal.
The way of serving parents,
filial piety to establish oneself.
The way of serving the ruler,
loyalty to establish benevolence.
Now you inherit virtue,
uniting ruler and kin.
Like the lushness of pines,
like the resilience of bamboo.
Merit intertwined with thorns,
duty commanding weapons of war.
North facing the Green Ridge,
south connecting to White Waves.
Straight clouds barring the pass,
long stars crossing the river.
Battle lines opened, sands severed,
troops shifted, many stoves.
Merits rewarded,
lands enfeoffed, positions granted.
Palaces adorned with jade,
mountains and rivers divided as territories.
Victory decided a thousand miles away,
plans deep and strategies secret.
Military achievements accomplished,
name linked with constellations.
Banners raised at Jì and Luò,
tokens held at Guīméng.
Silkworms nurtured on mulberry lands,
indeed pacifying Wútóng.
No different vessels in the wilds,
no separate winds on the river.
Wú pavilions and Chǔ barriers,
none dared draw their bows.
Swiftly, life passes,
suddenly, pines and catalpas.
Roads winding by Copper Fish,
mountains circling Stone Horse.
Temple of Marquis Wǔ,
altar of Duke Luán.
Gazing upon this lofty stele,
tears fall in sorrow.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, juan 919.
Stele Inscription for Dòulú Gōng, Senior Administrator of the Longyòu Command and Posthumously Awarded Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent of the Zhōu Dynasty
Stele Inscription for Dòulú Gōng, Senior Administrator of the Longyòu Command and Posthumously Awarded Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent of the Zhōu Dynasty
His name was Yǒng'ēn, courtesy name unknown,
a native of Túhé in Chānglí.
Originally surnamed Mùróng,
descendant of Mùróng Huàng, Emperor Wénmíng of Yān.
Enfeoffment of Jīzǐ in Cháoxiān,
state of Bóyí in Gūzhú,
Hàn had four cities,
Qín established one marquisate.
His ancestors preserved the surname and received the clan,
initially achieving merit at Liǔchéng;
founding the state and inheriting the family,
beginning by quelling the rebellion in Liáoyáng.
Since celestial portents and star anomalies,
military defeats at Lián and Jīn,
the senior official changed the surname to Dòulú,
and entered service under Wèi.
Grandfather Dài, General of the Left and Right, and Attendant of Emperor Wén of Wèi.
Father Cháng,
renowned from youth for grand strategies,
unfortunately passed away early.
The Zhōu court, because the Duke and his brothers assisted the mandate,
in righteousness remembered the distant past.
In the second year of Bǎodìng,
an edict posthumously awarded him Pillar of State, Grand General, and Duke of Fúlíng Commandery.
Thus it is known that spring rain moistens trees,
from leaves to roots;
Xībó practiced benevolence,
extending care to the living and the dead.
The Duke, with the essence of mountains and peaks,
the excellence of stars and constellations,
aura matching bells and tripods,
reputation moving wind and clouds.
Observing the Qín army, still called a youth; facing the Chǔ war, still in scholar's garb.
Emperor Tàizǔ Wén, seizing the time to quell chaos,
possessed the hegemonic enterprise.
From Yǐngchuān he followed me,
old affection never forgotten;
old acquaintance from Chōnglíng,
mutual understanding was profound.
In the second year of Pǔtài,
when righteousness was established west of the pass,
he was appointed General Who Exterminates Bandits.
Welcoming the imperial carriage,
he was enfeoffed as Count of Xīnxīng County,
with a fief of five hundred households.
Opening the lands of Xīn'ān,
he shifted Yáng Pú's pass back;
relieving the siege of Hóngnóng,
he entered again the commandery of Liú Kūn.
Grasping drumsticks and riding side by side,
both joining the vanguard.
In the third year of Dàtǒng,
there was the battle of Shāyuàn.
In the fourth year,
there was the campaign at Héqiáo.
Armor lice-infested,
warhorses bred in the suburbs,
the Duke's adaptability grew longer,
his vigor in the storm even braver,
steadfast as an enemy state,
somewhat satisfying to people's expectations,
appointed Dragon-Soaring General and Courtier for Miscellaneous Affairs.
In the eighth year,
appointed Attendant and Right Trusted Commander of the Guard.
Soon promoted to Grand Commander,
and additionally Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
In the sixteenth year,
appointed Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Chariot and Horse General, and Commandant with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies.
In the first year of Wèi,
appointed Piaoqi General and Commandant Equal to the Three Excellencies with Separate Establishment.
Dèng Zhì, as relative of the Hàn court,
first received the central ministry;
Huáng Quán, as meritorious official of the Wèi state,
first ascended to senior general.
The Duke repeatedly received these honored appointments,
a glory to court and countryside.
In the third year,
Commander of Military Affairs of Chéng Prefecture and Governor of Chéng Prefecture.
Soon additionally appointed Palace Attendant.
Externally commanding allied commanders,
authority shaking a hundred cities;
internally participating as a regular attendant,
honor surpassing the eight residences.
At that time, cunning Qiāng on the Lǒng ridges,
often infiltrated Shànggǔ;
gangs of bandits in Yúzhōng,
sometimes gathered in Yúyáng.
The Duke rolled up armor and sped like a star,
charging a thousand cavalry long distances.
Rebel forces at Huíluò,
seeing the wind, fell like grass;
powerful leaders of Guā Prefecture,
surrendered with bound hands.
In the first year of Later Wèi,
re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Lóngzhī County.
In the third year,
the court sent Grand General Ānzhèng Gōng to follow the Tūjué and Tǔyùhún back to the state.
The two prefectures of Hé and Shàn,
being at the head of the route,
the Duke led five thousand cavalry,
to serve as border defense.
Connecting south to Dānsù,
gazing west to Báilán,
passes and frontiers free from worry,
was the Duke's merit.
In the first year of the Zhōu era,
he was appointed as the military supervisor of Shànzhōu and Governor of Shànzhōu.
That same year,
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Wòyě County,
with an additional thousand households added to his fief.
In the second year,
he was appointed as the Chief Administrator of the Lǒngyòu General Administration Office.
In the first year of the Wǔchéng era,
he served as the military supervisor of Lì, Shè, and Wén provinces and Governor of Lìzhōu.
In the fifth year,
he led troops to defeat the Yángzhèn Mán in Wénzhōu,
and subsequently pacified the Lúshuǐ region.
In the first year of the Bǎodìng era, he led troops to defeat the Héngmàn Lǎo in Bāzhōu.
Crossing the Lú River in the fifth month,
Zhūgě Liàng had troops that ventured deep;
the winding slopes of Chángbǎn,
Wáng Zūn had the path of a loyal minister.
Frost and hail did not alarm him,
nor was there any shortage of water or grass,
heaven favored the general,
this is what is meant.
That year,
he was appointed as the Director of Revenues.
He oversaw the eight regulations,
and balanced the nine taxes,
managing affairs to complete the year’s tasks,
and contributing to the monthly assessments.
In the third year,
he returned,
and was appointed as the Chief Administrator of the Lǒngyòu General Administration Office.
The Duke repeatedly assisted illustrious vassals,
and frequently served in high offices.
When Běihǎi entered the court,
he was looked up to for responses;
when Dōngpíng paid homage to the emperor,
he established rituals accordingly.
Thus, even when horses turned their heads toward Yān,
there was no lack of Yuè Yì;
when foreign ministers compared themselves to Hàn,
many were like Tián Shū.
His elder brother, the Duke of Chǔ State,
through harmony and humility,
and with dignified support and joyful recommendation,
established a state and founded a capital,
extending his domain to the southern regions,
requested to transfer his earlier enfeoffment of three thousand households in Wǔyáng Commandery,
to augment the Duke’s fief in Wòyě.
The court, considering that brothers yielding to one another
was not without precedent in history,
and to extend grace by dividing the fief,
issued an edict granting it,
increasing the fief to a total of four thousand seven hundred households.
Later, as the six climatic influences clashed,
and the five tones conflicted,
his longevity did not reach its end,
and his wandering soul was about to change,
he passed away in his official residence,
at the age of fifty-eight.
An edict posthumously honored him as Junior Guardian, with military authority over Yōu, Jì, Dìng, and five other provinces, and Governor of Yōuzhōu.
He was given the posthumous title of Duke Jìng,
in accordance with ritual.
On the sixth day of the second month in the first year of the Tiānhé era,
he was buried at Hóngdúchuān in Xiányáng.
A minister’s tomb is planted with cypress trees,
and a feudal lord’s grave mound is higher than a pheasant.
Alas, how sorrowful!
The Duke embodied loyalty and fulfilled filial piety,
contained righteousness and embraced benevolence,
his integrity stood tall like a hundred-foot tree,
his clarity was vast like a thousand-acre pond,
he was attentive to his duties,
and fond of studying maps and books.
Official documents and records,
were never burdensome to him;
amidst the rush of military affairs,
he still maintained composure.
Brothers as dukes and marquises,
relatives of the state court,
Yíchūn had the grandeur of imperial baths,
yet Zhuólóng lacked the mechanism of flowing water.
With a thousand acres of bamboo in Wèinán,
he still feared excess;
with two hundred acres of land in Xiányáng,
he often thought of contentment.
In establishing himself, ten generations could be pardoned;
in bequeathing to his sons, a single classic was enough.
The stele of Governor Jiǎ Kuí,
already bore golden grains;
the tomb of General Wèi Qīng,
still retains stone unicorns.
Thus, the inscription reads:
Cháoxiān established a state,
Gūzhú became its lord.
The land was called Gāoliǔ,
the mountain named Mìyún.
Liáoyáng was split by Zhào,
Wǔsuì divided by Qín.
Precious jade for generations of nobility,
carved spears for old merits.
His name matched reality,
his words embodied refinement.
Endowed with such talent,
he descended with this brilliance.
He confronted without concealment,
the kingly way was upright.
With love and respect,
he forever maintained a pleasant countenance.
He immersed himself in the rites,
and lingered in scholarly pursuits.
Strategies planned in the tent,
merits earned through hardship.
In Hán’s formation, he wielded his spear;
in Qí’s city, he leaned on his chariot.
Plans of the leopard were established,
tactics of the dragon were unveiled.
He drilled troops in Qíyáng,
and displayed might at Lǒngdǐ.
City walls drawn on the ground,
mountains and forests gathered like rice.
Mounting his horse, he discussed books;
facing the army, he practiced rituals.
Jiǎ Fù opened his camp,
Lián Pō bowed in respect.
Composed in discussions,
eloquent in responses.
With such integrity and fairness,
he balanced leniency and strictness.
Greenwood bandits ceased,
Huángchí rebels quieted.
His fame shook Chìshān,
his authority towered over Qīnglǐng.
Mystical beasts floated on the river,
flying locusts left the borders.
Disaster emerged from Lǒng,
poisonous waters invaded Jīng.
By day, the earth’s pillar tilted;
by night, the constellation’s stars fell.
A stone altar received sacrifices,
a grand stele praised his spirit.
Cypress before Wèichéng,
courtyard below Chānglíng,
one must know the earthly market,
to read the mountain inscription.
○From *Yìwén Lèijù*, scroll 50.
From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, scroll 925.
〈Inscription for the Hot Springs〉
〈Inscription for the Hot Springs〉
Xiánchí bathed the sun,
first responding to the Green Armor Chart;
Dǐzhù floated in the sky,
first receiving the Xuányí’s command.
In benevolence, it washes away dust and haze;
in righteousness, it stirs clarity and turbidity;
in courage, it bears mountains with remaining strength;
in weakness, it cannot lift a goose feather.
In mid-spring, it flows with elm seeds;
in the third month, it descends with peach blossoms.
Those that change color,
flow as the nectar of five clouds;
those with exquisite taste,
condense as the dew of Sānwēi.
Its mist greener than the Tóngpǔ,
its color whiter than the Qiānxī.
Not a divine cauldron, yet perpetually boiling;
unlike a dragon pool, yet uniquely surging.
It cleanses the stomach and rinses the intestines,
reviving the weak and raising the frail.
The remaining stones of Qín Shǐhuáng,
still form steps like wild goose teeth;
the old pottery of Hàn Wǔdì,
is used as fish-scale tiles.
Water gushing from the mountains,
truly signifies loyalty;
rivers flowing within chambers,
further manifest pure filial piety.
How could sweet springs curing illnesses,
heard of in the Jiànwǔ era,
or divine waters dispelling ailments,
known in the Xiánkāng era, compare?
The three immortals’ lodge on Sōngshān,
does not solely boast of Tiānchí;
the hundred-zhàng spring in Huàyīn,
is not uniquely higher than Liánjǐng.
○From *Yìwén Lèijù*, scroll 9.
From *Chūxué Jì*, scroll 7.
〈Epitaph for Zhèng Wěi, Duke of Xiāngchéng and Grand General of Zhōu〉
The Duke, whose given name was Wěi,
courtesy name Zizhí,
was a man of Kāifēng in Xíngyáng.
King Xuān of Zhōu’s younger brother by the same mother
was enfeoffed at Zhèng.
The lands between the Hé and Luò rivers
already had their people;
the lords of Guó and Kuài
were not without their commanderies and towns.
Later, snakes fought at the gate,
a giant turtle was cooked in the cauldron,
Hán invaded Fùshǔ,
Jìn destroyed Yángchéng.
Its sacrifices abruptly ended,
and they took the state as their surname.
His grandfather, Chè,
was General-in-Chief of the Army
and posthumously granted the title of Governor of Jìzhōu.
His father, Xiānhù,
was General of Agile Cavalry, Pillar of State, Duke of Xiāngchéng Commandery, and Governor of Qīngzhōu.
During the Yǒng’ān era,
Luòchéng’s gates were closed by day;
the Huáng Hé’s ice congealed.
At Díquán, the site of the covenant assembly,
dark birds suddenly flew;
within the armory’s weapon racks,
scaled fish then appeared.
Three commanders were bound northward,
five steeds floated south.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng greatly intervened in the Central Plains,
establishing a ruler at Yī and Luò.
The Duke, leaning on the crossbar of his cart,
spoke of returning to his old homeland.
He was appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
Heaven grew weary of the Wèi’s virtue;
power lay with the strong ministers.
The Duke was ashamed to enter the ranks of disorder,
so he raised a righteous army at Chénliú.
The Grand Ancestor sealed Hángǔ Pass and awaited the lords;
he sat in Fēng Palace and received the assembled rulers.
Connecting with both awe and kindness,
he swept westward like a rolling mat.
In the third year of Dàtǒng,
the Duke entered the court
and was granted the title of Founding Baron of Wǔyáng County,
with a fief of six hundred households.
Soon he was appointed General of Soaring Dragons and Governor of Běixúzhōu.
He deployed formations at Héqiáo,
lifted the siege of Yùbì,
displayed banners at Fùpíng,
donned armor at Yīquè,
plunged into the tiger’s den and brandished his spear,
ascended Yúmén and hung up his helmet.
Thus his name was recorded in the Ministry of Merit,
his achievements lofty, deserving of fief and rank.
The Wèi general Hóu Jǐng,
glancing back like a wolf at Jīng and Hé,
the Son of Heaven commanded us
to dispatch a flank army to engage.
Dangling bait in the tiger’s mouth,
he broke the alliance midway.
The affair concluded with mutual withdrawal,
thanks to the Duke’s efforts.
He was appointed General of the Central Army, Regular Attendant, and Grand Governor,
inheriting the title of Duke of Xiāngchéng Commandery,
with a fief of two thousand households.
He was further appointed Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, General of Charlots and Cavalry, and Pillar of State.
His other titles remained unchanged.
He was promoted to General of Agile Cavalry with authority to establish a headquarters,
and given the additional title of Vice Director.
The position of Regular Attendant was weighty—
Huò Qùbìng ascending the court;
the office of Senior General was noble—
Gōngsūn Áo going beyond the frontier.
Comparing present to past,
different eras shared the same glory.
In the second year of Wèihòu,
he was appointed Grand General, Commander of Jiānglíng’s Defense, and Commander of Military Affairs of Fifteen Provinces.
Wú’s troops were trained soldiers;
their ships practiced river warfare.
Islands encroached;
waves crashed and surged.
The Duke briefly approached the river border
and already understood the troops of Nányuè;
just sailing the tower ships,
he excelled in the battles of Kūnmí.
Thus he could sing peacefully by the Lǐ riverbanks,
halt his journey at Cényáng,
detain the Marquis of Lǔ to feast at Zhāngtái,
face the men of Qí to hunt at Yúnmèng.
In the first year of Bǎodìng of Zhōu,
he was appointed Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Commander of Military Affairs of Yízhōu, and Governor of Yízhōu.
In the sixth year of Tiānhé,
he was appointed Commander and Governor of Huàzhōu.
His other titles remained unchanged.
Yáo and Hán formed layered barriers;
Qiān and Wèi divided their flows.
The flooding at Yánglíng had already subsided;
the scholars of Huàyīn still gathered.
But for years he suffered from wasting-thirst,
repeatedly afflicted with Xiàngrú’s ailment.
As it reached its critical stage,
it became like Fàn Zēng’s illness.
Tóng Jūn faced the medicines,
but they lacked divine efficacy;
Lǐ Zhù attended as physician,
yet no remedy was found.
On the seventeenth day of the fourth month in the sixth year of Tiānhé, he passed away,
at the age of fifty-seven.
An edict posthumously granted him his original office,
adding Junior Tutor, Commander of Military Affairs of Sī, Yù, Luò, Xiàng, and Jì Provinces, and Governor of Sīzhōu.
He was given the posthumous title Duke Sù,
in accordance with ritual.
The Son of Heaven suspended court,
deeply feeling the duty toward a minister;
the assembled lords gathered for the burial,
all observing the rites of alliance.
His wife, née Lǐ,
was of a noble clan from Dùnqiū.
A family of ministers and chancellors,
a house of worthies and talents.
Frost and dew assailed her first;
she was enfeoffed at the suburban altar.
On the sixth day of the eleventh month of that year,
she was jointly interred with him in a certain plain of Cháng’ān County in Xiányáng.
Joint burial was not ancient practice,
already differing from the era of the Three Kings;
yet “in death sharing the same grave”
still aligns with the beginning of the Six Classics.
Though two cranes bearing pearls
return together to the purple-canopied pines;
twin dragons emerging from the casket
vanish together into Yánpíng’s waters.
Alas, sorrow!
Thus the inscription is offered:
The state had its fortified cities,
the court many noble men.
Dukes Wǔ and Zhuāng,
King Píng’s ministers.
Wēn’s wheat broke the covenant;
Bēng’s fields saw sacrifices cease.
The outrider halted the carriage;
coming to court, they recognized the shoes.
Both grandfather and father,
both marquises and dukes.
Pivotal and secret, meticulous and close,
in issuing and receiving, clear and fluent.
Governing complexity with simplicity,
amid chaos, heart bold.
Jì and Hé left their kindness;
Hǎi and Dài bestowed their fiefs.
Generation after generation enhanced their beauty,
giving birth to this vessel.
Loyalty—nothing he did not undertake;
filial piety—never lacking.
Yōu and Jǐ tangled and blocked,
Guān and Hé seethed like a cauldron.
From north and south,
his fame reached Liáng and Wèi.
Raising banners at Rǔ and Yǐng,
his might shook the Three Rivers.
Grasping the command at Jiāng and Hàn,
he swept away the tower ships.
Chénggāo’s dust arose;
Guǎngwǔ’s beacon fires burned.
Elk sprang, deer were shot,
wild geese fell, startled by the bowstring.
Commanding guards at the orchid racks,
he displayed awe beyond the river.
Mountains like drum towers,
trees like carriage canopies.
Protector of two routes,
general alone receiving homage.
Wútóng in lush gardens,
yángliǔ in singing houses.
A thousand in gold for swirling snow,
a hundred days of flowing rosy clouds.
Withering, sudden and swift,
grieving the splendor and glory.
Héyáng’s ancient trees,
Jīngǔ’s fading flowers.
Lǒng dusky, clouds darkening,
mountains deep, road late.
The wind’s breath just rises high,
the pine’s sound already travels far.
Formerly, kin and friends,
joyful and congenial, bonded.
Not for a lifetime,
but for this parting.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 947.
〈Epitaph for Hùmòchén Dàoshēng, General of Agile Cavalry with Authority to Establish a Headquarters of Zhōu〉
The gentleman, whose given name was Dàoshēng,
styled Mǒu,
was a man of Wǔchuān in Shuòzhōu.
His lineage originated from Yīnshān,
descended from the imperial clan.
Descending to the time of Wèi,
in Qín he became a Liú.
His father, Shàoxīng,
was a garrison commander of Wǔchuān.
Mountains and rivers formed barriers,
frontier passes bordered the edges,
early on he possessed awe-inspiring reputation,
all were filled with heroic fervor.
The gentleman read books on horseback,
engaged in refined discourse with sword in hand,
alone devising the six stratagems,
specially mastering the three strategies.
Although he again held the position of a junior general,
his courage topped the banners at the gate;
though his rank was among the auxiliary troops,
his counsel participated in the headquarters.
In the fifth year of Zhèngguāng of Wèi,
he was appointed commanding general,
subordinate to Tiānzhù Ěrzhū Róng,
campaigning against the Prince of Běihǎi.
In the third year of Yǒng'ān,
he followed Grand Tutor Hèbá Shèng into the passes.
Soon he was transferred to a separate command.
At Huáyuán, armor was rolled up,
at the pass city, horses were tethered,
all were victories,
in which the gentleman had strength.
In the third year of Yǒngxī,
he was appointed as a commander.
The Grand Ancestor, Emperor Wén, swiftly held the passes and rivers,
his orders were carried out across the land,
considering the gentleman's ability and strategy,
entrusted him as a talon and fang.
His name was known among the inner attendants,
his merit participated in the highest creations.
When troops approached Héqū,
he first ascended the ford of Báimǎ;
when bandits arose from Púchéng,
he first fought in the garden of Huángshā.
At Línjìn, ships were arrayed across,
already capturing the Zhào general;
at Mǎlíng, trees were carved,
again subduing the Qí troops.
Distributing tokens, overseeing merits,
unfolding maps, bestowing ranks,
he was conferred the titles of Piāoqí Grand General, Gold and Purple Glorious Grand Master, Duke of È County with founding of a state,
with a fief of five hundred households.
When Zhào Yǎn became Piāoqí,
he stopped his carriage with a single chariot;
when Zhāng Zhàn received the title of Glorious Grand Master,
he long rode a white horse.
Comparing with these,
court and countryside honored him.
In the ninth year of Dàtǒng,
he changed his surname to Hóumòchén.
Following Grand General Tuòbá Yuǎn to begin at Yáng,
two waters long contended,
three rivers had no markets,
donning armor, he contracted illness,
died at the headquarters gate,
at the age of fifty-one.
He was posthumously awarded Commissioner with Discretionary Powers, Commander, and Governor of Shuòzhōu.
The gentleman, in Wǔchuān,
was of the same hometown as Emperor Wén.
When hegemon achievements were established,
and royal enterprise could be accomplished,
he did not forget to abandon lectures,
still discussing repayment of wagers.
Now the successor's virtue is renewed,
meritorious ministers are remembered from afar.
In the eastern capital, horses neigh,
not without sighs for seeing the sun;
by the northern mound, carriages pass,
finally recalling words of a lifetime.

There was an edict further awarding him Commissioner with Discretionary Powers, Piāoqí Grand General, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Commander of Military Affairs of Yí, Fū, and Jiàng Three Provinces, Governor of Fūzhōu.
Posthumously titled Duke Mǒu,
according to ritual.
His wife, of the Tuòbá clan,
was Lady of Ānyì Commandery.
The courtyard had bells and drums,
the family upheld admonitions and precepts,
teaching demeanor, teaching virtue,
words told, words returned.
In the fifth year of Tiānhé, sixth month, she passed away,
and in the tenth month of that same year, they were buried together in Hóngyuán Township of Mǒu County, Jīngzhào.
Wǔzǐ completed the resting place,
requested the western steps for joint burial;
Píngyáng married down,
immediately at Lúshān shared a grave mound.
The inscription says:
Condensed yin, distant silence,
vast desert, level cold.
Sands exhaust the vast sea,
land ends at Gāolán.
Frontier geese depart in autumn,
barbarian mulberries dry in summer.
Wind and earth strengthen spirit,
mountains and rivers sternly stand.
Armies from Shànggǔ,
might and heroism from Wǔchuān.
The gentleman then followed in footsteps,
generations did not lack worthies.
In the case, a loyal sword,
in the courtyard, flows a filial spring.
The Wèi house had many troubles,
remaining customs not yet extinguished.
Tiānbǎo yielded virtue,
Dāngtú abolished codes.
The senior general pointed the way,
the inner attendant exerted strength.
Luòchéng night victory,
Héliáng morning cut.
Iron sword, gold tortoise,
honor pursued jade pivots.
Personally enfeoffed with Hàn's mandate,
family inheriting Wèi's legacy.
Together excelling in illustrious clans,
both called those in power.
Husband and wife matched as a pair,
years and ages both passed.
Zhào zither, Qín sounds,
together become mound and tomb.
Xiǎolíng stone outer coffin,
Hóngyuán township grave.
Straw figures two lead,
pond willows both forward.
Tunnel paths still join,
pine city immediately connects.
Frost follows willow white,
moon pursues grave round.
How many generations for orchids?
What year for mound and valley?
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 947.
〈Epitaph Inscription for Yǔwén Xiǎn, Zhōu Chēqí Grand General, Posthumously Awarded Junior Minister of Works〉
The Duke, whose given name was Xiǎn,
styled Mǒu,
was a man of Wǔxiāng in Shàngdǎng.
Since great fog floated over the river,
long rainbow reflected on the islet,
receiving source from Ruòshuǐ,
continuing lineage from Cānglín.
Shàngdǎng lies west of Hán,
Chángshān is north of Zhào,
taking locality as surname,
can be briefly stated.
Grandfather, Qiúnán,
General of the Guards, Governor of Jìzhōu.
Father, Jīndiàn,
General Who Conquers the South, Governor of Dìngzhōu.
Both commanded crane troops,
both displayed martial music,
reputation and glory's flourishing,
followed footsteps of that time.
〈Epitaph Inscription for Yǔwén Xiǎn, Zhōu Chēqí Grand General, Posthumously Awarded Junior Minister of Works〉
The Duke was endowed with the essence of mountains and peaks,
and possessed the vigor of wind and clouds.
His demeanor was dignified and solemn,
and his reputation was widely renowned.
He could bend a strong bow,
shooting arrows while galloping left and right.
Thus, his fame rose high in Shànggǔ,
and his might shook Lóufán.
He inherited the title of Marquis of Ānjí County,
with a fief of five hundred households.
In the third year of Yǒngxīng,
Yōu and Bìng rebelled and defied authority,
harboring disloyal intentions toward the sovereign.
The Emperor turned to the Duke and said:
"The world is in turmoil and chaos,
what should be done?"
The Duke replied:
"Choose the good and follow it."
Then he recited from the *Book of Songs*:
"That beautiful person,
is a man from the west."
The Emperor said:
"This is my heart's desire."
Thus, the strategy to enter the passes was decided.
Because the Duke's mother was elderly and his family large,
he was ordered to plan ahead.
The Duke said:
"In today's affairs,
loyalty and filial piety cannot coexist.
If the ruler is not discreet, he will lose his ministers;
if a minister is not discreet, he will lose his life."
The Emperor, deeply moved, changed his expression and said:
"You are my Wáng Líng."
He was promoted to Zhūyī Zhígé and Grand Governor within the Gé,
and his title was changed to Duke of Chángguǎng County,
with a fief of one thousand five hundred households.
When Emperor Wǔ first arrived at Tóngguān,
Tàizǔ personally welcomed him at Qínshuǐ.
Tàizǔ had long known of the Duke's reputation but had never met him.
He looked among the crowd,
hesitated without asking,
and simply said:
"Have this man shoot the small bird by the water."
The arrow struck its target instantly.
Tàizǔ joyfully said:
"Now I know your name."
He was immediately appointed as Governor within the Tent, in charge of military affairs in Cāngzhōu, and Governor of Cāngzhōu,
with his fief increased to a total of two thousand five hundred households.
Huáng Gōnghéng's decisive actions
made the Wèi ruler trust him wholeheartedly;
Pān Chéngmíng's loyalty and valor
caused the King of Wú to lower himself in respect.
Different eras share the same glory,
as seen today.
The eastern frontier of Xià,
its lands connected to remote territories,
with Jǐngxíng's paths blocked,
and Fēihú's routes severed.
Thus, the Duke was appointed as Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, General of the Guards, Governor of Military Affairs in Dōngxiàzhōu, and Governor of Dōngxiàzhōu.
The troops of Báibō and Qīngdú,
and the rebellions of Tóngmǎ and Jīnshéng,
all without exception clasped their hands and knelt,
leading sheep and embracing horses in submission.
While in the province, he fell ill,
relinquished his post, and returned to court.
Small horses were left in the stables,
remaining tokens hung on lapels,
officials and people clung to him in reluctance,
and they carved a stone on Xíngshān.
Though not the walls of Hànyáng,
it resembled the road of Fúfēng.
He was appointed Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry, and given the rank of Yìtóng Sānsī,
with the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
In the first year of Wèi Hòu, his illness worsened,
and he passed away in Tóngzhōu,
at the age of fifty-seven.
The Son of Heaven ceased music,
the assembled lords gathered for mourning,
Tàizǔ personally attended to offer condolences and sacrifices,
grieving deeply, moving all around.
At that time, with warfare raging everywhere,
posthumous honors were generally suspended,
so he was temporarily buried with the seals and ribbons of his official position,
in the northern mountains of Tóngzhōu.
On the twenty-third day of the second month in the second year of Jiàndé,
he was reburied at Hóngdúyuán in Cháng'ān County, Xiányáng.
At a time when rites and music were changing,
and an era marked by shifts in songs and praises,
though the state's governance differed,
people could still pursue honor.

Thus, he was posthumously granted the titles of Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Grand General of Cavalry, Kāifǔ Yìtóng Sānsī, Junior Minister of Works, and Governor of Military Affairs in Dān, Yán, and Suí Provinces, and Governor of Yánzhōu.
He was given the posthumous title of Duke,
in accordance with rites.
His wife, Lady Gāo,
was from Bóhǎi.
Gentle, she participated in Jìn's governance,
rejecting Cáo Shuǎng's treacherous schemes;
rising in the Hàn court,
she stood with Wáng Líng in joint response.
Moreover, her admonitions were proper,
her speech and demeanor virtuous,
reverent and diligent in household duties,
a worthy talent in domestic principles.
Was it merely refusing to listen to miscellaneous music
to change the customs of Qí?
Or not eating fresh game
to halt the King of Jīng's hunts?
In the past, joint burials
were in Jì Wǔzǐ's western chamber;
today, sharing the same grave
is like Chángpínghóu's northern tomb.
The eldest son, Shénjǔ, and his brothers,
were of utmost sincerity and pure filial piety,
skillful in observing mourning rites,
consistent from beginning to end,
unchanging in their conduct.
Thus, they achieved official success and established reputations,
with filial piety evident and loyalty preserved.
The inscription says:
The northern peak has two names,
the Cōng River has two sources.
Its height is the utmost,
its origin is far-reaching.
Customs are shaped by mountains and rivers,
people rely on ministers and nobles.
Righteous and fierce, majestic and awe-inspiring,
talented and bold, sincere and devoted.
His ancestors and father,
followed in succession, mighty and heroic.
Striking metal in the northern land,
ringing jade in the southern palace.
Steadfast as Wú Hàn,
wise as Dòu Róng.
Guìshuāng relied on virtue,
Wúléi turned with the wind.
He stood out with inner brilliance,
born with this upholding of virtue.
Filial piety was his innate nature,
loyalty was his human principle.
With adorned chariot hubs and engraved breastplates,
in Yān's south and Zhào's north.
If the waters were to be opened,
the nine tribes could be governed.
Planning strategies within the tent,
overseeing duties within the palace.
Skilled in choosing loyal advice,
able to prevent changes in countenance.
The Fánruò bow was already strong,
the Qíyuán bamboo was straight.
The halberd struck the small branch,
the arrow pierced the left wing.
Raising banners at Chìgǔ,
brandishing spears at Wǔzhōu.
The Great Wall stretches ten thousand miles,
the river's waters flow in twin streams.
Yǐngchuān often ailed,
Huáishuǐ never healed.
Righteousness heavy as piercing walls,
favor deep as setting up postal stations.
At the mouth of the valley,
on the sunny side of the Wèi,
hills and mountains scattered,
stelae and gateways rising and falling.
Grass holds autumn fire,
trees embrace spring frost.
Books and swords both vanished,
man and lute perished together.
Mournful, mournful the heir,
pure heart with no reliance.
The Filial Waters not yet dried,
the sorrowful pines already fallen.
In the chamber, nesting owls enter,
at the gate, mourning cranes approach.
The meritorious minister's life ended,
his portrait will join the Qílín Pavilion.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, scroll 947.
〈Epitaph for Sīmǎ Yì, Duke of Lángyá Zhuāng, Grand General of Zhōu〉
〈Epitaph for Sīmǎ Yì, Duke of Lángyá Zhuāng, Grand General of Zhōu〉
The gentleman, whose taboo name was Yì,
styled Zūnyìn,
was a native of Wēn in Hénèi.
The Southern Rectifier oversaw the heavens,
the Northern Rectifier oversaw the earth—
these were the offices of Xī and Hé,
who succeeded to the governance of Zhòng and Lí.
When Áng returned to Chǔ,
he was enfeoffed alongside Zhāng Hán;
when Yù fled from Qín,
he departed together with Máo Gōng.
His grandfather, Jīnlóng,
continued to serve in the Ministry of Appointments,
a clear mirror to the Three Dukes.
His father, Yuè,
twice governed Jīng and Hé,
his awe-inspiring influence extending a thousand *lǐ*,
yet he fell victim to treacherous schemes,
and thus was mourned by Jì Bù.
That his surviving heir was preserved
truly relied upon the loyalty of Chéng Yīng.
The state, recalling its meritorious ministers,
again comforted the son of Shū'áo;
speaking of the official clans,
sought once more the descendants of Nǚ Qí.
The gentleman first accepted summons
as Registrar of Hénèi,
then appointed Gentleman in Attendance and Auxiliary Court Gentleman.
Training troops in Jí Commandery,
ferrying horses across the Yellow River,
he achieved victory breaking the enemy vanguard at Zhǐ Pass,
and routed them in battle at the Great Wall.
He was conferred the titles General Who Pacifies the East and Governor of Běixú Province.
Amidst the turmoil of Liǔquán,
he swept through three cities;
amidst the weapons' clash in Tángyīn,
a thousand households entered the passes.
Promoted to General of Chariots and Cavalry, Commander with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies, and Enfeoffed as Earl of Lóngmén County,
he was further appointed Governor of Bā Province.
Though the Bā River wound thrice,
and barbarian songs rose in number,
he merely encountered the white bamboo crossbows,
yet had already accomplished the merit of Qīngyī.
The court, considering the meritorious servants of Hàn,
must establish the headquarters of a senior general;
the descendants of Jìn's era,
should succeed to the state of Lángyá.
He was promoted to General of Agile Cavalry with the authority to establish a headquarters,
and his enfeoffment was changed to Duke of Lángyá,
with a fief of fifteen hundred households.
The palace's inner quarters, intimate and confidential,
truly awaited loyalty and steadfastness.
He was commissioned as Grand Minister of Ceremonies,
and further appointed Grand Minister of Justice.
In charge of the regular ministers,
overseeing the responsibilities of Kuí and Lóng,
the Kingly Way being already established,
his silk-bound words were solely trustworthy.
Soon he was appointed Governor of Shǐ Province and Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of Shǐ Province.
The barbarians relied on their perilous terrain,
glaring like wolves and spreading their wings like owls.
High mountains sought the clouds,
deep valleys held no sunlight,
the nine grounds crisscrossed,
the three gates rose and fell,
peaks perilous, horses constrained,
waters treacherous, bridges flying,
yet he managed to bring valleys to stillness and mountains to emptiness,
ice melting and mist dispersing.
He was then appointed Governor of Xìn Province and Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of Xìn Province.
Elite troops guarding Báidì,
sufficient to intimidate the cities of Bā Province;
ships' oars descending to Jīng Province,
greatly stirring the garrisons of Xīlíng.
He was then appointed Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Great General, Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of Xīníng Province, and Governor of Xīlíng Province.
About to open the way for the people of the northern gate,
towards communicating with the southern cloud countries,
he heard of favor as if startled,
and suddenly departed in the deep of night.
He passed away on the eighteenth day of the first month in the sixth year of the Tiānhé era,
at the age of sixty-five.
An edict posthumously awarded him his original office,
adding the governorships of Huái, Shào, Fén, and Jìn provinces,
and bestowed the posthumous title Duke Zhuāng,
in accordance with ritual.
On the thirteenth day of the seventh month in the first year of the Jiàndé era,
he was buried at Sānzhīyuán in Wǔgōng Commandery.
The gentleman's love and respect were pure and profound,
concealing faults without offending,
loyal, steadfast, bright, and upright,
knowing no action he did not undertake.
In military service for forty-two years,
he personally experienced sixty-nine battles.
As for the many stoves and counting tallies,
he consistently achieved success;
flying sand and heaped stones,
never did he violate discipline.
Sincere in teaching righteousness,
he had the style of Wú Qǐ west of the River;
composed in drums and banners,
he had the governance of Lǐ Mù at Chángpíng.
On the day of his death,
his household possessed no surplus wealth;
the timber from the mountains, the resources required,
all came from the imperial decree for burial.
Having a beginning and an end,
he lived in glory and died mourned.
The inscription says:
Zhùróng commanded it,
Zhòng and Lí could be raised.
The ducal clan was then established,
the celestial offices were put in order.
Fleeing the age to Qín,
inheriting the family in Chǔ.
The Metal Phase lost control,
the jade mirror's brilliance sank.
Our ardent ancestor,
recognized change and seized opportunity.
The yellow banner submerged in the east,
the blue canopy flew west.
Falling stars placed on the road,
the long isle emerged from siege.
And our imperial father,
again pacified Jīng and Hé.
The age beset by chaos and ruin,
his person lost to crafty underlings.
Alas, our surviving heir,
treading a rugged path like Zhào Wǔ.
Cold covering the bird's wings,
hunger swallowing the beast's milk.
Returned to Hénèi,
again inheriting Lángyá.
Years just of the bamboo horse,
resentment knotted with the long snake.
Concealing troops in the nine grounds,
placing swords in a thousand homes.
Snowy mountains burying horses,
icy rivers trapping chariots.
Then having distributed governance,
transcendently glorious in his duties.
Vermilion egrets frequently flying,
golden tortoises turning their pivots.
Building fortifications at long elms,
encamping armies at high willows.
Jade trays pushing food,
river bridges urging wine.
Stone Gate's ice melting,
Golden Dike scattering like lightning.
Lú River's gate and pass,
Máojīn becoming a spectacle.
Riding the wind, soaring wings,
the long road just half begun.
Meritorious servants of Jiànwǔ,
first mourning Wú Hàn.
Vast and empty, leaves falling,
the hunting grounds gradually fading.
Golden City's road severed,
Méiwù's people sparse.
Wind in pines, cloud canopies,
white waters, mountain robes.
The worthy already, stars fallen,
men gone, orchids withered.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 947.
〈Epitaph for Wú Míngchè, Duke of Huáidé and Great General of Zhōu〉
〈Epitaph for Wú Míngchè, Duke of Huáidé and Great General of Zhōu〉
The gentleman, whose taboo name was Míngchè,
styled Tōngzhāo,
was a native of Qín Commandery in Yǎn Province.
Among the ranked states of the Western Capital,
the Prince of Chángshā's merit covered mountains and rivers;
among the honored ministers of the Eastern Capital,
the Grand Marshal's name towered to the heavens.
Was it merely that Xīhé had a defender,
whose wisdom sufficed to resist Qín,
or that Jiànpíng had a city,
whose might could stir Jìn—nothing more than this!
His grandfather, Shàng,
was Governor of Nánqiáo.
His father, Biāo,
was General of the Right Army.
Resisting at Huái and Yí,
pacifying Jì and Luò,
generations of famous generals,
are seen herein.
The Duke's ambition was vast and unrestrained,
his demeanor elegant and free-spirited.
Like picking up the shoe at the Yí Bridge,
he early grasped military strategy;
like encountering the gibbon in the bamboo grove,
he fully understood swordsmanship.
Thus he earned a brave rank at court,
and was selected as a capable officer.
He began his career as Sīzhí of the Eastern Palace,
and later was appointed to the Left Army.
Zhān Gé had just inherited military command,
when Shǔ fell;
Lù Jī had only begun discussing achievements,
when Wú perished.
The Duke's service under Liáng,
was not yet illustrious.
Since Liáng received the mandate's end,
and the Qí ministers gained power,
rites, music, and military campaigns,
all returned to Shùn's descendants.
Thus authority extended across the four seas,
virtue instructed the feudal lords,
clearing the misty clouds,
brightening the sun and moon.
The Duke, with brilliant strategy aiding the times,
and grand plans assisting governance,
renewed scales and wings,
and his influence spread far like wind and storm.
Champion Hóu's use of troops,
did not necessarily follow antiquity;
Wǔ'ān Jūn's nurturing of men,
could win people's hearts.
Comparing him to his peers,
this describes the Duke.
As General of the Left Guard,
he soon rose to General Who Guards the Army and Governor of Dānyáng.
As North Army Central Inspector,
he oversaw the six divisions' administration;
as Governor of Hénán and the Capital,
he stood foremost among the hundred commanderies.
Entrusted with civil and military affairs,
the Duke was without shame.
In the campaign at Xiāo Xiāng,
he pressed upon the islands.
With wind-driven ships and fire vessels,
Zhōu Yú had the troops of Chìbì;
with covered warships and great fleets,
Hè Qí had the battle of Héngjiāng.
He was then made General Who Pacifies the South, with authority equal to the Three Dukes, Commander of the four provinces of Xiāng, Héng, Guì, and Wǔ,
thus causing the left guard to turn its keys,
and chariots to run smoothly again.
Chángshā's Chǔ iron,
re-entered the armory;
Dòngpǔ's stored rhinoceros horns,
were again delivered to the armor treasury.
Though war songs repeatedly celebrated victory,
and military tents still spread,
in Huáinán they watched for prisoners of the Court Minister,
in Héféi they spoke of the general's invasion,
none failed to lose their dens, startle their nests,
sink in water, or fall into fire.

As Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Palace Attendant, Minister of Works, General of Chariots and Cavalry, Commander of Military Affairs of the five provinces of North and South Yǎn, Qīng, and Qiáo, Governor of South Yǎn, Duke of Nánpíng Commandery,
with a fief of eight thousand households,
and a set of drums and pipes.
The central terrace was in the Xuánwǔ Palace,
the supreme general ranked among the Wénchāng stars,
high cicada ornaments graced his temples,
singing egrets accompanied his carriage.
With a fief of ten thousand households like Píngyáng,
and four thousand horses like Línzī,
seated, jade tables pushed food toward him;
traveling, he divided his followers equally.
Such was his life,
and such his achievements.
Then, as the metal essence grew vigorous,
the army marched with just cause;
the stone drum's sound rose high,
the clash of arms could be heard afar.
Thus where his fleets reached,
they covered the Huái and Sì rivers;
where his banners struck,
they encompassed the Guī and Méng regions.
The Wèi general had already fled,
yet they still wrote on the trees of Mǎlíng;
the Qí army was in retreat,
vainly gazing at the birds of Píngyīn.
Soon, Nán Zhòng sent out his chariots,
Fāng Shū arrived to oversee,
with long-axled carriages and patterned mats,
breastplates hooked and bridles adorned,
then, as Heaven's way lay in the north,
the southern wind could not compete.
In the past, when a lieutenant lost discipline,
General Wèi thus awaited punishment;
when the central army contended for crossing,
Xún Huánzǐ thereby met execution.
With a heart full of sorrow,
how could he serve his lord?
In the first year of Xuānzhèng,
arriving at the eastern capital's pavilion,
an edict released his phoenix bridle,
cleansed his covenant altar.
First expanding the rites of receiving at the guesthouse,
he then received the platform's mandate,
appointed General with Extraordinary Powers, Duke of Huáidé Commandery,
with a fief of two thousand households.
Returning to Píngjīn's lodge,
he sometimes heard the stable horse's neigh;
staying at Guǎngchéng's post station,
he barely saw the guests of feudal lords.
Lián Pō longed and lingered,
did he ever hear of being used again?
Lǐ Guǎng paced and hesitated,
with no more hope of leading the vanguard.
The drunken captain at Bàlíng,
his insults can be imagined;
the former marquis of Dōnglíng,
his life was over.
On the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month in the second year of Dàxiàng,
his breath illness suddenly worsened,
and he passed away in the guesthouse,
at seventy-seven years of age.
On the nineteenth day of the eighth month of that same year, he was temporarily buried in the eastern suburbs of Wànnián County, Jīngzhào.
An edict posthumously awarded him a certain office,
and the posthumous title of...,
according to ritual.
The eight thousand子弟 of Jiāngdōng,
followed Xiàng Jǐ and did not return;
the five hundred soldiers on the island,
died for Tián Héng together.
Alas, sorrow!
Máo Xiūzhī buried beyond the frontier,
lost and not preserved;
Lù Píngyuán defeated at Héqiáo,
in death and life ashamed and regretful.
To return Gōngsūn's coffin,
is still not timely;
to bring back Lián Yǐn's corpse,
who knows on what day?
A wandering soul in a sojourner's life,
enough to grieve Wēn Xù's heart;
in the dark night longing for home,
finally having Sū Sháo's dream.
Thus causing the lanes of Guǎngpíng,
to forever detain a wronged spirit;
the pavilion of Rǔnán,
long to hear night weeping.
Alas, sorrow!
Then the inscription says:
Nine rivers settled the land,
three rivers paid tribute.
That beauty of the central states,
was your fiefdom.
Proud of talent, boasting wisdom,
riding danger, relying on strength.
Floating chimes gathered scales,
solitary paulownia hung wings.
The five weapons early exhausted,
the first drum already faded.
Moving camps, reducing stoves,
empty tents, birds flying.
Could sheepskin redeem him?
What use painting a horse to pursue?
Xún Yīng gone forever,
Suí Huì never returning.
Existence and extinction in a moment,
time and light sorrowful and bleak.
The mountain cracked, the central terrace,
the stars empty, the supreme general.
Turning to speak of wife and children,
far away the border posts.
The soul perhaps can be summoned,
the funeral rites, what can be hoped?
Great ambition sunk and submerged,
grand plans buried and lost.
The western mound enough to stumble,
yellow dust, shattered bones.
Where are the ponds and terraces?
Whose breeze and moonlight?
The tomb path distant and confined,
the camp soul drifting and lodged.
No mound by the Bà riverbank,
no trees at Pínglíng.
The mound of a strong warrior,
the tomb of a general.
In what age, what year,
will it become an armory again?
○ From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 947.
〈Epitaph for Zhèng Cháng, Duke of Guǎngráo with Authority Equal to the Three Dukes, Great General of the Zhōu Dynasty〉
The Duke, whose given name was Cháng,
styled Mǒu,
was a man of Xíngyáng.
The younger brother of King Xuān of Zhōu
first enfeoffed his state;
the grandson of Duke Mù of Zhèng
first established his surname.
His grandfather, Sīqìng,
was General Who Establishes Might and Governor of Shānyáng.
His father, Xū,
was Pillar of State with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies and Governor of Yùzhōu.
When Nányáng sat and whistled,
it encountered this lord of the state;
when Xīhé erected the falcon banner,
it met this inspector’s recommendation.
Dukes and marquises followed in succession,
caps and coronets linked bridle to bridle—
this can be spoken of
and transmitted in the historical records.
The Duke knew ritual from his childhood,
and his reputation spread early.
He attended the classics in the schoolhouse,
briefly glimpsing the study hall;
he practiced martial arts in the military barracks,
particularly mastering swordsmanship.
Although still young in years,
he was already praised by Confucian scholars;
though his rank was that of a minor officer,
he entered into the general’s rewards.
In the third year of the Dàtǒng era,
he raised an uprising at Huáyáng,
and was granted the title of Founding Baron of Yǒng’ān County.
When Emperor Wén first laid the foundation of his hegemony,
heroes gathered like spokes to a hub;
the Duke drew his sword at the camp gate,
and Yǐngchuān followed me.
In the battle against the rebels at Luòchéng,
he was mightier than the troops of Báimǎ;
in relieving the siege at Héqiáo,
he was braver than the strategy of Wūlín.
He was appointed General Who Pacifies the East and Commander-in-Chief,
inheriting his father’s fief.
In the second year of the Wèihòu era,
he was granted the authority of Commissioner with Credentials, General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Pillar of State with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies.
The General of Chariots and Cavalry drew on the merit of Guō Huái,
and the Pillar of State took the nobility of Wáng Chén—
for this appointment of the Duke,
all said the right man was chosen.
He was advanced to Duke of Guǎngráo County,
with a fief of one thousand households.
In the third year of the Bǎodìng era, he was appointed Commissioner with Credentials, Commander of All Military Affairs of Qiānzhōu, and Governor of Qiānzhōu.
He then took overall command of the troops and horses of Jīnzhōu,
opening up the northern frontiers.
The high mountains sought the clouds,
the deep valleys held no shadows;
only by ladder and rope could one ascend,
only by floating bamboo rafts could one pass.
The influence of Mǐnyuè,
the prestige of Gōuwú.
The Duke went forth to battle with short weapons,
and all fled northward,
disintegrating like ice shattering,
leaving the mountains empty and valleys still.
He was appointed Commissioner with Credentials, General Who Opens the Mansion with Equal Honor.
At the high feast of Bǎiliáng,
there was the poem of the great general;
when the command tent first opened,
there was the state of the Marquis of Pínglíng.
Compared to today,
how could they be spoken of in the same breath!
From then on, his envoy’s carriage
was adorned with embroidered robes;
he observed local customs,
and inspected punishments and governance.
The Duke, bearing his credentials, drove eastward,
the wind hastening the bands of bandits;
he buried his wheels in the road,
his might shaking the Central Plains.
When Emperor Wǔ had his army at Méngjīn,
he made the Duke the strong central force,
externally following the decisive victory,
internally attending to military strategy.
And when the tracks of writing were unified,
and the banners of war had been laid down,
the Director of Merit performed the rewards,
the military officials raised their achievements,
and he was appointed Commissioner with Credentials, Senior General Who Opens the Mansion,
with an increase of five hundred households to his fief.
He was granted the surname Yǔwén,
the honor of sharing the state’s chariot;
in the ancestral covenant of Zhōu,
he was no longer a descendant of a different surname.
Entrusted as a protective screen,
the focus of high favor,
the ducal house was not estranged—
this is what is meant.
The commander of the nine provinces
must have the right talent;
the lords of a thousand li
truly await his governance.
He was then made Commissioner with Credentials, Commander of All Military Affairs of Dōngxúzhōu, and Governor of Xúzhōu.
Soon he was transferred to Commander of All Military Affairs of Nányǎnzhōu and Governor of Nányǎnzhōu.
The Duke repeatedly oversaw the six regulations,
twice toiled over the ten departments;
customs changed and morals shifted,
people cherished and officials feared.
Leftover sheaves and forgotten bundles
benefited the weary people;
mountain mulberries and wild silkworms
sufficed for tribute and taxes.
His transformation reached different customs,
his might extended to neighboring borders;
when reporting affairs to the capital,
he was first among the four directions.
Is this not what is called a true governor?
Was it not in this?
His years were not yet advanced,
when suddenly he encountered illness.
In the first year of the Dàxiàng era, he passed away at the provincial garrison,
at the age of sixty-three.
Alas, sorrowful indeed! The officials and people clung in longing,
