birds and beasts changed color;
the Hé and Jì rivers ceased their pounding,
the Huái and Yí rivers halted their markets.
This year he was returned for burial in the mountains of Xíngyáng.
An edict posthumously granted him the office of Mǒu,
in accordance with ritual.
Alas for the shifting of hills and valleys,
fearing the eternal loss of fine plans;
as earth endures and heaven lasts,
I dare to inscribe this steadfast stone.
The inscription says:
Jīng and Hé define Yù,
the foundation where Luò feeds.
Waters wind around the waves of Xíng,
mountains slant to Lùhún.
The star of virtue still shines,
the auspicious wind has not gone far.
Each generation does not lack worthies,
the patterns do not lack embroidered robes.
When the Duke was born,
he truly descended as an heroic spirit.
Loyalty was the root of his virtue,
filial piety he received from heaven’s constants.
He read books in the tiger hall,
he studied swordsmanship in the dragon pavilion.
His carved bow curved like the moon,
his running horse shot like a meteor.
He deployed formations at Líyáng,
wielded troops at Guāndù.
At Píngyīn he listened to crows,
at Mǎlíng he wrote on trees.
His spirit watched the turning ford,
his stars divined flying steps.
Fire severed the Qiāng camps,
sand collapsed the bandits’ roads.
And when he drove with the rhinoceros tally,
he governed a mighty province.
Officials did not startle dogs,
people had no panting oxen.
Western silkworms obtained the year,
eastern plowing met autumn.
Grass rotted at the prison gate,
stars lowered over the market tower.
The five generals’ stars perished,
the three terraces’ peaks split.
Alas, the way of heaven,
thus claimed the wise man.
Beams and pillars crumbled,
wind and clouds fell silent.
The northern wall long mourned,
the eastern capital forever parted.
Deep and secluded is this place,
the burial ground relies here.
Mountains encircle the tiger pen,
roads ascend the fish mound.
Sad winds rage at night,
bitter dew congeals at dawn.
Orchids fragrant, chrysanthemums lush,
through eternity they endure.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 947.
“Epitaph for Liǔ Xiá, Duke of Wénxǐ and Great General of Zhōu”
“Epitaph for Liǔ Xiá, Duke of Wénjiāxǐ and Great General of Zhōu”
The gentleman, named Xiá,
styled Zǐshēng,
was a man from Xiè County, Hédōng.
When Qín first annexed the lands of Jìn,
and Hàn opened the region of Píngyuè,
the pitch-pipe matched Yízé,
and the stars resided under Chúnshǒu.
Moreover, Zhuāng plotted in Wèi,
already serving as a minister of the state;
Xǐ responded in Qí,
never neglecting the duties of the feudal lords.
His grandfather, Shūzhēn,
served as a Gentleman Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Governor of Yìyáng under the Sòng.
Possessing the responsive eloquence of Xú Miǎo,
he served in the bureau of the Cavalier Attendants;
with the upright integrity of Jí Àn,
he administered the commandery of Huáiyáng.
His father, Jìyuǎn,
served as Advisory Army Advisor to the Prince of Línchuān and Governor of Yídū.
The Orchid Terrace and Stone Chamber
were where he broadened his knowledge;
White Horse and Flying Fox,
surpassed in lofty rhetoric.
Wú Róng of the Western Capital,
renowned south of the Yangtze,
when meeting in conversation,
found him as if an old acquaintance.
The gentleman, endowed with the spirit of virtuous virtue,
imbued with an aura soaring to the heavens,
from his childhood days with bound hair,
displayed early wisdom and maturity.
Love and reverence came naturally from heaven,
piety and respect were inherent to his nature,
embracing benevolence and upholding righteousness,
practicing faithfulness and residing in integrity.
His paternal uncle, the Commandant Equal to the Three Excellencies, Lord Zhōnghuì, especially valued his exceptional talent,
and once said to him:
"I once served our late uncle, the Grand Commandant,
and he told me:
'I dreamed last night that you ascended a tall tower,
the tower was exceedingly lofty and splendid,
and I gave you my seat.
You may attain wealth and honor,
but I regret I will not live to see it.'
I recently took a nap during the day,
and again dreamed of giving you that former seat,
once more bestowing it upon you.
Your official rank shall surely reach that level."
Wáng Xiáng's girdle knife,
passed down for generations among high ministers;
Bào Yǒng's piebald horse,
handed down in a family of Directors of Retainers.
Comparing him to these,
he was in no way ashamed.
When the Light-Chariot General, Marquis of Xīchāng, established his fief in Xiāng-Hàn,
the gentleman was twelve years old at the time.
He paid a visit according to commoner etiquette,
his advance and halt dignified and proper, his demeanor elegant and upright.
The Marquis could not take his eyes off him,
and tested him by sending an attendant
to step on the hem of his robe,
wishing to observe his reaction.
The gentleman slowly stepped forward a little,
without ever looking back.
When Marquis Wèi met Liú Yì,
he unconsciously composed his expression;
when the Hàn sovereign observed Tián Fèng,
he then ordered an inscription on the pillar.
Compared to this day,
how could they suffice!
When the Swift-as-Flight Cavalry General, Prince of Lújiāng, an imperial son, went out to his fief,
he held the scales and selected with high standards,
and due to the gentleman's illustrious reputation,
summoned him to serve as Registrar.
Zhāng Tǎn's straightforward admonitions,
were praised as the fragrance of Prefect Xún;
Zōu Zhàn's discerning words,
further revealed Lord Yáng's virtue.
When the Advisory Army Advisor, his father, passed away in the capital,
the gentleman rushed to attend,
and reached the capital in just six days.
His body was emaciated and haggard,
unrecognizable.
As the coffin traveled upstream on the river,
in midstream as evening approached,
the currents grew turbulent and swift,
a contrary wind turned the sails,
and the people in the boat
looked at each other, their faces pale.
Clutching the coffin, he wailed in grief,
vowing not to seek survival.
In a short while,
the wind and waves calmed,
and all believed it was due to his utmost sincerity.
The filial son of Chéngdū,
who threw himself into the river;
the worthy of former times from Guìyáng,
whose body was revealed by a wildfire.
Both preserved the coffins,
all lamentable and sigh-worthy.
When the Grand Lady developed sores between her breasts,
the physician said:
"Only if someone sucks the pus and blood,
might there be hope of recovery."
The gentleman, his heart in turmoil,
responded immediately and sucked.
Within ten days,
she recovered fully.
In serving his parents,
he can be said to have reached the utmost.
His elder cousin of the Right Guard,
holding authority south of the mountains,
insistently brought him along.
In the past, Mǎ Yóu's aspirations
were recognized by Mǎ Yuán;
Bān Sì's talent and learning
were appreciated by Bān Biāo.
This was heard of again in the present day.
He was then appointed Magistrate of Yǒnghuà County.
Quietly clearing his tilted desk,
he might chant of distant Chángcén;
occasionally strumming his singing zither,
he did not consider Héyáng crude.
The golden pillars of Rìnán,
the pearl springs of Hépǔ,
he never harbored in his heart,
nor ever cast his eyes upon.
He took up the kerchief as Legal Advisor to Prince Shàolíng of Píngxī,
and then transferred to Vice Director of the Ministry of Works.
Upon first entering the ceremonial gates,
and ascending the Orchid Pavilion,
the Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs of Chén Commandery, Xiè Jǔ,
a man of renown and national treasure,
engaged him in conversation,
and said to those seated with him:
"The heroic spirit of Jiāng-Hàn
is seen here today!"
The Central General of the West, Prince Yuèyáng,
with the weight of the green carriage,
oversaw the governance of Xīhé.
By decree, he employed the gentleman as Administrator of this province,
and soon promoted him to Assistant.
Wáng Shūlǐ was famed for grading the flow of beings,
Chén Zhòngjǔ renowned for inscribing the carriage.
The gentleman's display of his steed's talents,
combined both.
When the great bandits shifted the state,
and the royal house was thrown into turmoil,
the moon shook and stars swayed,
clouds leveled and rainbows stood straight.
Prince Yuèyáng received authority east of Shǎn,
and held the jade disc south of the Hàn,
where the net of heaven gathered,
and all the worthy and wise assembled.
He appointed the gentleman Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel, and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
concurrently serving as Tutor to the Crown Prince.
Overseeing the stores at the Jiǎguān,
his duty was as weighty as Shǐ Dān's;
lecturing at the Cassia Palace,
his fame as high as Zhāng Yǔ's.
He soon advanced to General of Chariots and Cavalry, Grand Commander,
enfeoffed as Duke of Wénxǐ County, Palace Attendant, Commandant Equal to the Three Excellencies with authority to establish a mansion,
retaining his previous positions.
Compared to riding as escort,
Huò Qùbìng served as Palace Attendant;
likened to commanding troops,
Gōngsūn Áo was Swift-as-Flight Cavalry General.
Sufficient to illuminate the six ministries,
and wisely plan the nine virtues,
how could it merely mean harmonizing with the supreme general,
and assisting the central army!
Afterwards, he followed words to the state of Liáng,
and served in office at Fēngdū.
Guǎn Zhòng, with his words,
received the rites of a lower minister;
Zāng Sūn, seen for his virtue,
was again honored with a feast for distinguished guests.

There was an edict appointing him Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Swift-as-Flight Cavalry General, Commandant Equal to the Three Excellencies with authority to establish a mansion, in charge of all military affairs of Huò Province, and Governor of Huò Province.
With the rhinoceros tally leaving the pass,
and the embroidered robes speeding by relay,
he was welcomed in the suburbs with scholars leading the way,
and as an honored guard, the regional lord bore the crossbow.
Simply because the Five Streams were remote and distant,
like Mǎ Fúbō's longing to return;
and the Three Xiāngs low and damp,
like Jiǎ Chángshā's unwillingness.
Therefore, the Governor of Yíchéng,
went straight to meet at Lùmén;
the ancient land of White Sands,
still retained the dragon's seed.
Heaven's pestilence gave no warning,
and suddenly he reached his end.
In a certain year of the Tiānhé era,
he was returned and buried in the old graves at White Sands, Xiāngyáng.
Your bearing is auspicious and upright,
your discernment broad and keen,
you cleanse your body and bathe in virtue,
cultivate arts and rely on benevolence,
a man of esteemed reputation in Rǔnán,
a respected elder in Fúfēng.
Not speaking of wealth and profit,
like Wáng Yífǔ in his virtue;
not discussing people and affairs,
like Ruǎn Sìzōng in his conduct.
Composed amid the turmoil of chaos and separation,
you preserved this fine reputation;
unfolding and rolling amid the winds and clouds,
it did not hinder your noble service.
After Zhāng Héng's armillary sphere,
he composed "Returning to the Fields";
since Dù Yù sank his stele,
he settled in his hometown.
Wáng Zhòngxuān had a tower for reading,
Zhūgě Liàng had a residence for playing the qin—
truly wishing to retire due to illness,
to live in leisure until the end.
With the singing qin upon your knees,
you might face an old friend;
with a treasured sword at your side,
you would at times encounter a young child.
A hundred years pass in an instant,
alas, how sorrowful!
Thus, the tomb of a gentleman
holds only a buried bronze sword;
the grave of a worthy minister
bears only an inscribed stone casket.
The inscription reads:
There were Zhuāng and Huì,
dwelling in Lǔ and Wèi.
Righteousness adapts to the times,
talent capable of aiding the age.
Minister of the Northern Department,
Metropolitan Commandant of the Eastern Capital.
Surely to restore its beginning,
the marquises succeed one another.
A single peak of the Huágài,
a single star of Wénchāng.
Blue-collared youths discern their aspirations,
young boys depart from the classics.
In righteousness, he urged the "non-horse,"
in study, diligent as the firefly's glow.
In past years, the spirit carriage
drifted upon the river's isles.
Through your grief and sorrow,
the river god stilled the waves.
Fame spread to the Northern Sea,
renown raced to the Western River.
Who ascends the nine bends,
yet does not enter Cháogē?
Luxuriant brilliance, all transformed,
climbing and accompanying, then far removed.
White deer follow the carriage,
red halos adorn the crown.
Position ranked among high generals,
honors combined with original selection.
Snakes coil on ribbon knots,
turtles circle on seal turns.
Coming to court at Pínglè,
returning governance to Xiányáng.
The frontier defenses thus opened,
the military tent still spread.
Rising with these rites and measures,
steepening these martial regulations.
The long phoenix, graceful and winding,
preens its feathers over the river's heights.
The age urgent as rushing streams,
years hasten the startled falcon.
Vanishing, reining in abruptly,
Fúsāng shakes the carriage shafts.
The wise man's stone splits,
the worthy's star falls.
Western È's mushrooms wither,
Nányáng's chrysanthemums exhaust.
Sorrowfully, opening the hands,
life's glory reaches its end.
The pestle halts its pounding,
the loom ceases its weaving.
Lonely, the descendant son,
watches the shadows, with remaining breath.
Frost and dew tread upon him,
alas, the sorrowful thorny jujube.
Dragon's nest gazes northward,
phoenix tower viewed ahead.
Pines tall, wind distant,
earth thick, springs cold.
Books buried, tablets scattered,
qin overturned, strings slack.
The volume presented at parting,
inscribed and placed in the coffin.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 948.
Epitaph for the Late Great General of Zhōu, Duke Yìxīng of the Xiāo Family
Epitaph for the Late Great General of Zhōu, Duke Yìxīng of the Xiāo Family
In ancient times, when the Minister of Education spread the five teachings,
it was at the beginning of Yáo's abdication;
when the Chancellor oversaw all affairs,
it was after Qín's downfall.
Like the Yīn people receiving their clan name,
they inherited the fief of Wēizǐ;
when the Liáng dynasty responded to the charts,
it truly opened the state of Yánlíng.
The Duke, named Tài,
courtesy name Shìyí,
was from Lánlíng,
grandson of Emperor Wén, the Great Ancestor, and son of Prince Zhōngliè of Póyáng.
His lineage diverged from the celestial river,
his branch split from the Ruòmù tree,
the straight trunk naturally tall,
the clear source already distant.
A close relative of illustrious virtue,
he was praised for the achievements of Máo and Bì;
the imperial clansman guarding the walls,
he established the states of Xíng and Máo.
In the first year of Dàtóng,
at age sixteen,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Fēngchéng County,
with a stipend of five hundred households.
The mountains overlook the Crane Pass,
not without Táo Kǎn's guests;
the aura connects the Dipper and Ox,
there was indeed Zhāng Huá's sword.
He took up the scarf as Gentleman of the Palace,
and concurrently served as Crown Prince's Assistant.
A young lord entering service,
not a court gentleman yet of equal rank;
a palace assistant,
different from the road-clearers yet advancing ahead.
With the Duke occupying this post,
it was truly a distinguished selection.
In the first year of Dàtóng,
he entered duty in the palace departments.
That same year,
he transferred to Crown Prince's Secretary in the Central Secretariat.
Guarding the Southern Palace,
his duty was at the orchid racks;
attending the Northern Pavilion,
he was honored to participate in consultations.
Registered in both palaces,
his worthiness was thus present.
In the third year of Dàtóng,
he was appointed Commissioner with Credentials, General of Benevolent Authority, and Governor of Qiáo Prefecture.
Lifting the curtains in the realm of auspicious airs,
he inspected and recommended in the land that dispels sorrow.
In Nányáng's customs,
literary arts abound;
in Měijì, welcoming him,
children came from afar.
Then came chaos and separation, distress ensued,
the royal house was in turmoil,
great officers had the sorrow of distant service,
gentlemen had grievances without end.
Turning his back on the pass, longing for Chǔ,
he traveled by small boat,
on the Jiāng and Hàn, serving the rightful ruler,
returning to Zhānghuá with the restoration lord.
In the first year of Chéngshèng,
he was appointed Palace Attendant.
Unparalleled in responding to inquiries,
he truly followed in the steps of Dīng Hóng;
knowledgeable in ancient statutes,
he equaled Wáng Càn in balance.
In the second year,
he was appointed Commissioner with Credentials, General Who Pacifies the West, and Governor of Línchuān,
then transferred to General Who Pacifies the South and Governor of Guìyáng.
The Imperial Workshop cast swords,
again turning the golden turtle;
the Censorate distributed tallies,
doubly sealing the bronze tiger.
Was it merely Dèng Yōu's purity,
praised in the song of the fifth drum;
or Liú Chǒng's integrity and ability,
renowned as the one-coin commandery?
Thus, as the Heavenly Protection era was not yet settled,
and the royal roads were fraught with obstacles,
returning to Wú was impossible,
and there was no path back to Shǔ.
Línzī faced the sea,
so he abruptly changed his course,
fleeing to Qīngzhāng,
and folding his wings at Bóhǎi.
He was granted the titles of General of Chariots and Cavalry and Regular Attendant of the Imperial Court,
and still served as Commissioner with Special Powers, Regional Commander, and Governor of Yǒng Prefecture.
Yet the Qín pavilion pressed upon the border,
and the watchtowers of Zhū sounded the alarm within the city walls.
Drums and horns echoed from the earth,
and generals fell from the sky.
Although he listened for sounds in jars and pots,
it did not prevent the enemy tunnels;
though he tied ropes and bundled firewood,
it could not repel the cloud ladders.
He pleaded for surrender,
only to be returned to the Protector-General.
The Zhōu court, valuing talent from Chǔ for use in Jìn,
did not cease in its governance;
and the Zhào jade sought by Qín,
was not hindered by distance or captivity.

In the fifth year of the Bǎodìng era, he was appointed Commissioner with Special Powers, General of Agile Cavalry, Pillar of State with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies, and Duke of Yìxīng Commandery with a fief,
with an estate of 1,300 households.
In the second year of the Tiānhé era,
he was appointed Commissioner with Special Powers, Regional Commander of Military Affairs in Cài Prefecture, and Governor of Cài Prefecture.
Like the beloved son of King Qǐngxiāng of Chǔ,
who wore commoner’s clothes and guarded the valley;
or the maternal younger brother of King Ānxī of Wèi,
who was also a traveler in Hándān.
Worries wounded the man,
and his allotted years were not long.
At the age of fifty-one,
he passed away at the garrison of Cài Prefecture.
When his remains were sent back to the capital,
only his ceremonial robes remained;
as his carriage returned on the road,
the curtains were drawn once more.
Alas, how sorrowful!
An imperial decree granted him posthumous honors,
and he was given the posthumous title of Mǒu,
in accordance with ritual.
In the eleventh month of the fifth year,
he was buried on the northern plain of Cháng’ān.
The tomb of Chūlǐzǐ
faced the armory directly;
the grave of the Grand Historian
aligned straight with the Gāo Gate.
The inscription reads:
The distant achievements of the Dark Bird,
the grand plans of Xiàngtǔ.
Enfeoffed in the east at the Sòng altar,
gathering maps in the west from Qín.
Men served to assist Hàn,
the state succeeded in founding Wú.
There was the beauty of virtuous conduct,
a close relative in the princely residence.
Establishing a state for the imperial branch,
continuing the family as the emperor’s younger brother.
Following the hidden workings of fate,
bright and upright, enlightened by heaven.
Yuángù heard the "Odes,"
Tángdū studied the "Rites."
In the gardens of Bówàng,
the palaces of Jīnhuá.
In the literary grove, he lectured on virtue,
in the military tent, he participated in strategy.
His name was inscribed on the pillars,
his plans filled the curtains.
He settled to the west of Zī,
governed to the east of Huái.
The Qín pavilion pressed from the west,
the Chǔ marshes ended in the south.
At times startled by hunting fires,
or fearing the autumn wind.
Entrusted with far-reaching strategies,
he encountered this crisis.
Formations stretched for ten lǐ,
troops besieged from one side.
The moon haloed the solitary city,
dust alarmed the empty reinforcements.
Spring bamboo shoots were not provisions,
autumn mugwort had no arrows.
Folding wings like a crouching dragon,
he laid down his pride and ceased battle.
At a time of reconciliation,
favor was added with initial rewards.
The royal rank grew more lofty,
military honors rose further.
The scarlet egret had just taken flight,
when the songs of Yú resounded.
Weeping for the son, leaving regrets behind,
his books stored away, he departed forever.
Heat and cold alternate in succession,
scattered and fallen upon the hills.
Frosty air veils the moon,
pine scent ascends in autumn.
Alas, the prince of the southern state,
became the former marquis of the eastern tomb.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 948.
Epitaph for the Late Great General Zhào of Zhōu
Epitaph for the Late Great General Zhào of Zhōu
The gentleman’s personal name was Guǎng,
courtesy name Qiánguī,
the great-grandson of Duke Shàohuì,
and the eldest son of Duke Bīnxiào.
Like Ruòmù brushing the sun,
the long serpent entrusting itself to heaven,
the dragon chart veiling the river’s light,
the divine tripod connecting to the clouds’ aura,
the six hexagrams constructing characters,
the five cycles manifesting auspicious signs.
Thus, the sacred mountain descended its spirit,
and virtue was born from heaven.
His skin was smooth as congealed fat, his eyes dark as lacquer,
his forehead broad like the sun, his brow like pearls.
As a son, his fame surpassed the five capitals;
as a minister, his radiance illuminated a thousand lǐ.
The peak of Huágài reaching the mid-heavens
could not match his loftiness;
the waters of Yúyuān bathing the sun
could not exhaust his depth.
In the year of the carved chariot,
at the age of bamboo horses.
The cassia tree within the moon,
he inquired earnestly and could be instructed;
the wood growing upon the stone,
he pondered deeply and immediately understood.
At the age of eleven,
Duke Xiào passed away.
Alone in sorrow,
he mourned with the devotion of a child beyond ritual,
startling the springs of filial piety,
stirring the bamboo in the cold forest.
The three virtues were fully manifested,
the eight wings thus raised.
When the Great Zhōu founded the state,
the imperial clansmen formed its walls.
Altars were established for the enfeoffed,
and duties were divided according to mandate.
He was enfeoffed as Duke of Tiānshuǐ Commandery,
with an estate of 2,000 households.
In the first year,
he was appointed Commissioner with Special Powers, General of Agile Cavalry, and Pillar of State with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies.
In the fourth month of that year,
he was appointed Regional Commander and Governor of Qín Prefecture.
Duke Xiào had long governed Qiānlǒng,
leaving behind love among the people.
Now, as he was entrusted with this task,
he was the son of our lord.
Was it only the office of the Director of Uprightness
where Bào Xuān’s lineage accumulated?
Or the residence of the Chancellor,
where Wéi Xián’s generations succeeded?
In the second year,
he was appointed Great General.
Like Wèi Qīng setting up his tent,
he was recorded among the great meritorious officials;
akin to Hán Xìn ascending the platform,
he was honored with a unique appointment.
In the first year of the Wǔchéng era,
he was transferred to Regional Commander of Military Affairs in Xīng, Liáng, and seventeen other prefectures, and Governor of Liáng Prefecture.
Bōzhǒng guides the Yàng River,
which becomes the eastern flow of the Hàn;
Càiméng’s journey levels,
truly the western extremity of Huáyáng.
In the ninth month of that year,
he was re-enfeoffed as Duke of Cài,
with an estate of 10,000 households.
His lands bordered Hánchéng,
his passes neighbored the Chǔ barriers.
With eight counties in his fief,
the favor ran as deep as Kòu Xún’s achievements;
with a household of ten thousand families,
the reward reached the heights of Cáo Shēn’s recognition.
In the first year of the Bǎodìng era,
he was appointed Junior Minister of Justice.
Prison doors grew moss,
and jail keys remained still.
Wine-laden carriages passed by,
fortunately free from grievances;
inspecting prisoners in the military headquarters,
he sometimes listened to the zither’s melody.
In the second year,
he was ordered to guard Púchéng,
serving as Commander of the Six Defenses including Tóngguān.
In the intercalary month of that year,
he was promoted to Commander of the Twelve Provinces including Qín and Wèi, and Governor of Qín Province.
He repeatedly governed Jìchéng,
frequently defended Lǒngdǐ,
causing the powerful to restrain their hands,
and the corrupt to resign their seals.
With the elite troops of Shànggǔ,
and the war drums of Yúyáng,
facing Gāoliǔ to the north,
and gazing at Chángyú to the south,
from the mountains where the Xiōngnú dismounted,
to the valleys where the noble stored wine,
all from afar admired his authority,
and received his civilizing influence.
In the second year,
he was ordered to welcome the empress in Gānzhōu.
With a mark on his hand,
Zhòngzǐ returned;
when Jì Lièrú came,
the minister acted as the ruler’s envoy.
Had he not been renowned across the realm,
and his might felt by neighboring states,
how could he have been entrusted with such an honorable mission?
In the fourth year,
he was appointed Pillar of State and Grand General.
Zhāoyáng was employed for his great achievements,
and Xiàng Liáng was appointed for his fame as a general,
but compared to him now,
they would feel ashamed.
In the third year of the Tiānhé era,
he was appointed Commander of the Eight Provinces including Shǎn and Yú and the Gān Defense, and Governor of Shǎn Province.
Qūchǎn and Chuíjí,
already had armies to destroy Guó;
Wángguān and Jīmǎ,
were not without routes to cut off Qín.
He properly arranged banners and drums,
and orderly managed chariots and tracks,
subduing rebels and intimidating the borders,
with strategies leaving no room for error.
But due to long toil at home and abroad,
illness accumulated from this,
mountains and rivers were visited with prayers,
and guests filled the doors like visiting lords.
Thus, he requested an audience at Chéngmíng,
speaking of returning to his fief,
seeking the sacrifices of the Xià suburbs,
or discerning the hauntings of Sānglín.
He was further appointed Governor of Qín Province,
and inherited his father’s title, Duke of Bīn.
Before he could ascend the ridge of divided streams,
he gazed in vain at the city of the evening frontier.
His mother, seeing him frail and thin,
wept sorrowfully by his side,
until chest qi clashed violently,
and she suddenly passed away.
He prostrated himself on the mourning mat,
refusing food and drink,
and though envoys urged him to relent,
his grief only deepened.
The mother died for her son,
the son died for his parent,
the ways of kindness and filial piety,
were gathered in a single moment.
At the time of his decline,
he was twenty-nine years old.
Markets ceased in the four passes,
and the three armies wept as they marched.
Seeking where he once heard cases,
one still sees the cold pear tree;
looking back at the empty camp,
only the withered willows remain.
He was posthumously granted a certain office,
as was fitting.
In the sixth year, in the sixth month,
he was buried in the plains of Qínzhōu.
Black armor cleared the way,
recalling the achievements of the swift cavalry;
dragon banners escorted his journey,
deeply mourning the distance of Dōngpíng.
He was upright and loyal,
gentle and filial,
dwelling in benevolence and righteousness,
adorned with ritual and music,
his demeanor alert and keen,
wise and discerning,
with depth like palace walls,
and no trace of joy or anger on his face.
Records like the Golden Plates and Jade Tablets,
he pored over tirelessly;
illustrations of orchid leaves and mushroom flowers,
he studied diligently.
Autumn clouds over Jiéshí,
the setting moon at Zhāoyáng,
thoughts like wind filling his heart,
words flowing like a spring from his lips.
In elegant secretarial work,
he was like Ruǎn Yǔ and Chén Lín;
in graceful refinement,
he resembled Wáng Méng and Xiè Tiǎo.
Speaking of his hundred shots,
his bow surpassed the ape’s cry;
discussing his hundred hits,
his sword pierced deeper than the goose formation.
Like Méi Chéng gazing at the Liáng estate,
he did not fear abandoning office;
like Yuè Yì seeking the road to Yān,
he did not refuse a journey of a thousand miles.
As for adapting to changing tactics,
he achieved them like lightning;
in devising strategies within the tent,
he unknowingly matched Sūn and Wú.
He had the ambition to evaluate human character,
and the heart to bring peace to the world.
But the roc’s path was suddenly cut short,
and the dragon’s ford was blocked.
Alas, how sorrowful!
The Grand Steward early flourished in the three Jīng,
and long departed from all beginnings,
raising the orphaned child,
as branches of the same tree, sharing the same breath.
Like Mǎ Yuán instructing his nephews,
his righteousness lay in caution and discipline;
like Wáng Chén serving his uncle,
his feelings were deep with love and respect.
Sharing virtue and matching righteousness,
this is what is meant!
Thus, the inscription reads:
He governed the Qian trigram and followed the Ji constellation,
riding the Li trigram to become a sage.
The white jade ring yielded to virtue,
the black jade tablet received the mandate.
He pacified the earth's axis,
adding radiance to the heavenly mirror.
Shading numerous states to the side,
facing the seven regulators ahead.
The land belonged to the first ascendant,
the time met with the succeeding martial one.
The jade huang pendant quelled chaos,
the golden casket illuminated assistance.
Wei and Jin inherited the family,
Xíng and Máo bestowed the land.
Waves divided at Jiànmù,
tributaries flowed from Xuánhù.
The great destiny followed the Yin order,
the profound plans were deep and secure.
Loyalty had splendid designs,
filial piety was complete virtue.
With mountain-like austerity he attended to governance,
holding the huangui jade he guarded the state.
The vast sea was about to be reached,
Yān Mountain would soon be inscribed.
At Pínglè, high feasts were held,
in Jīnhuá, classics were expounded.
Discussing Confucianism at Bìshuǐ,
personally observing rites in the bright court.
Awaiting compositions from the wind-measurer,
requiring inscriptions for the dew-collector.
Sailing a boat toward the sun,
guiding a horse following the stars.
Virtuous actions were able to be illustrious,
capable and worthy, truly virtuous.
The high general bestowed the sacrificial meat,
the supreme commander pushed the chariot.
Zhào lost its eastern fishing grounds,
the Hú perished in southern pastures.
Arrows fell upon Liáochéng,
mud sealed Hángǔ Pass.
The dragon robe was frequently revealed,
the red carriage curtain repeatedly rolled up.
Laws were simplified with empathy,
complex arguments were dismissed with reason.
Thieving crows were exposed upon investigation,
doubtful snakes were distinguished immediately.
People shared the official gardens,
households alike had wild silkworms.
Grasping clouds pushed aside shadows,
shifting winds brought down cliffs.
The star of the central terrace split,
the mountain of the left garrison collapsed.
Summer pillars set aside the wine cups,
Yīn steps opened the funeral.
The fringed canopy trod the path,
bright banners led in the courtyard.
Gazing straight toward Qínchuān,
the Lǒng River waters parted in flight.
Mountains and rivers filled the eyes,
the retinue and guards escorted the spirit home.
The tomb illustration showed stone horses,
the carriage depicted dragon robes.
Small hills shed their leaves,
tall forests turned to decay.
Mournful were the plains and lowlands,
desolate the burial grounds.
Trees dense, people sparse,
mountains many, paths small.
Ten lǐ of pine walls,
a millennium-old ornamental pillar.
The night terrace now silent,
the deep spring knows no dawn.
○From *Wenyuan Yinghua*, scroll 948.
Epitaph for Lady Bùlùgū, Wife of the Duke of Qiáo of Zhōu
The lady's given name was Mǒu,
her courtesy name Mǒu,
originally surnamed Lù,
from Wújùn commandery.
When the Son of Heaven expanded the borders,
the Bǎiyuè came to court;
when the Chancellor led troops,
the Three Rivers were swept up.
Her great-great-grandfather Zài
served as Chief Clerk to Liú Yìzhēn,
remaining to guard Guānzhōng.
After perishing under Hèlián,
he subsequently served Wèi.
On his deathbed,
he admonished his descendants:
"To delight in the native airs
is not to forget one's roots.
Remembering your ancestors,
do not betray this heart."
Her grandfather Zhèng
was General of Agile Cavalry, Commandant with Equal Honor to the Three Excellencies, and Governor of Héngzhōu.
Her father Tōng
was Pillar of State General, Grand Marshal, and Duke Wén'ān.
Assisting in statecraft,
participating in planning the abdication,
his fame surpassed Guǎngwǔ,
his merit outweighed Chángpíng.
The lady contained the splendor of the seven virtues,
her four stars shone in conjunction,
reverent and loving by heavenly nature,
her speech and demeanor followed ritual codes.
On the ninth day of the ninth month ascending heights,
she composed inscriptions on autumn chrysanthemums;
at the beginning of the three primordial festivals,
she sometimes praised spring pepper.
At the age of fourteen,
she was married into the household of the Duke of Qiáo.
In harmony with her zither and se,
she grew more respectful and frugal in heart;
pruning its branches,
she truly upheld the virtue of diligence and concern.
The brocade from ascending heights in Yè,
she washed herself in the river waves;
at the ferry where mulberries were gathered in Píngyáng,
she personally labored in the silkworm month.
In the first year of the Tiānhé era,
she was appointed Lady of Qiáo.
The wife of the Lord of Dōngwǔ Pavilion,
was already said to have rank;
the wife of the Marquis of Nánchéng,
was also heard to have received a fief.
His Highness the Pillar of State, with his illustrious reputation shining separately,
added to the towering earth of Zēngchéng,
raised banners on the thorny road,
inquired into governance in Qiōngdū.
At the stream of Báiláng,
the way was arduous as the slope of Huángniú;
at Lìzhī Mountain,
the land perilous as the state of Pútáo.
The lady parted from her relatives,
the passes and rivers presented repeated obstacles.
A single song of the barbarians
could not dispel her sorrow;
three cries of the gibbons,
made her robes endlessly damp.
Thus an illness sent by heaven
became a deep-seated affliction.
Jade nectar was hard to obtain,
golden ointment truly distant.
On the ninth day of the seventh month in the first year of the Jiàndé era,
she passed away at her private residence in Chéngdū,
at the age of twenty-one.
In the same year, on the twenty-second day of the eleventh month, she was returned for burial at the northern plain of Cháng'ān.
By decree she was posthumously granted the title Lady of Qiáo,
in accordance with ritual.
The lady served her superiors with utmost loyalty,
attended her parents with exhaustive filial piety,
advanced the worthy in proper order,
and treated those below with kindness.
When about to be covered by the dark spring,
she spoke as midnight approached.
Relatives both internal and external
all deeply felt the grief of the chaste woman;
the few small stars
truly held the attachment of the household manager.
His Highness grieved under the autumn moon,
hid his tears by the tall pines.
Zhōu Jìzhí's remaining letter
further deepened the obscurity;
Pān Ānrén's literary grace
only added to the sorrowful lament.
How could one speak of the woman of Xīhé,
alone seeing the silver terrace;
or the woman of Dōnghǎi,
first encountering the golden gate?
The inscription says:
The banners turned back at Shānlíng,
The halberds were laid to rest at Jiāoshān.
The golden essence held the peaks,
The Chāng Pavilion soared over the waves.
To the west, ministers and chancellors traveled,
To the east, mountains and rivers were cleft.
The crown and robes of Huátíng,
The strings and songs of Gǔshuǐ.
The clan migrated from the region of Zhèn,
Following official posts to the northern borders of Yān.
The frontier entered Fēihú,
The pass linked to Míngyàn.
Strategies were devised upon ascending the heights,
Merits were achieved overlooking the streams.
The precious tripod left its inscription,
The carved halberd retained its praise.
Corresponding to the charts, virtuous and fair,
Upholding rites, she spoke of returning.
The fish-adorned carriage leaned on its crossbar,
The marsh pheasant in patterned attire.
The bright moon shone upon the mirror,
The immortal stone propped the loom.
Drifting clouds rose gently,
Whirling snowflakes flew lightly.
To the north, the imperial son descended,
To the south, the governor of Shǔ waved his banner.
When Ruòshuǐ was opened,
Língshān had already been carved.
Apes cried in the Moon Gorge,
River deities battled like bulls.
The starry loom turned northward,
The sun’s reins circled westward,
Yángquán’s breath lay dormant,
Yīnlǜ’s ashes sank deep.
The crane left the market of Wú,
The phoenix departed from the terrace of Qín.
Divine light flickered and merged,
Lamp shadows lingered and wavered.
The double streams returned for burial,
A hundred carriages turned back their banners.
The young maiden left her position,
The noble lady departed the city.
Curtained halls were set in the wilds,
Tented palaces camped in the outskirts.
Strange events among mountains and rivers,
The wind and moon, devoid of sentiment.
Withered and fallen, the hills and mounds,
Desolate and barren, the sealed domain.
Every tree echoed with autumn sounds,
Every mountain wore a cold hue.
Grass short, leveling the ground,
Pines tall, turning ever straighter.
The festival tomb stood firm,
The garden mausoleum planted forever.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 963.
Epitaph for Lady Hédòulíng, Wife of the Duke of Zhào of the Zhōu Dynasty
Epitaph for Lady Hédòulíng, Wife of the Duke of Zhào of the Zhōu Dynasty
The lady’s given name was Hánshēng,
Originally surnamed Dòu,
A native of Pínglíng in Fúfēng.
At the court of Wèi,
No marquis could rival her in propriety;
Ānfēng presented the charts,
And all meritorious officials yielded the highest seat to her.
The biographies of imperial relatives,
Already recorded in the annals of Jiànwǔ;
The ancient tripod of Zhòngshān,
Sometimes marked the tribute of the Chányú.
Her grandfather, Lüè,
Junior Guardian, Duke of Jiànchāng Commandery.
Her father, Chì,
Pillar of State, Grand General, Grand Minister of Rites, Duke of Dèng.
At the great oath of Mèngjīn,
He was ever among the ministers of shared virtue;
At the breach of covenant in Xiányáng,
He aided the lord who led the vanguard.
Both attained positions among the six ministries,
And their merits were counted among the eight handles of power.
The lady bore markings on her palm,
And her image corresponded to the charts,
Her glory and brilliance evident from youth,
Her virtue and splendor flourishing early.
Reverent and respectful in propriety,
She received instruction in the ducal palace;
Her speech and demeanor guided by virtue,
She was renowned among the instructresses.
When she advanced the worthy gentleman,
She became the mistress within Hándān,
Lute and zither in the hall,
Carriages and robes her attire.
Long devoted to chastity,
She was not without inscriptions of autumn chrysanthemums;
At the beginning of the year,
There were odes to pepper flowers.
How could it be limited to Zhuāng Jī covering her mouth,
Or the Chancellor of Chǔ knowing shame;
Dìng Jiāng inquiring of omens,
And the armies of Qí not entering?
In the second year of Wǔchéng,
She was enfeoffed as Lady of the Duke of Zhào.
The King of Hàn, hearing of a woman who upheld righteousness,
Enfeoffed her with Yánxiāng;
The Marquis of Qí, seeing a wife who observed propriety,
Granted her Shíliù.
Different eras, shared glory,
With no cause for shame in virtue.
His Highness the Pillar of State, dwelling on a branch of the Ruòmù tree,
A separate stream of the celestial river,
Raised banners at Yùlěi,
Drove his carriage through Tónglíng,
Reaching south to the people facing the sun,
Extending east to the land without thunder.
The lady assisted in governance at Yuèxiá,
And praised virtue at Yúnmén.
Brocades washed in river waves,
Returned to the weaving chambers;
Mountains brightened by stone mirrors,
Faced directly the dressing tower.
Then, as the jade pitch-pipes shifted frequently,
The golden incense burner remained unchanged.
Four liǎng of foreign incense,
Lamented the rarity of envoys from the Western Regions;
A single stalk of divine herb,
Regretted the severed path to the jade fields.
On the twenty-second day of the fourth month of the fifth year of Tiānhé,
She passed away in Jǐnchéng of Chéngdū,
At the age of twenty.
Sūn Zǐjīng’s grief for the departed,
Stirred resentment with the autumn wind;
Pān Ānrén’s mourning for his lost wife,
Deepened sorrow with the long mat.
How much more, with the eternal parting at the immortal terrace,
No more sound of flutes;
The instructress long gone,
Only the lute melody remains.
In the seventh year, on a day in the second month,
She was returned for burial at Hóngdú Plain in Cháng’ān.
By decree, she was posthumously honored as Lady of Zhào,
In accordance with propriety.
Clouds and rain come and go,
Already lingering with the Queen of Chǔ;
Time and light part and meet,
Truly causing melancholy for the Prince of Chén.
The inscription reads:
Héxī stands steep as the Dipper,
Guānjīn rises alone.
Zhāngwǔ, the worthy minister,
Ānfēng, the worthy official.
Wooden towers a thousand rèn high,
Golden mountains ten thousand li afar.
Continuing blessings like Aunt Xíng,
Laying foundations like Lady Sòng.
Bestowing the sash north of Zhào,
Serving the mother south of Qín.
Rites of headdress and ribbons,
Side horses of the ceremonial carriage.
Righteousness surpassing “Jiāngsì,”
Benevolence flowing through “Gétán.”
Jade basket welcoming swallows,
Golden cage aiding silkworms.
Respect and love pure and deep,
Dignified, virtuous, and well-spoken.
Bringing glory to the state’s history,
Showing no trace of joy or anger.
Humbly presenting the tray outside,
Halting the loom to instruct below.
Fragrant as the orchid,
Years fleeting as the hibiscus.
Wind and rain disperse,
Divine spirits part forever.
The widow returns to the stars,
Cháng’é goes back to the moon.
Evening offerings at the left pillar,
Morning departure from the high hall.
Vainly raising the surging waves,
No more whirling snow.
Low and level is called marshland,
High and level is called plain.
To the west lies Huǒjǐng,
To the north, one gazes toward Sàimén.
Still hangs the pheasant-feather robe,
Still rides the fish-adorned carriage.
The plain vanishes suddenly,
What words has the Way of Heaven?
Mountains encircle the earthly market,
Roads vanish at Téngchéng.
Pines mourn, cranes depart,
Grass runs wild, fireflies emerge.
New clouds rise apart,
The old moon shines alone.
The tomb of the virtuous, an eternal model,
The mound of chastity, ever steadfast.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 963.
Epitaph for Lady Zhèng, Wife of the Duke of Ānchāng of the Zhōu Dynasty
The lady, née Mǒu,
was a native of Yángwǔ in Yíngyáng.
King Xuān of Zhōu's maternal younger brother
was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Zhèng;
through successive generations from Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng,
they served as ministers at the Zhōu court.
Taking the state as their clan name,
this began from that time.
Her grandfather, Qióng,
was Grand Minister of Ceremonies and the Reverent Marquis.
Her father, Mù,
was Minister of Works and the Chaste Duke.
Composing poems in the Western Capital,
he attended the Bǎiliáng Terrace banquet as Grand Minister of Ceremonies;
prophesying in the Eastern Capital,
he served as the Military Guard official as Minister of Works.
Their lineage connected to the imperial genealogy,
already firm as a great rock;
their gate was known for its pervasive virtue,
never neglecting the scholarly tradition.
The lady observed ritual propriety within the women's quarters,
dignified, upright, virtuous, and gentle.
Lush and abundant as the plantain,
thick and flourishing as the vine.
When she became the spouse of a gentleman,
serving her parents-in-law,
with softened voice and cheerful tone,
bearing towels and holding brooms,
she treated relatives only according to ritual,
harmonizing the inner chambers.
In the second year of the Bǎodìng era,
she was enfeoffed as the Lady of Yíngyáng Commandery.
Her rank rose according to kinship,
her status derived from her husband's position.
Was she not like the righteous woman
whose fief was Yánxiāng;
or the wife who observed ritual,
enfeoffed at Shíjiào?
While the Grand General guarded the Two Rivers,
the lady heard gibbons in the Three Gorges.
The perils of the bright moon at Língguān Pass,
the hardships of the Shǔ road in autumn wind,
were veiled by jade-like blossoms,
preceded by spring dew.
On the twentieth day of the fifth month in the eighteenth year of the Tiānhé era,
she passed away in Chéngdū,
at the age of thirty-six.
By imperial decree, she was posthumously honored as the Lady of the State of Ānchāng,
according to ritual.
On the sixteenth day of the eleventh month of that same year, she was returned for burial at Báiqǐ Plain in Xiányáng.
Thus causing the mountains to turn back the soil,
first enclosing the tomb of the chaste woman;
as the sun sets at Yúyuān,
truly covering the grave of the worthy lady.
Alas, sorrowful indeed!
Therefore, the inscription reads:
The Heavenly River founded the state,
dividing the domains and establishing governance.
The land had ten cities,
its people held the nine ranks of honor.
The fief of old,
now becomes the surname.
Her discernment and conduct passed on tradition,
her participation in the carriage left blessings.
The Three Stars were at the door,
a hundred carriages announced her return.
Reverently devoted to domestic affairs,
her splendor shone in the inner chambers.
Serving her mother-in-law with ablutions,
instructing her sons, pausing her loom.
In mulberry gardens, silkworms spun;
in brocade chambers, phoenixes flew.
Pendants regulated her steps,
waterweed and fire adorned her robes.
The Bā River flows with muffled sobs,
gibbon cries are severed.
The moon sets, pearls grieve;
spring withers, cassia breaks.
The Zhào zither is forever silent,
the Qín flute eternally parted.
The chaste lady's path is sealed,
the faithful woman's tomb is mounded.
By the Luò's banks, no moon;
on the Jīng Terrace, clouds are lost.
Birds mourn, sorrowful to hear;
pine sounds, grievous to listen.
For a thousand years, since ancient times,
for a hundred generations, her fragrance remains.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 963.
〈Epitaph for Lady Dòu, Wife of the Great General and Duke of Lǒngdōng Commandery, Hóumòchén of the Northern Zhōu〉
The lady, née Mǒu,
was a native of Pínglíng in Fúfēng.
When Zhāngwǔ founded the state,
his fame ranked above the imperial relatives;
when Ānfēng entered the court,
his position stood above the meritorious officials.
Her grandfather, at the beginning of the Xiàochāng era,
governed Huáiyáng;
her father, at the start of the Zhèngguāng era,
administered the region of Hǎidài.
The lady was born into a family of ritual and righteousness,
rooted in the virtue of admonition and warning,
reverent and respectful, observing ritual,
virtuous and gentle, conforming to propriety.
When the hundred carriages announced her return,
and the Three Stars were at the door,
she began her duties with ablutions and admonitions,
following the principles of branches and twigs.
With a son in government service,
she still harbored no mind for ease and pleasure;
with a husband on campaign,
she herself recognized the omen of the mountains and mounds.
In the sixteenth year of the Dàtǒng era,
she was enfeoffed as the Lady of Yǒng'ān Commandery.
A wife is honored through her husband,
a mother esteemed through her son;
court honors and family celebrations,
she possessed both.
In the second year of the Bǎodìng era,
she was re-enfeoffed as the Lady of the State of Lǒng.
Carriages, robes, ritual protocols,
ceremonial gowns and regulations,
like the fine bream of the river,
sufficient to glorify the vermilion records.
Then, as wind and frost reached her,
the ash in the pitch-pipes was encroached upon,
what words for one who did good?
Until her great decline.
On the seventh day of the fourth month in the sixth year of the Tiānhé era, she passed away,
at the age of sixty-six.
On the tenth day of the tenth month of that same year, she was moved for burial at Dù Plain in Wànnián County, Xiányáng.
The undulating forms of the mountains
already matched the auspiciousness of the white crane;
the terrain's winds and mists
conformed to the energy of the green crow.
The inscription reads:
A hereditary clan of Guānjīn,
a prominent family of Pínglíng.
Four marquises entered official service,
three lords served in government.
The white wolf achieved merit,
the red snake inherited blessings.
Vast indeed was the Hàn,
first hearing of her virtuous goodness.
The gentleman at court's forefront,
the worthy talent managing the household.
Hairpins and earrings according to ritual,
carriages and canopies by command.
Yielding fruit cultivated integrity,
declining pearls halted contention.
A hundred years pass swiftly,
a thousand pieces of gold cannot be relied upon.
The chamber bids farewell to the worthy husband,
the courtyard takes leave of the noble son.
The returning saddle halts the dew,
gathering artemisia, the sacrifices cease.
The room leaves silkworms to sleep,
garments retain the painted pheasant.
Clouds descend upon the low marsh,
the sun veils the high dusk.
Empty curtains in the old lodge,
void canopies over the new mound.
Mountains curve around the broad willows,
the road vanishes into deep pines.
How many changes for the wandering soul?
Where does the great person go?
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 963.
〈Epitaph for Lady Wūshílán, Wife of the Duke of Guànjūn of the Northern Zhōu〉
The lady, née Mǒu,
was a native of Lèlíng.
She was a descendant of Bāo, Duke of Lèlíng and Minister over the Masses of the Jìn.
His descendants received the fief,
and thus made their home there.
In the old city of Fúfēng,
the iron market still remains;
at the former estate in Hénán,
the Golden Valley yet endures.
Some resided at the Yān frontier,
still serving in Dài Commandery.
Her grandfather, Xíng,
was Governor of Dài Commandery.
Her father was Minister of Works of the Wèi and Duke of Lánlíng Commandery.
The Minister of Works assisted the founding,
serving as Junior Tutor of the Wèi court;
supporting the Zhōu house in doubt,
both were great clans,
and both were granted surnames.
A match between Qín and Jìn,
this is called an interlinked family.
At the age of seventeen, the lady
married into the Yǔwén family.
Virtuous, graceful, dignified, and proper,
she embodied inner refinement and steadfast purity.
Her conduct in washing and serving was exemplary,
and she maintained perfect order within the women's quarters.
In a certain year,
she was appointed Lady of Jīnxiāng Commandery.
In a certain year,
she was reassigned as Lady of the Champion State.
Possessing the Four Virtues of a noble lady,
she brought harmony to her household;
though capable of handling the three major domestic affairs,
she modestly declined involvement in administrative matters.
In the fourth month of the fifth year of the Bǎodìng era, she fell ill and passed away,
at the age of forty-four.
In a certain month and day of that same year, she was returned for burial at a certain plain in Jīngzhào.
The world is but mist and smoke;
mountains and rivers are remote and fleeting.
Should green wheat grow upon the burial mound,
it may mark the grave of a chaste lady;
if white poplars stand at the ridge's head,
they might signify the tomb of a worthy consort.
Thus, the inscription reads:
The Three Stars adorn the heavens,
the Five Peaks stabilize the earth.
Ritual has its proper order,
and humans occupy their rightful places.
Yān and Zhào abound in marvels,
their mountains and rivers imbued with heroic spirit.
From this arose this virtuous lady,
endowed with such inner refinement.
Jade shone in the courtyard's light,
orchids bloomed, filling the chamber with fragrance.
Like the Xíng aunt in her plain robe,
or the Sòng maiden with river bream.
A hundred carriages heralded her marriage procession,
the Nine Rituals accompanied her betrothal.
Her pheasant-patterned robe of seven colors,
her carriage borne by a team of six—a rank of high nobility.
She left her parental home for the tripod-adorned chamber,
and aided governance within the locust-tree court.
Generations pass like flowing water,
human life becomes a great dream.
The tent is rolled at the mountain gate,
the lamp is moved to the spring-fed cave.
The golden jujube is held forever in the mouth,
the silver silkworm is sent off for eternity.
Incense fills the cypress outer coffin,
the path is closed by the pine-tree city.
The grieving phoenix laments its solitary shadow,
the male sword cries out alone.
Lingering notes of the Zhào zither,
plaintive strains of the Qín sheng.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, scroll 163.
〈Epitaph for Lady Zhèng, Wife of the Grand Tutor and Duke of Zhèng of the Zhōu Dynasty〉
The lady's given name was [a certain character],
a person from Yuǎn Village, Kāifēng County, Xíngyáng.
The seven sons composing poems
sufficed to honor guests;
the three ministers administering affairs
truly brought peace to the feudal lords.
When riding as attendant, she caused the Jìn queen to halt her carriage;
when coming to court, the Hàn sovereign recognized her slippers.
Her illustrious lineage, continuous as cicada wings,
is fully recorded in historical texts.
Her grandfather, Nà,
served as Assistant Administrator of Qín Prefecture.
Her father, Màobó,
was General of the Pacifying Army, Governor of Liáng Prefecture, and Marquis of Bóyáng County.
The lady's virtue and goodness were renowned from an early age;
like orchids and irises, she flourished uniquely.
Possessing both beauty and virtue,
she was betrothed and married.
Fraternal and truly warm and respectful,
reverent and mindful in her serving duties.
The Grand Tutor assisted in harmonizing the Zhōu court,
a crucial pillar of support;
the lady aided her lord,
diligently managing her responsibilities.
Lute and zither were in harmony,
branches and twigs were not cut—domestic peace prevailed.
Thus she was able to serve the state,
and fulfill filial piety and respect.
On a certain year, month, and day,
she was enfeoffed as Lady of the Zhèng State.
Once adorned with the pheasant-patterned robe,
she devoted herself to the ceremonial cap-strings.
Though her husband possessed the nobility of Ān Shì,
she personally attended to washing clothes;
though her son held the尊status of Wén Bó,
she never forgot the loom and shuttle.
Internal and external affairs were peaceful,
and the women's quarters were properly ordered.
Though the physician's door had illness,
the prescribed remedies proved ineffective.
On the twentieth day of the third month in the third year of the Tiānhé era, she passed away,
and was buried at the Shí'ān Plain in Cháng'ān.
Her eldest son, [a certain person].
The brothers all heeded her kind instruction,
and revered her maternal example.
Deep grief as for frost and dew,
increased sorrow like cold springs.
The inscription reads:
Dwelling in virtue at Pǔtián,
holding office in the educational bureau.
Horses were stationed for arriving guests,
schools were opened to gather scholars.
Blessings filled the household,
worthy talents followed in succession.
Flowers of the cherry tree,
wings of the katydid.
The seven virtues of human relations,
the transforming influence of the Two Souths.
Gathering the plantain herb, lush and abundant,
thick and flourishing like the kudzu vine.
Her conduct and integrity rang like jade,
her hairpins and ornaments were added appropriately.
In the willow garden she grasped the shuttle,
at the mulberry ford she bathed the silkworms.
Spring and autumn pass swiftly,
decline and fall know no fixed time.
The family has lost a virtuous lady,
the state mourns a worthy consort.
The fragrant grave sees her off forever,
the dancing crane bids a long farewell.
Mountains are deep, the moon is dim,
the wind is urgent, the pines grieve.
After a thousand years, when it opens again,
it will verify the spirit turtle.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, scroll 963.
〈Epitaph for Lady Yuán, Wife of General of Agile Cavalry and Governor of Jīng Province Hèbá of the Later Wèi〉
"On the river's islet,"
we hear of the gentleman's virtuous match;
"I gather the fern,"
we see the lady's propriety.
Applied to influence customs,
human relations are thereby enriched.
The lady's given name was Ān,
courtesy name Dàluó,
a person from Luòyáng, Hénán.
Her grandfather, [a certain person],
was Prince Kāng of Jīngzhào.
Her father, Zhāo,
was General of Agile Cavalry, Pillar of State with Honors Equal to the Three Excellencies, Supervisor of the Imperial Secretariat, Governor of Sī Province, and Prince of Rǔyáng Commandery.
The calyx and sepals of a grand design,
the foundation and steps of hegemonic achievements.
From a family of dukes and ministers,
generations of generals and chancellors who safeguarded the state and the family.
The lady was able to cultivate proper conduct,
never contemplating violation of ritual.
Reverent, frugal, and economical,
her concern lay in advancing the worthy.
In the fifth year of the Dàtǒng era,
she was enfeoffed as Princess of Lè'ān.
She married into the Hèbá family,
at the age of thirteen.
Thoughtful in service, diligent and concerned,
she transformed into a model of wifely virtue.
The red-tube brush recorded her radiance,
the cherry tree flourished early.
And when the songs of praise found their home,
the pheasant robe's rank was lowered,
yet in assisting her lord,
she remained content within her chamber.
In the first year of the Zhōu Tiānhé era,
she was then enfeoffed as Lady of Zhāngwǔ Commandery.
Frost and dew do not linger,
wind and mist drift fleetingly.
Stricken by illness for several weeks,
she suddenly departed her residence.
On the twenty-sixth day of the second month in the fourth year of the Zhōu Tiānhé era, she passed away in Wànnián Ward, Cháng'ān,
at the age of fifty-two.
By imperial decree, she was posthumously granted the title Lady of Dùnqiū State,
in accordance with ritual.
On the twentieth day of the third month of that same year, she was returned for burial at the Shí'ān Plain in Xiányáng.
Unlike those who ride a phoenix,
she has suddenly departed forever;
though not a dancing crane,
she is now shut behind the spring gate.
Wishing to record this fine burial ground,
the inscription is thus composed:
How distant, those grand strategies;
How remote, those hegemon’s tracks.
The nine domains silently shifted,
The three rivers’ flow ceased within.
Ministers and chancellors rode side by side,
Worthy talents danced to their end.
Jade-like, virtuous and fair,
She donned the sash and tied the bridal knot.
Compared to the flowering pear,
Or likened to the katydid’s brood.
Perfect in wifely virtue,
She was also praised as a motherly model.
The flowing waters rush on,
The perilous road stretches far.
No answer came when medicine was sought,
Elixirs steamed proved ineffective.
The Di robes lay empty,
The zither’s mechanism left untouched.
The city gate road turns,
The mournful dirge ends on the path.
Deep on the ridge, mist gathers,
High on the pines, winds assemble.
Spring orchids, autumn chrysanthemums,
Only the beginning, only the end.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 963.
Epitaph for Lady Luó, Wife of Chángsūn Xiá, Yánglín Bó and Grand Governor of Zhōu
Epitaph for Lady Luó, Wife of Chángsūn Xiá, Yánglín Bó and Grand Governor of Zhōu
The lady’s given name was Mǒu,
A person of Tàipíng County, Dàijùn, Héngzhōu.
Her grandfather was Mǒu.
Her father was Xié,
Great General of Zhōu and Duke of Nányáng Commandery.
The lady’s nature suited serving her parents,
Personally receiving instruction and admonition,
Educated within the clan,
She was well-versed in the *Book of Songs* and *Book of Rites*.
When it came time for her marriage,
She was reverent and respectful as in serving,
Devout in offering duckweed and algae,
Diligent in managing caps and ribbons,
Harmonious in her domestic duties,
Peaceful within the women’s quarters.
Her years did not contend,
Frost and dew encroached first,
No cup of longevity remained,
Thus lacking the pillow of eternal life.
In the fourth year of Tiānhé of Zhōu, on the eighth day of the second month, she passed away in Hónggù Township of Cháng’ān,
At the age of twenty-three.
On a certain day of a certain month in that year,
She was buried in Shòu Village of Wànnián County.
The mountain is not in the state of Sòng,
Yet becomes the tomb of a chaste woman;
The land differs from Jīngtái,
Yet holds the grave of a virtuous consort.
The inscription reads:
Bì and Láng established the state,
Língwǔ opened the capital.
The land connects to Tiānzhù,
The mountain overlooks Bǎofú.
People embody righteous fervor,
Generations display heroic plans.
The kudzu spreads lushly,
The flowering pear blooms early.
Secure in her virtuous character,
She thus followed the mandate of marriage.
The four teachings widely proclaimed,
The three stars correctly aligned.
Frost withers the cassia garden,
Wind scatters the orchid fields.
The three obediences lack her nature,
The five blessings grieve her years.
Return and peace forever severed,
Words of farewell long abandoned.
Desolate the outskirts and wilds,
Winding the lowlands and plains.
Wind bleak, clouds sorrowful,
Pines mournful, dew weeping.
Bright moon vainly sighs,
How can wounded spirit be reached!
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 963.
Epitaph for Lady Yùchí, Wife of Tuòbá Jìng, Duke of Sōngzī and Commandant Equaling the Three Excellencies of Zhōu
Epitaph for Lady Yùchí, Wife of Tuòbá Jìng, Duke of Sōngzī and Commandant Equaling the Three Excellencies of Zhōu
The lady’s given name was Mǒu,
A person of Luòyáng, Hénán.
Her grandfather was Mǒu.
Her father was Grand Preceptor and Pillar of State Duke.
When the Wèi court fell into chaos,
Plans and order were disrupted,
The Zhōu dynasty established its state,
Assisting in the abdication.
Consulting the imperial genealogy charts,
There were internal and external kinships;
Dividing the mountains and rivers,
They still became states of uncle and nephew.
The lady’s appearance and demeanor were dignified and proper,
Her bearing and model virtuous and graceful.
The six principles reveal virtue,
The “South Wind” contains poems of a lady;
The eight trigrams take form,
The east holds the position of the youngest daughter.
Tutors taught speech,
The ducal palace instructed in duties,
Admonishing while washing, spinning thread and floss,
Wearing sachets with angelica and orchids.
At the age of twelve,
She married Commandant Equaling the Three Excellencies Tuòbá Jìng.
Wearing her pheasant-feather robes,
She fulfilled the rites of a clan wife;
Riding in her fish-scale carriage,
She followed the rituals of ranked states.
Plums marked thrice ripened,
Not missing their season;
Peach blossoms ninefold splendid,
Able to cultivate governance.
In a certain month of a certain year,
She was enfeoffed as Lady of Huíluò County.
Her mother,
Princess Jīnmíng,
Eldest daughter of Emperor Wén of Wèi.
In spring, the imperial daughter gathered mulberry leaves,
In autumn, the royal princess built lodges.
The lady entered and left the ruler’s household,
Roamed among the relatives’ estates,
The gardens of Zhuólóng,
The palaces of Chángmén.
Then, rich soil breeds fine ailments,
Luxuriant growth harms years,
A stubborn illness confined her to bed curtains,
Feverish separation through cold and heat.
The arts of three lifetimes,
Could not match the physician’s gate;
The roots of a hundred herbs,
Were exhausted in vain for their medicinal properties.
She died on the seventh day of the fifth month in the third year of Jiàndé,
At the age of thirty.
In the past, a woman of Xīhé
Obtained calamus of nine nodes;
A woman of Dōnghǎi
Gained magic mushrooms from three mountains.
No way to encounter them again,
How sorrowful!
On the fifteenth day of the eleventh month of that year, she was buried in the Běilíng Plain of Jīngzhào.
Turtle and milfoil divination announced the date,
The mound opened for offerings,
To the west facing the temple of the Weaving Maid,
To the south gazing toward the tomb of the Xiāng consorts.
Alas, sorrowful!
Thus the inscription reads:
Her father called Imperial Preceptor,
Her mother called Royal Princess.
Carriages and robes not tied,
Jiāng and Hàn without thought.
Thus was born this virtuous lady,
Observing rites and devoted to poetry.
Her fame surpassed Sòngzǐ,
Her virtue flourished like Xíngyí.
Inheriting generations of abundant virtue,
Thinking of worthies, she could be recommended.
Wild geese presented at the gate,
Duckweed soaked filling the sacrificial vessel.
Serving the washing as in duty,
Moving the mat in proper order.
Spring ice for bathing silkworms,
Autumn loom holding the shuttle.
Imperial homeland, close kin,
Imperial city, close minister.
Zhuólóng relatives,
Píngyáng host.
Golden waves reflect the moon,
Jade trees face spring.
Nòngyù’s phoenix,
Chāngróng’s purple herb.
From this time a thousand years,
No one attains the Way.
Shùn blossoms glorious and bright,
How early they drift and fall.
Wèi River’s northern plain,
Pínglíng’s former garden.
Just reaching the valley mouth,
Already gazing toward the cold gate.
Alas, this place,
Gone, the returning soul.
The tenth month of early winter,
Tall pines for nine years.
Relatives and guests hide tears,
What words for such grief!
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 963.
Epitaph for Lady Lǐ, Wife of Chái Liè, Champion Bó, General of Swift Cavalry, Grand General Who Opens the Manor, Commandant Equaling the Three Excellencies
Epitaph for Lady Lǐ, Wife of Chái Liè, Champion Bó, General of Swift Cavalry, Grand General Who Opens the Manor, Commandant Equaling the Three Excellencies
The lady's given name was so-and-so,
and she was from Dídào in Lǒngxī.
In the Zhou dynasty, there was the Pillar Historian,
whom the Master likened to a dragon;
in the Han dynasty, there was a general,
through whom Wǎnchéng offered horses in tribute.
Again, there was one who presented a memorial after traveling west,
and still became the prime minister of the state of Qín;
and one who sought counsel facing east,
who was precisely the teacher of the King of Hán.
Her father, Yí,
was Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Grand General, Governor of the Northern and Southern Huá Provinces, and Duke of Shùnyáng Commandery.
He was the eldest maternal uncle of Emperor Wǔ of Wèi.
Lord Rǎng of Wèi, Rǎn,
resided in the palaces of Xiányáng;
the Prince of Qūyáng, Gēn,
borrowed the Hall of Brilliant Light.
Speaking of their noble relatives,
they are somewhat comparable;
but discussing their humility in retirement,
they are much ashamed in virtue.
The lady was intelligent and quick-witted from childhood,
and her virtuous nature was known early.
The red-tube brush recorded her beauty,
and her worthy talent was praised.
Playing with paper and brush,
she feared to disappoint her elder brothers' expectations;
cutting her hair in childhood,
she was careful not to grieve her grandmother's heart.
At the age of eleven,
she married Grand General of Agile Cavalry, Pillar of State, Chái Liè.
Liè, as a high general, promulgated the calendar,
and received appointments from the central ministry.
Loyal and diligent in military and state affairs,
he managed numerous responsibilities with great scale.
The lady assisted her husband,
her words and demeanor providing support and counsel,
adding luster to the Three Stars,
and reverently illuminating the Four Virtues.
Presenting towels and pouring water for washing,
she was respectful in serving her mother-in-law;
cutting the loom's threads and halting the shuttle,
she never forgot to instruct her sons.
In the second year of the Bǎodìng era,
she was enfeoffed as Lady of Dàxià County.
Honored through her husband,
and also elevated through her sons,
she was then transferred to Shùnyáng,
and her title changed to Commandery Lady.
The lady's fief,
sometimes took the name of her hometown;
the title of lesser lord,
often followed her husband's rank.
With the ceremonial edicts bestowing honor,
it was truly a glorious favor.
She originally suffered from a wind-qi illness,
which worsened over the years,
and she often lay resting on her pillow.
The flying turtle powder,
sent to treat the illness, showed no effect;
the painted dragon talisman,
meant to prolong life, proved ineffective.
On a day in the third month of the fourth year of the current Jiàndé era, she passed away in her residence,
at the age of forty-nine.
In the eighth month of the same year, she was buried at Hóngdú Plain in Cháng'ān.
The divine light flickers,
still lingering by the riverbank;
the clouds drift and linger,
as if returning beneath the tower.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Thus, the inscription reads:
Presenting memorials to the Qín minister,
achieving merit as a Hàn general.
The Lǒng waters divide and flow,
gazing afar toward Qínchuān.
Autumn land, customs of bravery,
metal element, land of strength.
In the army of Guǎngwǔ,
on the river of Ānpíng.
A wife is an equal,
marriage is called returning.
Three stars shine at night,
a hundred carriages fly at dawn.
Ceremonial robes have their rules,
demeanor and rites without transgression.
Equal in rank at court,
sharing robes of noble attire.
Sons uphold the mother's model,
husband hears of household governance.
Seven clans receive harmony,
nine chambers share celebration.
Tidy and respectful,
warm in winter and cool in summer, filial and reverent.
Shuttles held in autumn harvest,
silkworms follow spring's decree.
Years not yet fallen,
lightning's shadow passes first.
Vainly consuming the sun's breath,
emptily drinking the Milky Way.
Stars fade at the Jade Well,
the moon abandons golden waves.
Sunset at Yúyuān,
the mournful song of "Xièlù."
Lonely and empty offerings,
desolate and barren semblance.
Dark mound sealed by turtle,
deep springs knotted by ants.
Autumn colors bleak and mournful,
pine sounds severed and cut off.
A hundred years, how brief,
ending in this parting.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 963.
Epitaph for Lady Ěrzhū, Wife of the Duke of Péngchéng
Epitaph for Lady Ěrzhū, Wife of the Duke of Péngchéng
Lady Ěrzhū
was from Luòyáng in Hénán.
As for the Yīn Mountains, inside and out,
they align with the mechanism of the Northern Dipper;
the vast sea stretches boundlessly,
directly facing the constellations of Bì and Mǎo in the four streets.
The four seasons bear fire,
the Torch Dragon illuminates the light of the earth;
in the sixth month, riding the wind,
the great Peng spreads its sky-covering wings.
Thus, they came to possess the capital's counties,
and eventually ruled the central lands.
Chariots, writing, rites, and music—
the adaptations of the Three Kings are known;
generals, ministers, dukes, and marquises—
the mountains and rivers of a hundred generations remain unbroken.
Her grandfather, Chǎng,

served as Pillar of State of the Suí, Grand Master of the Golden and Purple, Governor-General of the Seven Provinces of Qí, Tóng, Jīn, Shēn, Xìn, Lín, and Xú, Minister of War, and Duke of Jīnchéng Commandery.
In heaven, he ranked among the stars of the Minister;
on earth, he was marked by the cold of the Grand Master.
Rising from a journey of ten thousand *li*,
he knew the great merit of Lǚ Dài;
commanding a region alone,
he understood the heavy trust of Liú Hóng.
Her father, Xiūzuì,
served as Left Thousand Oxen Guard, Grand Master for Court Service, and Marshal of the Prince of Qí's Mansion in the Suí,
and inherited the title of Duke of Jīnchéng.
The Grand Master spoke of achievements,
and the feudal lords granted lands.
The Huái immortal brought rain,
still climbing the mountain of cassia trees;
the Chǔ guest facing the wind,
entered further into the waters of lotus flowers.
The lady possessed the chaste aura of the Jade Terrace,
and the immortal essence of the Golden River.
Like the daughter of Cài Zhōngláng,
she early understood the beauty of colored silk;
like the inner chambers of Xiè Tàifù,
she first displayed elegant principles.
The Duke of Péngchéng traced his origins to the Earl of Yīn,
and inherited the legacy of the Hán minister.
The aura of mountains and rivers
revealed the white tiger to Gāoyáo;
the auspicious signs of celestial phenomena
brought down the azure dragon to Mànqiàn.
The three stars shone at night,
awaiting the time of the calling geese;
the seventh day of autumn,
sitting to present the omen of the flying phoenix.
The lady, just eighteen years old,
then married into our family.
Gazing south toward Wū Mountain,
she encountered the evening rain with Yáojī;
looking west toward Huà Mountain,
she descended as a bright star with the Jade Maiden.
Her actions matched the *Book of Songs* and *Rites*,
her words formed rules and standards.
Morning and evening, she showed reverence,
serving to the utmost in moving heaven;
with duckweed and algae, she upheld sincerity,
fulfilling her duty in managing the household.
The maiden's washing stone
echoed the bright moon and longed for the autumn wind;
the weaving woman's loom
listened to the cold crickets urging the weft.
She followed the teachings of Cáo Dàjiā,
and upheld the chaste integrity of Sòng Bójī.
Moreover, her heart rested in the Eight Awakenings,
her mind comprehended the Three Emptinesses,
wielding the blade of wisdom in the sandalwood grove,
sailing the immortal boat on the sea of Dharma.
Her subtle spirit shone alone,
silent in form and image, without exertion;
emptiness and existence both forgotten,
she discarded traps and snares, unused.
Man lives between heaven and earth,
his lifespan is not like metal or stone.
Stealing the elixir at the Silver Terrace,
she longed to fly to the moon—but in what year?
Burning incense in the golden hall,
she yearned for the soul’s return, yet no day came.
She passed away on such-and-such date in the private residence at Píngkāng Lane.
On the twentieth day of the tenth month in the third year of the Shàngyuán era,
she was jointly buried at Bìyuán south of the city,
in accordance with ritual.
By the side of Marquis Qí’s resting place,
before the steps of the Dù family,
facing King Wén’s Bìyuán,
the joint burial of Duke Zhōu was employed.
The reclining pines endure a thousand ages,
long free from the sorrow of the lone crane;
the patterned catalpa stands a hundred fathoms tall,
still seen where a pair of mandarin ducks alight.
The inscription reads:
Joint burial is not ancient,
yet preserved by Duke Zhōu.
Death and life span a thousand years,
coffins enclose twin souls.
The wilds are vast, the wind urgent,
the sky cold, the sun dim.
Mist veils the distant peaks,
fog obscures the remote village.
Recording the stele with yellow silk,
facing the tomb gate with green pines.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 964.
Epitaph for the Lady of the Eastern Peace Commandery, Madame Lǐ, Paternal Aunt
The lady’s surname was Lǐ,
from Dídào in Lǒngxī.
Since the time of the Martial and Illustrious King of Liáng,
three dukes in one family,
they became a prominent clan throughout the land,
as detailed in state histories and family records.
Her grandfather, Chōngyǐng,
was Grand General of the Later Zhōu, Prefect of Huá Province, and Duke of Liújiāng Commandery.
Her father, Xuánmíng,
was Grand Master of the Imperial Court with Ceremonial Rank, Prefect of three provinces—◇, Jì, and Sānzhōu—and Baron of Chéngjì County.
Serving across three reigns,
bearing tallies and bamboo tokens of authority,
in the regions of Qín, Lǒng, Hé, and Jì,
people to this day praise him.
All scholar-officials under heaven, whether acquainted or not,
none did not admire his demeanor.
The lady was pure and profound from birth,
reverent and respectful in childhood,
harmonious and amiable as she grew,
gentle and kind in maturity.
At the age of capping,
she first joined our family.
Holding broom and dustpan,
serving parents-in-law,
no discord arose from the words of sisters-in-law, concubines, or attendants;
within the women’s quarters,
all was harmonious.
Thus the clan praised her fine reputation,
and the village regarded it as a beautiful tale.
The Duke of Eastern Peace upheld a foundation of purity and integrity,
encountering an era of peace,
appointments and summons came in succession,
his fame reached the heavens.
By decree, he was appointed as a Secretary in the Imperial Secretariat,
promoted to Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and sent out as Prefect of four provinces: Dì, Cáo, Héng, and Cháng.
The lady assisted her lord,
diligently managing internal affairs.
At dawn, with hairpins arranged,
there was the solemnity of ruler and minister;
in washing and offering food,
there was the reverence of father and son;
in reporting returns and departures,
there was the principle of brothers;
in accepting assignments with earnest caution,
there was the trust of friends.
Such were her wifely virtues.
Serving in both central and provincial posts,
his fame grew ever greater.
Harmonizing like lute and zither,
rectifying the state and household—
the lady contributed greatly to this.
She once sighed and said:
“In ancient times, the inner consorts of ministers,
as ladies of the great sash and appointed women,
completed sacrificial garments for the altar and presented their achievements—
how could one not strive!
How could one not strive!”
Thus she wore laundered garments,
personally engaged in spinning and weaving.
Baskets, hampers, pots, and cauldrons—
these she labored to handle;
duckweed, southernwood, pondweed, and algae—
these she used to manifest her virtue.
If not one broadly learned, understanding ritual,
chaste, gentle, and obedient,
who could have achieved this!
When the duke begged to retire in old age,
withdrawing to his original station,
the lady was past sixty,
yet her sight and hearing remained undiminished.
Every year as spring commenced,
or at the winter solstice when days lengthen southward,
when the younger generations raised cups to offer longevity wishes,
often numbering tens or even a hundred,
she never failed to speak joyfully and guide kindly,
bestowing a warm countenance.
Earnestly and sincerely,
courteously and respectfully,
she had the manner of Mother Mèng,
the instruction of Jìng Jiāng.
In the first year of Yǒngchún, on the day after the last quarter of the eighth lunar month,
she fell ill and lingered gravely,
passing away at Wàngxiān Lane in Huàyīn,
at the age of eighty-one.
On the first day of the eleventh lunar month, bǐngchén,
she was moved and interred in the plains of Yǒngfēng Township,
following the former burial site.
The Duke of Eastern Peace, cherishing memories and mourning the departed,
was deeply pained in his heart.
Those near and far all gathered,
clan relatives assembled completely,
honored in life, mourned in death—
this describes it well.
On this day,
the Crown Prince was overseeing Cháng’ān,
and I, Jiǒng, unworthily serving as Senior Secretary of the Household Administration,
was unable to attend the funeral proceedings,
or accompany the spirit carriage,
but dare to offer the words of Lǐ Yóng,
hoping to match the elegy of Pān Yuè.
Alas, sorrowful indeed!
Thus the inscription reads:
Upon the lofty peak,
