floating clouds soar;
beyond Hángǔ Pass,
upright spirit soars.
Establishing merit against the northern Dí,
campaigning against the western Qiāng;
enfeoffed in Nánzhèng,
the household flourished in simplicity.
Oh, illustrious ancestors,
radiant as dragons;
governing provinces and commanding commanderies,
adorned with silver and gold.
Born was this virtuous nature,
endowed with auspicious signs;
as reed flowers bloom and chrysanthemums flourish,
orchids and pollia emit fragrance.
She possessed noble virtue,
like jade tablets and scepters;
seeking through divination,
the phoenix cried out.
The lord arrived,
jade pendants chiming;
household in harmony,
lute and zither strung.
Holding her hemp and flax,
she provided clothing;
presenting her offerings of food,
she clarified wine and broth.
Aunts and elder sisters-in-law,
harmonious, warm, and kind;
younger sisters-in-law and cousins,
joy unending.
When the duke went out to govern,
guarding the four directions;
the lady’s transforming influence,
virtue overflowing.
When the duke begged to retire,
returning to his mulberry fields;
within the women’s quarters,
the Way shone ever brighter.
On the first day of the first month,
the solstice sun long in the south;
descendants rejoicing,
each raising cups.
Like Duke Sòng, Mother Mèng, and Lady Jì of Lǔ—
not with anger but with teaching,
following ancient ways.
Just when expecting to rise high,
ascend the purple chamber;
who would have thought it unsuitable,
to be sealed in the dark hall.
Solemn are the pines and catalpas,
luxuriantly forming rows;
profound is the deep night,
never to see dawn again.
○From *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 964.
“The Seventh Night”
The Herdboy shines distantly upon the water,
The Weaving Maid ascends her carriage.
The starry bridge leads to the Han envoy,
The shuttle-stone pursues the immortal raft.
Gazing across the river, so near,
Yet after autumn, parting stretches far.
Sorrow turns tonight’s regret,
To bloom again next year’s flowers.
○From Yùtái Xīnyǒng, scroll 8.
From Gǔjīn Suìshí Záyǒng, scroll 25.
“Untitled”
Not troubled by the gentle breeze,
But helpless before the hanging snow.
Spirits rely solely on wine,
Yet deliberation demands poetry.
○Quoted in Quánfāng Bèizǔ‧Qiánjí, scroll 1, plum blossom section.
White clouds emerge from the cliff’s edge,
A clear moon ascends amid the waves.
○Chéngzhāi Shīhuà attributes this to Yǔ Xìn.
“Cuckoo”
“Cuckoo”
Text missing.
○From Cánghǎi Shīhuà.
“Untitled”
How many generations have collected these books?
Viewing their breadth spans a thousand years.
○Quoted in Shēng’ān Shīhuà, scroll 1, as a poem by Yǔ Zǐshān.
“Poem on Passing the Tomb of Prince Sī of Chén”
“Poem on Passing the Tomb of Prince Sī of Chén”
The prince alone grieved over life,
His mound retains a lasting fame.
Gathering firewood, the withered trees are gone,
Plowing the fields, the overgrown path is leveled.
Would he still seek pleasure at Yàn Pínglè?
Could he still hope to attend at Chéngmíng?
Now I come bearing the mandate,
And speak of matters long concluded.
Drifting far to the north of the river,
Whistling and howling, the gale roars.
Wild geese and clouds form ranks together.
Sand and tumbleweeds share alarm.
Withered mulberries fall by the ancient shrine.
Cold birds return to the lonely town.
At Lǒng River, a mournful reed-pipe melody.
At Yúyáng, the grim sound of drums.
Leaving home, a traveler from afar,
How can he not be wounded in heart?
○Wényuàn Yīnghuá, scroll 306, attributes this to Yǔ Jiānwú.
“Rhapsody on Sorrow”
Assault the fortress of sorrow, yet it never falls,
Storm the gate of sorrow, yet it never opens.
What can boil sorrow till it’s done?
What can burn sorrow till it kindles?
Shut the door to drive sorrow away,
Sorrow simply refuses to leave.
Hide deep to avoid sorrow,
Sorrow already knows your place.
○From Hǎilù Suìshì, scroll 9.
Also quoted in Mànsǒu Shīhuà with the rhyme for “place.”
Who would know that within one inch of heart,
There could be ten thousand hu of sorrow?
○From Hǎilù Suìshì, scroll 9.
“Untitled”
Wind sweeps over Yúnmèng,
Ice seals the shipyard.
○Mànsǒu Shīhuà quotes this as from a rhapsody by Yǔ Zǐshān.
Also in Tiáoxī Yúyīn Cónghuà‧Qiánjí, scroll 49.
“Rhapsody on Mandarin Ducks”
Once there was a pair of phoenixes,
That flew into the Wèi palace.
Now they are two trees,
Which one is Hán Féng?
○From Guānlín Shīhuà.
“Rhapsody on the Wandering Son”
Adorned with pearls and jade,
Hairpins inlaid with millet-grain.
○From Hǎilù Suìshì, scroll 5.
Shaking the cold frontier pass,
Vast and dim the evening sun.
○From Shī Gù Zhù Sū Shī, scroll 3.
Spring robes hastily cut by hand.

Indulging in reciting beacon-fire words,
Solely wielding the staff of discourse.

Mixed with duckweed, all floating together,
Amidst lotus blossoms, blooming outward.

Roaming the pole, the Dipper spreads,
Setting the mark, rosy clouds rise.

“Epitaph for Yǔwén Shèng”
Receiving the charts from Huáng Shí,
He surely had a mentor’s heart;
Learning swordsmanship from the white ape,
He thus attained the ambition of wind and clouds.
